articles.title: Lymph Node Structure And Function
articles.markdown: # Lymph Node Structure And Function # Introduction Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped organs strategically located along lymphatic vessels throughout the body.  These specialized structures serve as filtration stations and immune response hubs, playing a crucial role in the body's defense against infections and surveillance of abnormal cells.  This article provides an overview of lymph node anatomy and physiology, with particular emphasis on their structural organization and functional significance within the immune system. # Structure and function Lymph nodes have a complex internal architecture that facilitates their immune functions ((Figure 1)).  An outer capsule composed of dense connective tissue encases and protects the node.  Underneath are trabeculae, which are internal fibrous extensions that project inward from the capsule, providing structural support and creating compartments for cellular organization.  Each lymph node contains a hilum, a concave region allowing passage of arterial and venous blood and containing efferent lymphatic vessels. Each node is organized into 3 distinct but interconnected regions:  cortex, paracortex, and medulla. ## Cortex The cortex is the outer region of the lymph node.  It primarily houses **B lymphocytes** and is organized into distinct structures: - **Primary follicles**:  Consist of spherical collections of **quiescent** B cells awaiting antigen encounter. - **Secondary follicles**:  Develop after antigen stimulation and contain **germinal centers** where B cells proliferate and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells (eg, through isotype/immunoglobulin class switching) and memory B cells. - **Subcapsular sinus**:  Filters incoming lymph from afferent vessels and contains specialized macrophages that capture and present antigens to lymphocytes. ## Paracortex The paracortex is located between the cortex and medulla and primarily houses **T lymphocytes** and dendritic cells.  It contains high endothelial venules (HEVs) that allow lymphocytes to enter the node from the bloodstream (ie, via extravasation).  The paracortex enlarges when there is an extreme immune response (eg, due to infection), causing lymphadenopathy.  This region is underdeveloped in DiGeorge syndrome (ie, thymic hypoplasia affecting T-cell development). ## Medulla The medulla is the innermost region, containing the following: - **Medullary cords**:  House plasma cells and lymphocytes organized into rope-like structures. - **Medullary sinuses**:  Contain reticular cells (synthesize fibers that create a supportive meshwork) and macrophages, draining filtered lymph into efferent vessels and removing remaining pathogens. # The lymphatic system ## Lymphatic fluid Lymph, a clear fluid consisting of interstitial fluid, proteins, lipids, lymphocytes, and other immune cells that have been collected from tissues throughout the body, enters the node via multiple afferent lymphatic vessels.  Within the node, lymph is filtered as it passes through the cortex and medulla, removing pathogens and debris.  The cleansed lymph then exits the node via 1 or more efferent lymphatic vessels at the hilum ((Figure 2)).  From there, it continues through the lymphatic system before eventually draining into the venous circulation. ## Lymphatic vessels Lymphatic fluid flows through a complex network of lymphatic vessels.  Fluid from the right upper extremity, right side of the head, portions of the heart and lungs, and the right thorax drains into the **right lymphatic duct**.  The right lymphatic duct empties into the venous circulation at the junction of the right internal jugular vein and the right subclavian vein, forming the right brachiocephalic vein. In contrast, the **thoracic duct** drains lymphatic fluid from the remainder of the body, including both lower extremities, the abdomen, the left thorax, the left upper limb, and the left side of the head and neck.  The thoracic duct originates from the **cisterna chyli** in the abdomen and ascends through the thorax to empty into the venous circulation at the junction of the left internal jugular vein and the left subclavian vein, forming the left brachiocephalic vein.  The left and right brachiocephalic veins merge to form the superior vena cava, which then drains directly into the right atrium of the heart ((Figure 3)). ## Lymph node anatomy Lymph node anatomy for various structures is illustrated in the following figures:  head and neck ((Figure 4)), axillary region ((Figure 5)), lower extremities ((Figure 6)), large intestine ((Figure 7)), anorectal region ((Figure 8)), male genitalia ((Figure 9)), and female reproductive organs ((Figure 10)). # Clinical relevance Changes in lymph node characteristics provide crucial diagnostic information across multiple disciplines: - **Lymphadenopathy**:  Enlarged or tender lymph nodes frequently indicate localized infection, inflammation, or heightened immune activity in the drainage area.  The pattern of lymph node involvement may help clinicians identify the source of infection or disease.  Physical examination of lymph nodes (eg, evaluating size, consistency, tenderness, and mobility) offers valuable clinical insights.  Nodes that are hard, fixed, or painless raise concern for malignancy, whereas tender, mobile nodes typically suggest inflammatory processes. - **Regional patterns**:  The location of affected nodes corresponds to their drainage territories: - Cervical lymphadenopathy may indicate head and neck infections or malignancies. - Axillary nodes reflect upper extremity or breast pathology. - Inguinal lymphadenopathy suggests lower extremity or genitourinary conditions. - **Systemic disease markers**:  Persistent, generalized lymphadenopathy (affecting multiple nodal regions) may signal systemic conditions, including: - Autoimmune disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus). - Hematologic malignancies (lymphomas, leukemias). - Infectious diseases (HIV, tuberculosis, mononucleosis). - Metastatic cancer. - **Biopsy importance**:  Lymph node biopsy represents a critical diagnostic procedure when malignancy is suspected, providing definitive tissue diagnosis and staging information.  Fine-needle aspiration or excisional biopsy may be performed depending on the clinical context.  The **sentinel lymph node** (first node receiving drainage from a tumor site) is often evaluated to determine whether cancer has spread beyond the primary site, guiding treatment decisions, particularly in breast cancer and melanoma.  This minimizes unnecessary extensive lymph node dissection and associated complications. - Benign, reversible enlargment due to antigenic stimulus is called reactive hyperplasia.  It is classified as follicular hyperplasia (follicles increase in size and number), sinus hyperplasia (sinuses enlarge and fill with histiocytes), and diffuse hyperplasia (nodal architecture diffusely effaced by sheets of lymphocytes). - Evaluation for monoclonality of the lymphocyte population is important when lymphoma is suspected.  The clonality of a T-cell population is assessed by molecular methods (eg, PCR) that examine the rearrangement of T-cell receptor (TCR) genes.  If a single allele for the V region of the TCR predominates in a lymphocytic population, monoclonal proliferation is suspected.  Similarly, monoclonal rearrangement of the genes for immunoglobulin variable regions is suggestive of a B-cell lymphoma.  # Summary Lymph nodes are organized into cortical B-cell zones, paracortical T-cell regions, and medullary cords/sinuses.  They filter harmful substances, detect threats, and activate specific immune responses through coordinated lymphocyte interactions.  Their streamlined structure ensures efficient immune surveillance while helping to maintain fluid balance. ​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌

articles.title: Lipid Metabolism And Overview Of Dyslipidemias
articles.markdown:
# Lipid Metabolism And Overview Of Dyslipidemias # Introduction Dyslipidemias are disorders characterized by abnormal lipid levels in the blood, including cholesterol, triglycerides (TGs), and lipoproteins.  These abnormalities are often chronic and are frequently associated with complications, including atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).  Dyslipidemias most commonly arise from interactions between genetic and environmental factors but also can be inherited in a monogenic fashion (familial disorders).  This article discusses lipid classification and metabolism, etiology of dyslipidemias and complications including atherosclerosis, and clinical presentation and screening.  Management of dyslipidemia is presented in a separate article. # Main categories of lipids Lipids discussed in this article include cholesterol and TGs; because they are insoluble, lipids are carried within lipoproteins.  This section provides an overview of cholesterol, TGs, and lipoproteins (with their associated surface apolipoproteins). ## Cholesterol - **Synthesis:**  Cholesterol is endogenously synthesized or consumed through diet.  It is most commonly synthesized in the liver and intestines; the rate-limiting step is the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate by the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase ((Figure 1)). - **Functions:**  Cholesterol is important for cell membrane integrity and is a precursor to steroid hormones, bile salts, and other compounds (eg, myelin). - **Homeostatic regulation:**  Hepatic synthesis of cholesterol is decreased during increases in exogenous (dietary) cholesterol (negative feedback regulation).  Circulating cholesterol is primarily cleared by the liver; blood cholesterol levels are primarily regulated by expression of cholesterol-binding hepatocyte receptors (discussed further below). ## Triglycerides - **Synthesis:**  TGs are endogenously synthesized or consumed through diet.  TGs are formed by esterification of fatty acids (eg, saturated, unsaturated) with glycerol; in contrast, when needed (eg, for energy), TGs undergo lipolysis within tissue and in the circulation to become free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol. - **Functions:**  TGs serve as an important form of **energy storage** in the body.  FFAs derived from TGs can be used for ATP production (eg, beta-oxidation within mitochondria).  Glycerol is used by the liver (glycerol kinase) for glucose formation via gluconeogenesis ((Figure 2)).  Conversely, fatty acids can be reesterified in cells (eg, adipose tissue) into TGs; these stored TGs can subsequently be mobilized for energy (eg, during exercise). - **Homeostatic regulation:**  Dietary TGs are lipolyzed by pancreatic lipase.  In addition, lipoprotein lipase (LPL) located within the endothelium promotes lipolysis of TGs for uptake within cells, effectively decreasing circulating FFA levels ((Figure 3)).  In contrast, hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) promotes lipolysis of stored TGs for release into the circulation, increasing circulating FFA levels.  Excess FFAs are taken up by the liver. ## Lipoproteins and apolipoproteins Lipids are insoluble and therefore are carried within the core of lipoproteins ((Figure 4)).  Lipoproteins deliver TGs and cholesterol to tissues then return to the liver (binding to hepatocyte receptors) for processing, storage, and recycling.  Lipoproteins are classified based on density (determined by their relative proportions of cholesterol, TGs, and proteins), which in turn determines their primary functions ((Table 1)). Each class of lipoproteins has specific **apolipoproteins** (eg, Apo B-48), which assist with assembly, enzymatic signaling, transport, and hepatocyte binding ((Figure 5)).  Apo deficiencies (eg, genetic syndromes) are implicated in pathogenesis of dyslipidemias, as discussed in the subsequent sections. The following section details how lipids and lipoproteins are metabolized. # Lipid metabolism Pathways for metabolism of dietary lipids (primarily involving chylomicrons) and endogenously synthesized lipids (primarily involving hepatic synthesis of VLDL and HDL) are each discussed in the following sections. ## Transport of dietary lipids: Chylomicrons TGs and cholesterol consumed through diet are metabolized via the following steps: - **Fat emulsification and micelle formation:**  The presence of dietary TGs and cholesterol in the gut triggers bile secretion into the small intestine, which emulsifies fat droplets (increase surface area) to facilitate further enzymatic processing ((Figure 6)).  TGs are lipolyzed by pancreatic lipase, forming FFAs and monoglycerides, which aggregate into micelles ((Figure 7)). - **Chylomicron formation and circulation:**  Micelles are absorbed by enterocytes, where FFAs are reassembled into TGs and packaged along with cholesterol esters and **Apo B-48** into chylomicrons.  Chylomicrons cannot enter the bloodstream due to their large size; instead, they exit into the lymphatic circulation via lacteals, eventually emptying via the thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein. - **TG uptake into cells, clearance of chylomicron remnants, and cholesterol recycling:**  Assisted by **Apo C-II**, LPL facilitates lipolysis of TGs within chylomicrons for cellular uptake.  TG-depleted chylomicron remnants enter the liver by receptor-mediated endocytosis, a process requiring **Apo E** and Apo B-48 to interact with the remnant receptor.  Cholesterol within chylomicrons is recycled for production of bile acids or other lipoproteins. ## Endogenous lipid transport: VLDL and LDL Endogenous lipid metabolism begins in the liver with VLDL synthesis, formed by TGs and a small amount of cholesterol.  After exiting the liver, VLDL undergoes the following steps: - TGs contained in VLDL undergo lipolysis (LPL action, supported by Apo C-II), in a manner similar to chylomicron processing, for uptake and storage in tissue. - As TG content of VLDL is progressively depleted, it becomes IDL and then cholesterol-rich LDL. - LDL enters cells via r**eceptor-mediated endocytosis**, a process requiring binding of Apo B-100 to the LDL receptor (located on hepatocytes and certain other peripheral tissue, such as adrenocortical cells).  The hepatic LDL receptor is the greatest contributor to cholesterol clearance from the circulation (~70% of LDL clearance); its expression is in part controlled by the serine protease proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (**PCSK9**) and is subject to negative feedback: - **High intracellular cholesterol:**  PCSK9 binding to the LDL receptor increases, causing receptor degradation, decreasing LDL receptor expression and hepatic cholesterol uptake.  The net effect is increased circulating LDL. - **Low intracellular cholesterol:**  PCSK9 binding to the LDL receptor decreases, and LDL receptor expression and hepatic uptake increases.  The net effect is decreased circulating LDL. ## Reverse transport of cholesterol to the liver: HDL HDL, synthesized in the liver and intestines, serves 2 important functions in lipid metabolism: - **Scavenges intracellular cholesterol** (eg, from macrophages, other lipoproteins):  This process requires entry of HDL into the cell (involving binding of Apo A-1 to the cell surface ATP-binding cassette transporter-1) and an esterification of free cholesterol by lecithin cholesterol-acyl transferase (LCAT).  HDL carries this esterified cholesterol to the liver, binding to hepatocyte surface scavenger receptors to enter hepatocytes. - **Supports function of other lipoproteins:**  HDL is a carrier of Apo C-II and E, passing them to other lipoproteins (eg, VLDL, chylomicrons) to enable lipolysis of TGs and hepatic clearance. When TG levels are high, HDL accepts TG from VLDL and LDL in exchange for cholesterol, a process catalyzed by cholesterol ester transferase protein (**CETP**).  The resulting TG-rich HDL is unstable and prone to breakdown of HDL, with a net effect of decreasing HDL concentration and impairing HDL transport of cholesterol to the liver. Several key enzymes involved in endogenous cholesterol synthesis and transport are summarized in this table ((Table 2)). # Common patterns of dyslipidemia Common patterns seen in dyslipidemia and their causes are presented in this table ((Table 3)). # Dyslipidemias and atherosclerosis A primary clinical consequence of dyslipidemia involves its association with ASCVD. ## Role of LDL Chronic exposure to excess LDL is causally linked to ASCVD.  LDL generates ASCVD through the following steps: - LDL (especially small, dense LDL) can penetrate the endothelial barrier and accumulate under the subendothelial space, a crucial step in atherogenesis ((Figure 8)).  It undergoes reactive oxygen species modification, becoming ox-LDL. - Ox-LDL is taken up by macrophages and rapidly accumulates (because uptake of ox-LDL is not subject to normal feedback inhibition), resulting in formation of foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) and proliferation of smooth muscle cells with increased production of extracellular matrix proteins (eg, collagen, proteoglycans) - The ensuing inflammatory cascade leads to the development of the lesions typical of atherosclerosis, starting from the fatty streaks within the intima (composed mainly of lipid-laden foam cells) that transition into atherosclerotic plaques, such as fibrous cap atheromas and fibrous plaques.  These can become calcified and obstruct blood flow, or can rupture and lead to acute thrombosis. ## Role of HDL and TGs High TG and low HDL levels are often seen in combination with high LDL.  Their effects on the pathogenesis of ASCVD are as follows: - **HDL** has antiatherogenic properties (eg, scavenging excess cholesterol from macrophages before it can be oxidized) and appears to increase nitric oxide production to improve vascular function. - **TG** has theoretical proatherogenic effects because high levels are associated with increased CETP activity and decreased HDL and reverse cholesterol transport. No direct causal link between either high TG or low HDL and ASCVD has been established, although both laboratory abnormalities are often seen in other conditions increasing risk for ASCVD (eg, metabolic syndrome). # Clinical presentation The clinical manifestations of dyslipidemia vary depending on the specific lipid abnormality, severity of the disorder and the presence of associated conditions.  In most cases, dyslipidemia is diagnosed in asymptomatic patients during routine lipid screening (eg, lipid panel), obtained during health maintenance visits (eg, in asymptomatic patients).  In other cases (especially with familial syndromes), patients may manifest with dyslipidemia-associated complications (eg, ASCVD) or signs on physical examination.  This section covers common asymptomatic and symptomatic manifestations of dyslipidemia. # Screening in asymptomatic patients The optimal time to screen for dyslipidemia depends on the presence of other ASCVD risk factors for ASCVD (eg, family history, obesity, presence of hypertension). - **No ASCVD risk factors present:**  Low-risk, asymptomatic patients are generally recommended to undergo one-time screening in childhood and early adulthood (age 9-11 and between age 17 and 21). - **Other ASCVD risk factors present:**  Patients with a family history of familial hypercholesterolemia or other risk factors should initiate screening earlier (early childhood, or when the risk factor is identified). Because age is a primary risk factor for ASCVD, frequent (eg, annual) monitoring of lipids is not usually recommended for low-risk, younger patients (no ASCVD risk factors, age <35 for men and age <45 for women) because it will usually not affect management (ie, lifestyle management for prevention is universally recommended for such patients as first-line treatment).  However, for motivated patients interested in monitoring lipid values to inform lifestyle changes and prevention, lipid screening may be performed earlier. # Symptomatic presentations In some cases, patients with severe elevations in LDL or triglycerides (often reflecting familial syndromes) may manifest with premature ASCVD (eg, childhood, teenage years), pancreatitis, and/or characteristic physical examination findings. - **Atherosclerosis:**  Manifestations can involve the coronary, cerebral (especially internal carotid), and/or systemic (eg, ileal, popliteal) circulation; symptoms can range from myocardial infarction, aortic aneurysm or dissection, ischemic stroke, or limb symptoms of peripheral artery disease (claudication, nonhealing ulcers) to sudden cardiac death. - **Fatty liver disease:**  Accumulation of lipids (especially TG) within hepatocytes results in hepatic steatosis, the first stage in nonalcoholic fatty disease ((Figure 9)).  Chronic metabolic inflammation and oxidative stress (eg, from obesity and insulin resistance) downregulates the nuclear receptor protein peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha, which normally promotes FFA beta-oxidation.  Reduced beta-oxidation of FFAs leads to further lipid accumulation and lipotoxicity, ultimately inciting hepatocyte necrosis, inflammation, and fibrosis (eg, progression to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis). - **Pancreatitis:**  Increased TGs are lipolyzed by pancreatic lipase in pancreatic capillaries; the resulting FFAs are highly inflammatory and cause cellular damage, inflammation, and necrosis.  The serum TG level generally is >1,000 mg/dL (eg, familial syndromes) to be a potential cause of pancreatitis (lower levels may be associated with pancreatitis with concomitant excess alcohol intake). ## Physical examination findings Physical manifestations of dyslipidemia are most often seen in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia and other genetic syndromes.  Presence of any of these findings warrants obtaining a diagnostic lipid panel: - **Xanthoma** is a flat, yellowish deposit of cholesterol that presents as lipid-laden histiocytes in the dermis; it can form in the skin or in tendons (eg, Achilles tendon).  It may be tuberous (over knees, elbows), eruptive (acute onset), or tendinous (over tendons). - **Xanthelasma** is a type of xanthoma usually found on the medial eyelids ((Image 1)); it presents as dermal accumulations of benign-appearing macrophages with abundant, finely vacuolated (foamy) cytoplasm containing cholesterol (free and esterified), phospholipids, and triglycerides.  Unlike other types of xanthomas, xanthelasma does not always signal severe dyslipidemia; it can be seen in milder cholesterol elevations or also seen in ~50% of healthy patients.  Chronic cholestatic processes including obstructive biliary lesions and primary biliary cholangitis result in hypercholesterolemia due to leakage of bile back into the circulation, leading to the formation of xanthelasmas. - **Arcus corneae** appears as an opaque ring or arc around the cornea; although it can occur in older adults as a benign finding, its presence in children or younger adults (eg, age <40) suggests an underlying dyslipidemia (eg, familial syndrome).  Lipemia retinalis (milky-appearing retinal vasculature) may also occur. - **Lipemic serum** is often a clue to high chylomicron levels, indicative of high circulating chylomicrons in the blood, and often indicate a genetic defect. # Risk factors Most cases of dyslipidemia are acquired through a polygenic mechanism involving interaction of possible genetic factors with environmental triggers (eg, diet, lifestyle behaviors, obesity).  Dyslipidemia may also be the result of another comorbid condition (eg, insulin resistance) or part of a monogenic familial syndrome. ## Lifestyle factors Lifestyle is a major factor influencing the risk for acquiring dyslipidemia in the general population (eg, 50%-60% of attributable risk).  Factors that adversely impact lipid profile include diet (eg, high saturated fat/trans fat intake, high sugar intake), sedentary lifestyle, excessive alcohol intake, and smoking. ## Insulin resistance Insulin resistance (eg, diabetes mellitus, obesity) is associated with increased VLDL, elevated LDL, and low HDL.  This occurs due to aberrant insulin action.  Normally, insulin upregulates LPL, which increases FFA uptake in adipose tissue and lowers blood TG and FFA levels, while inhibiting HSL (which releases stored FFAs and promotes increased TG levels).  Insulin resistance leads to the following effects: - Impaired LPL activity and increased HSL activity lead to an increase in circulating FFAs. - Acquisition of excess FFAs by the liver causes increased VLDL and TG levels. - Increased TG levels stimulate CETP to transfer TGs to HDL, resulting in lower HDL levels. Increased TGs also affect the morphology of LDL, leading to the generation of small dense LDL, which is more strongly associated with atherogenesis and inflammation. ## Familial syndromes Dyslipidemias are inherited as familial syndromes through a primarily monogenic (eg, autosomal recessive or dominant) or polygenic fashion involving mutations or dysfunction of various apolipoproteins, lipoproteins, receptors, or enzymes required for optimal lipid metabolism.  These familial dyslipidemias and their syndromes are often associated with specific physical examination findings or other manifestations.  Common genetic syndromes are presented in this table ((Table 4)). # Summary Dyslipidemias represent a diverse group of lipid disorders that manifest with high LDL, low HDL, and/or high triglycerides.  They involve defects in lipid metabolism and enzymatic processing, lipoproteins and apolipoproteins, lipid transport, and/or cellular receptor binding, which can result from genetic and lifestyle factors.  Although many patients with dyslipidemia are asymptomatic, some experience sequelae of atherosclerosis, pancreatitis, skin and tendon findings, and fatty liver disease. ​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​

Lipoproteins

Structure & synthesis

Function & clearance

VLDL

  • Formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ TGs, ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs
  • Becomes IDL as TG content reduces
  • Requires Apo C-II (LPL co-factor) & ApoE

LDL

  • Formed when IDL is depleted of TGs; also formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ cholesterol, ↓ TG
  • Transports cholesterol
  • Mainly cleared by liver; can be taken up by other tissues
  • Requires LDL-R & apo-B100

HDL

  • Formed in intestine & liver
  • Begins as nascent HDL (↓ TG & ↓ cholesterol); mature HDL has more cholesterol
  • Scavenges excess cholesterol & returns to liver
  • Supports function & clearance of other lipoproteins
  • Requires Apo A-I

Chylomicron

  • Formed in intestines from dietary lipids; ↑↑ TGs & ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs from diet
  • Becomes chylomicron remnants when TG content depleted
  • Requires Apo B-48, ApoE & Apo C-II (LPL cofactor)

Apo B-48 = apolipoprotein B-48; Apo B-100 = apolipoprotein B-100; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; ApoE = apolipoprotein E; IDL = intermediate-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; TG = triglyceride.

Key enzymes involved in cholesterol transport & synthesis

HMG-CoA reductase

  • Rate-limiting step in endogenous cholesterol production
  • ↑ Cholesterol synthesis

PCSK9

  • Binds to & promotes degradation of LDL-R
  • ↓ LDL-R & ↑ cholesterol levels

LPL

  • Lipolyzes TGs within lipoproteins into FFAs for cellular uptake → catabolizes VLDL & chylomicrons into remnants
  • ↓ Level of FFAs & TG in the blood

CETP

  • Transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to LDL/VLDL
  • ↑ TG content of HDL → ↓ quality & ↓ levels of HDL

LCAT

  • Esterifies free cholesterol for transport by HDL
  • ↑ Reverse transport of cholesterol to liver

CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; FFA = free fatty acid; LCAT = lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

Common patterns of dyslipidemias & their causes

High LDL (eg, >100-130 mg/dL)

  • ↑ LDL formation (eg, excess VLDL or Apo-B hepatic synthesis)
  • ↓ LDL clearance (eg, ↓ LDL-R expression, ↑ PCSK9, ↓ LDL-R binding caused by defective Apo B)

High TGs (eg, >150 mg/dL)

  • ↑ Hepatic VLDL synthesis
  • ↓ Chylomicron or VLDL clearance (eg, defective Apo E)
  • ↓ HDL activity (eg, ↑ CETP activity)
  • ↓ LPL activity (eg, defective Apo C-II → ↓ TG lipolysis)
  • Worsened by metabolic inflammation (eg, insulin resistance)

Low HDL (eg, <40-50 mg/dL)

  • Most commonly a sequela of ↑ LDL & TG
  • Isolated ↓ HDL can occur if ↓ synthesis (eg, defective Apo A-1)

Apo A-1 = apolipoprotein A-1; Apo B = apolipoprotein B; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; Apo E = apolipoprotein E; CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

Important inherited hyperlipoproteinemias

Dyslipidemia

Protein defect

Elevated lipoproteins

Major manifestations

Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
(type I)

  • Lipoprotein lipase
  • ApoC-2

Chylomicrons

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Lipemia retinalis
  • Eruptive xanthomas

Familial hypercholesterolemia

(type II A)

  • LDL receptor
  • ApoB-100

LDL

  • Premature atherosclerosis
  • Tendon xanthomas
  • Xanthelasmas

Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
(type III)

  • ApoE

Chylomicron & VLDL remnants

  • Premature atherosclerosis
  • Tuboeruptive & palmar xanthomas

Familial hypertriglyceridemia
(type IV)

  • Polygenic

VLDL

  • Associated with coronary disease, pancreatitis & diabetes

LDL = low-density lipoprotein; VLDL = very low-density lipoprotein.

articles.title: Lac Operon
articles.markdown: # Lac Operon # Introduction Bacteria regulate gene expression in response to environmental conditions (eg, nutrient availability) by controlling whether RNA polymerase transcribes specific genes.  One common strategy is the operon, a group of functionally related genes transcribed together and regulated as a unit.  The *lac* operon, first described in *Escherichia coli*, is a prototypical inducible operon that uses a negative feedback mechanism for transcriptional regulation in prokaryotes.  It enables bacteria to express genes required for lactose metabolism only when lactose is available and glucose is limited, aligning gene expression with energy efficiency. # Structural organization of the *lac* operon Bacteria can use either glucose or lactose as a carbon source, but glucose is metabolically preferred.  The *lac* operon enables the cell to activate lactose metabolism when glucose is unavailable and to avoid unnecessary enzyme production when lactose is absent. The *lac* operon is a polycistronic transcriptional unit, meaning multiple genes are transcribed together as a single mRNA.  It includes 3 structural genes related to lactose metabolism: - ***lacZ***:  Encodes beta-galactosidase, which hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose and converts a small fraction of lactose into allolactose. - ***lacY***:  Encodes lactose permease, which facilitates lactose entry into the cell. - ***lacA***:  Encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase, which is not essential for lactose metabolism but may detoxify nonmetabolizable galactosides. Upstream of the structural genes are regulatory DNA elements that control transcription by determining RNA polymerase access.  They include the following: - The **promoter (lacP)** is where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. - The **operator (lacO)** is a DNA sequence that is the binding site for the *lac* repressor, which blocks transcription when bound. - The **catabolite activator protein (CAP) binding site** is located upstream of the promoter and serves as a docking site for an activator protein that enhances transcription of genes required for lactose metabolism when cAMP concentrations are high.  A separate, constitutively expressed gene, *lacI,* encodes the ***lac*** **repressor**, which is produced continuously and diffuses to act on the operator. These elements determine whether transcription of the downstream genes occurs by controlling RNA polymerase access and efficiency. # Regulatory logic of the operon Regulation of the *lac* operon reflects 2 questions. 1. Is lactose present?  (Is expression of the genes required for lactose metabolism currently necessary?) 2. Is glucose available?  (Can a preferred energy source be used instead of lactose?) The inputs are handled by 2 interacting control systems: - A **repressor**, which blocks transcription unless lactose is present (negative control). - An **activator**, which increases transcription when glucose is low (positive control). This creates a 2-step regulatory logic: Lactose determines whether transcription is blocked or allowed, and glucose determines whether transcription is low or high. ## Induction by lactose (allows transcription when lactose is present) When lactose is absent, the *lac* repressor is bound to the operator and transcription of genes required for lactose metabolism is blocked ((Figure 1)).  When lactose is present, a small amount enters the cell and is converted to allolactose.  Allolactose acts as an inducer by binding the repressor and causing a conformational change that prevents operator binding and allows transcription to proceed ((Figure 2)). The *lac* operon is therefore classified as inducible; expression is activated by the presence of substrate. ## Activation by low glucose (increases transcription when glucose is low) When glucose levels are low, intracellular cAMP levels rise.  cAMP binds to CAP, and the cAMP–CAP complex binds to its site upstream of the promoter.  This complex interacts with RNA polymerase, stabilizes the open complex, and substantially increases the rate of transcription initiation ((Figure 3)). Intracellular cAMP levels are inversely related to glucose availability: - High glucose levels lead to low cAMP levels, resulting in minimal CAP binding and basal or low transcription. - Low glucose levels lead to high cAMP levels, resulting in active CAP binding and strongly enhanced transcription. This mechanism couples *lac* operon expression to cellular energy status, ensuring that lactose metabolism is upregulated only when glucose is scarce. # Integration of regulatory inputs Because both control systems operate simultaneously, transcription of lactose metabolism genes depends on the combination of lactose and glucose availability: - **No lactose, high glucose**:  The repressor is bound and CAP is inactive; transcription is off. - **No lactose, low glucose**:  The repressor is bound and CAP is active; transcription is off. - **Lactose present, high glucose**:  The repressor is unbound and CAP is inactive; low-level transcription occurs ((Figure 4)). - **Lactose present, low glucose**:  The repressor is unbound and CAP is active; high-level transcription occurs ((Figure 5)). CAP activity alone cannot drive transcription if the repressor remains bound.  Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for high-level expression.  This dual control ensures that lactose metabolism genes are strongly expressed (ie, high-level transcription) only when both lactose is present and glucose is low. ## Functional dynamics of induction Induction is not instantaneous.  Because some *lac* repressor molecules periodically dissociate from the operator even in the absence of allolactose, basal transcription continuously produces low levels of permease and beta-galactosidase.  When lactose becomes available, this basal activity allows the following events to take place: - Initial lactose uptake via basal permease. - Conversion of a small fraction of lactose to allolactose via basal beta-galactosidase. - Allolactose binding to the repressor, releasing the operator and increasing transcription. - Increased production of permease and beta-galactosidase, allowing more allolactose to be generated. This constitutes a positive feedback loop that amplifies and sustains operon activation when lactose is present.  It also explains why induction is not all-or-none at the single-cell level but instead builds progressively as intracellular allolactose accumulates. # Effects of mutations - **Repressor or operator defects**:  Mutations that prevent the *lac* repressor from binding the operator result in transcription that is always allowed, regardless of lactose availability (constitutive expression). - **Promoter defects**:  Mutations that impair RNA polymerase binding to the promoter decrease transcription of genes required for lactose metabolism, even when regulatory conditions would otherwise permit expression. - **CAP or CAP binding site defects**:  Mutations that disrupt CAP function or its binding site prevent increased transcription when glucose is low, so transcription remains low despite the presence of lactose. - **Structural gene mutations**:  Mutations in *lacZ*, *lacY*, or *lacA* prevent proper lactose uptake or metabolism, so the operon may be transcribed normally but lactose cannot be effectively used. # Inducible vs repressible operons The *lac* operon is an inducible system under negative control, with additional positive regulation.  This contrasts with repressible operons, such as those governing amino acid biosynthesis, in which gene expression is typically on by default and is turned off by the end product, which acts as a corepressor. # Summary The *lac* operon regulates transcription of genes required for lactose uptake and metabolism by integrating lactose and glucose availability.  Lactose determines whether transcription is blocked or allowed by controlling repressor binding to the operator, whereas glucose determines how strongly those genes are transcribed through cAMP–CAP activity.  This creates a graded, condition-dependent response: Transcription is blocked when lactose is absent, allowed at a low level when lactose is present but glucose is high, and increased when lactose is present and glucose is low.  These effects are mediated by DNA elements that control RNA polymerase access and activity, allowing for coordinated, condition-dependent expression of multiple genes from a single promoter. ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌

articles.title: Hypoxemia: Physiology
articles.markdown:
# Hypoxemia: Physiology

# Introduction

Hypoxemia, hypoxia, anemia, and ischemia are related, yet distinct processes:

-   **Hypoxemia**:  Low dissolved oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) content of arterial blood, commonly defined as an arterial partial pressure of O<sub>2</sub> (PaO<sub>2</sub>) <60 mm Hg.  Example:  parenchymal lung disease.
-   **Hypoxia**:  Low O<sub>2</sub> content at the end-organ and tissue level.  It can be caused by hypoxemia, anemia, or ischemia.  Prolonged hypoxia typically results in tissue necrosis.  Example:  myocardial infarction.
-   **Anemia**:  Low number of circulating red blood cells (and therefore, hemoglobin content) in arterial blood.  Example:  iron deficiency.
-   **Ischemia**:  Low perfusion of end-organs and tissues, resulting in decreased O<sub>2</sub> and other nutrients (eg, glucose).  Example:  arterial thrombosis.

This article discusses the mechanisms, pathophysiology, and evaluation of hypoxemia.

# Normal oxygenation

Normal oxygenation requires 3 elements:

-   Normal inspired O<sub>2</sub> (ie, normal PiO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, normal PaCO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, normal A-a gradient).

## Normal inspired oxygen (PiO<sub>2</sub>)

**PiO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of inspired O<sub>2</sub>) is the O<sub>2</sub> available in the atmosphere for breathing.  It is determined by the fraction of inspired O<sub>2</sub> (FiO<sub>2</sub>), the atmospheric pressure (P<sub>atm</sub>), and the water vapor pressure (P<sub>H2O</sub>).

Under standard conditions:  PiO<sub>2</sub> = FiO<sub>2</sub> × (P<sub>atm</sub> − P<sub>H2O</sub>) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ **150 mm Hg**:

-   **FiO**<sub>**2**</sub> = fraction of inspired O<sub>2</sub>.  It is the percentage of air molecules that are O<sub>2</sub>.  Normal FiO<sub>2</sub> is 21% everywhere on Earth.
-   **P**<sub>**atm**</sub> = atmospheric pressure.  Normal P<sub>atm</sub> is 760 mm Hg at sea level and decreases with altitude.
-   **P**<sub>**H2O**</sub> = vapor pressure of water in the atmosphere.  Normal P<sub>H2O</sub> is 47 mm Hg.

## Normal alveolar ventilation (PaCO<sub>2</sub>)

**PaCO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide) reflects the effectiveness of ventilation, which removes ("blows off") carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>).  It is determined by minute ventilation, the product of respiratory rate (RR) and tidal volume (V<sub>T</sub>).  Normal minute ventilation is 6-8 L/min because normal RR is 12-16/min and normal V<sub>T</sub> is 500 mL (= 0.5 L).

PaCO<sub>2</sub> is measured directly by arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis.  PaCO<sub>2</sub> is in equilibrium with PACO<sub>2</sub> (partial pressure of alveolar carbon dioxide) because CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses instantly between the pulmonary capillary blood and the alveolar airspace.  Therefore, under normal conditions, P<sub>A</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> = PaCO<sub>2</sub> = **40 mm Hg**.

In the alveolus, each molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> displaces 0.8 molecule of O<sub>2</sub>.  **PAO**<sub>**2**</sub> (partial pressure of alveolar oxygen) is the O<sub>2</sub> content present in the alveolar airspace after dilution by CO<sub>2</sub>.  Normally, P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = PiO<sub>2</sub> − P<sub>A</sub>CO<sub>2</sub> / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = **100 mm Hg**.

## Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (A-a gradient)

**A-a gradient** (alveolar-arterial gradient) is the difference between P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and PaO<sub>2</sub>.

-   P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is normally 100 mm Hg as previously described.
-   **PaO**<sub>**2**</sub> is normally **75-100 mm Hg** and is measured directly by ABG analysis.

A small A-a gradient is normally present due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, thebesian veins, bronchial circulation).  This expected A-a gradient can be predicted from age:  normal A-a gradient ≈ age / 3 ≈ (age / 4) + 4.  The A-a gradient is widened by conditions that disrupt the uptake of oxygen, such as V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, and abnormal right-to-left shunting.

# Five mechanisms of hypoxemia

There are 5 mechanisms of hypoxemia:

-   1\. Low PiO<sub>2</sub>.
-   2\. Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO<sub>2</sub>).
-   Abnormal (↑) A-a gradient.
    -   3\. V/Q mismatch.
    -   4\. Diffusion limitation.
    -   5\. Right-to-left shunt.

## Low inspired oxygen (↓P<sub>i</sub>O<sub>2</sub>)

Low PiO<sub>2</sub> refers to hypoxemia due to insufficient atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> available for breathing.  It occurs in 2 situations:

-   **Decreased FiO**<sub>**2**</sub> (ie, **normobaric hypoxemia**):  Normal FiO<sub>2</sub> is 21% everywhere on Earth.  It drops if another gas displaces O<sub>2</sub> in the inspired air.  For example, a massive nitrogen spill can severely depress FiO<sub>2</sub>, even though P<sub>atm</sub> remains the same.  In practice, this is a very rare scenario.
-   **Decreased P**<sub>**atm**</sub> (ie, **hypobaric hypoxemia**):  Normal P<sub>atm</sub> is 760 mm Hg at sea level.  Atmospheric pressure is decreased at **high altitudes**.  For example, P<sub>atm</sub> is only 250 mm Hg at the top of Mount Everest, even though FiO<sub>2</sub> is still 21%.  PaO<sub>2</sub> declines with rising elevation ((Figure 1)), with hypoxemia generally becoming problematic at >2,500 m (8,000 ft), corresponding to the development of high-altitude illness.

With low PiO<sub>2</sub>, hypoxemia occurs because the initial O<sub>2</sub> content reaching the alveoli is decreased.  However, the **A-a gradient is norma**l because O<sub>2</sub> transport across the alveolar membrane is unaffected.

## Alveolar hypoventilation (↑ PaCO<sub>2</sub>)

Alveolar hypoventilation ((Figure 2)) refers to hypoxemia due to the retention of carbon dioxide.  An increase in PaCO<sub>2</sub> **(hypercapnia)** occurs in 3 situations:

-   **Central hypoventilation** ("won't breathe"):  Central hypoventilation occurs when neural respiratory drive is diminished.  Etiologies include opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and damage to brainstem respiratory centers (eg, tumor, stroke).  Patients have **slow and shallow** breathing (↓ RR × ↓ V<sub>T</sub>), indicating a lack of drive.
-   **Peripheral hypoventilation** ("can't breathe"):  Peripheral hypoventilation occurs when respiratory mechanics are impaired, even though neural respiratory drive is intact.  Etiologies include neuromuscular disease (eg, myasthenia gravis), chest wall deformities (eg, severe kyphosis), advanced obstructive lung disease (eg, emphysema), and advanced restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis).  Patients have **rapid and shallow** breathing (↑ RR × ↓↓ V<sub>T</sub>), and minute ventilation decreases when tachypnea cannot compensate for low V<sub>T</sub>.
-   **High dead space** (wasted ventilation):  Dead space refers to the portion of the V<sub>T</sub> that does not participate in gas exchange.
    -   **Anatomic** dead space is formed where no gas exchange occurs in the conducting airways (eg, trachea, bronchi).  It remains constant but can be increased if additional tubing is added to the respiratory circuit (eg, mechanical ventilation).
    -   **Alveolar** dead space is formed by alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused.  It is normally negligible but can be increased by conditions that block alveolar perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism).  Minute ventilation is decreased **despite** rapid and deep breathing (↑ RR × ↑ V<sub>T</sub>) because most of the V<sub>T</sub> does not participate in gas exchange.

With alveolar hypoventilation, hypoxemia occurs because O<sub>2</sub> is displaced by CO<sub>2</sub> retained in the alveoli.  However, **A-a gradient is normal** because O<sub>2</sub> transport across the alveolar membrane is intact.

## V/Q mismatch

V/Q mismatch ((Figure 3)) refers to hypoxemia due to a regional imbalance of air flow (V) and blood flow (Q) reaching the alveoli.  Normally, both V and Q are highest at lung bases and lowest at the lung apices.  Across the entire lung, this averages to a global V/Q ratio = 1 ((Figure 4)).  Defects in either V or Q can cause deviations from this ratio:

-   **Low V/Q** ((Figure 5)):  Alveoli are poorly ventilated but continue to be perfused.  Etiologies include **airway and airspace disorders** such as lobar pneumonia, asthmatic bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, and atelectasis.
-   **High V/Q** ((Figure 6)):  Alveoli are poorly perfused but continue to be ventilated.  Etiologies include **pulmonary vascular disorders** such as segmental pulmonary embolus and pulmonary arterial hypertension.  (These high V/Q areas also contribute to increased alveolar dead space, as previously described.)

With V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia occurs because Q and V are not efficiently localized together, producing an **elevated A-a gradient**.

## Diffusion limitation

Diffusion limitation ((Figure 7)) refers to hypoxemia due to factors that impair O<sub>2</sub> transfer across the alveolar membrane.  Normally, O<sub>2</sub> diffuses quickly and is fully extracted by the time blood has traveled only a third of the pulmonary capillary length.  This explains why exercise, which can increase pulmonary Q, does not result in hypoxemia.  However, 2 major processes can limit diffusion:

-   **Destruction** of the alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) decreases the surface area available for O<sub>2</sub> uptake.
-   **Thickening** of the alveolar membrane (eg, interstitial lung disease) increases the diffusion distance for O<sub>2</sub>.

Unlike V/Q mismatch, which involves regional or focal abnormalities (eg, segmental pulmonary embolus), diffusion limitation involves diffuse abnormalities of the lung parenchyma.

With diffusion limitation, hypoxemia occurs because O<sub>2</sub> transit across the alveolar membrane is impaired (ie, **elevated A-a gradient**).  In many cases, patients can be normoxic at rest but develop hypoxemia with exertion.

## Right-to-left shunting

Right-to-left shunting refers to hypoxemia due to the direct mixture of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated blood.  It occurs in 3 scenarios:

-   **Intracardiac anatomic shunt**:  An intracardiac communication is seen with atrial or ventricular septal defects.  Normally, oxygenated blood flows from the left chambers (higher pressure) to the deoxygenated right chambers (lower pressure).  However, the flow can reverse if the right-sided pressures increase, such as with the development of pulmonary hypertension, known as Eisenmenger syndrome ((Figure 8)).
-   **Intrapulmonary anatomic shunt**:  An intrapulmonary anatomic shunt is seen with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, which are anomalous connections between the deoxygenated pulmonary arteries and oxygenated pulmonary veins (bypassing the alveolar capillaries).
-   **Intrapulmonary shunt effect**:  In patients with extensive alveolar edema (eg, severe acute respiratory distress syndrome), the V/Q ratio can be close to 0, such that blood passing through the lungs barely receives oxygen.  This produces a functional right-to-left shunt, even though no direct anatomic connection is present.

With right-to-left shunting, hypoxemia occurs because deoxygenated blood mixes directly with oxygenated blood.  The **A-a gradient is elevated**.  Hypoxemia is often severe and **does not correct** with supplemental O<sub>2</sub> because a portion of the blood flow never reaches the lungs to be oxygenated.

# Evaluation of hypoxemia

ABG analysis can be approached in 2 ways.  A physiologic method, emphasizing stepwise interpretation without clinical context, is presented here.  In contrast, a clinical method, in which ABG is reserved for complex cases of hypoxemia in which clinical data alone are insufficient, is discussed in a separate article.  When reviewing an ABG, it is a good habit to apply a systematic framework even when the condition seems clinically obvious.

Formal stepwise ABG analysis of hypoxia ((Figure 9)) involves the 3 steps illustrated below.

## Step 1:  Compare PaO<sub>2</sub> and SaO<sub>2</sub>

PaO<sub>2</sub> is measured on ABG, and SaO<sub>2</sub> (O<sub>2</sub> saturation) is measured by pulse oximetry.  They are related by the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ((Figure 10)).  Dyshemoglobinemias can lead to discrepancies between these 2 values.

-   **Methemoglobinemia**:  Methemoglobin is hemoglobin in which iron is oxidized to the ferric (Fe<sup>3+</sup>) state, which cannot bind oxygen.  Therefore, the amount of functional hemoglobin available is reduced, leading to decreased SaO₂.  However, the amount of O<sub>2</sub> dissolved in plasma is normal (ie, arterial blood is normoxic), meaning that PaO<sub>2</sub> is normal.
-   **Carboxyhemoglobinemia**:  Carboxyhemoglobin forms when carbon monoxide (rather than oxygen) binds to hemoglobin.  Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light at a similar wavelength to oxyhemoglobin, causing pulse oximeters to misclassify it.  Therefore, SaO<sub>2</sub> (measured by pulse oximetry) reads as normal (or even artificially high), and blood may appear deceptively pink, even though functional oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced and true hypoxemia (eg, PaO<sub>2</sub> <60 mm Hg) may be present.

Additional testing for abnormal hemoglobin species (eg, multiwavelength CO-oximetry) may be indicated to explain the PaO<sub>2</sub>\-SaO<sub>2</sub> gap.

Severe acidosis or alkalosis can shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right or left, respectively.  For example, acidosis leads to the SaO<sub>2</sub> reading higher than expected for PaO<sub>2</sub> because it favors unloading into tissues.

## Step 2:  Calculate A-a gradient

The A-a gradient is a 4-step process that follows inspired gas as it moves from the atmosphere into the alveolar capillaries.

-   First, **calculate PiO**<sub>**2**</sub>:
    -   When breathing room air at sea level, PiO<sub>2</sub> = FiO<sub>2</sub> × (P<sub>atm</sub> − P<sub>H2O</sub>) = 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150 mm Hg.  This value changes at different altitudes or with the use of supplemental oxygen.
-   Second, **calculate P**<sub>**A**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>:
    -   As discussed previously, P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is the alveolar O<sub>2</sub> content after dilution by CO<sub>2</sub>.  Each molecule of CO<sub>2</sub> displaces 0.8 molecules of O<sub>2</sub>.  PaCO<sub>2</sub> is taken from the ABG and is normally 40 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal PAO<sub>2</sub> = PiO<sub>2</sub> × PaCO<sub>2</sub> / 0.8 = 150 – 40 / 0.8 = 100 mm Hg.
-   Third, **calculate A-a gradient**:
    -   A-a gradient is the difference between P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (calculated above) and PaO<sub>2</sub> (measured from ABG).  For example, a normal PaO<sub>2</sub> = 90 mm Hg.  Therefore, normal A-a gradient = 100 − 90 = 10 mm Hg.
-   Finally, **determine expected A-a gradient for age**:
    -   The physiologic A-a gradient increases with age.  Expected A-a gradient = (age / 4) + 4 ≈ age / 3.  The calculated A-a gradient in the previous step should be compared to this expected value.  A normal A-a gradient is due to low PiO<sub>2</sub> or alveolar hypoventilation.  An elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunt.

An example using real patient data is provided in the table ((Table 1)).

## Step 3a:  If A-a gradient is normal

Hypoxemia with normal A-a gradient is due to alveolar hypoventilation (most common) or low PiO<sub>2</sub> (usually clinically obvious).

-   **Alveolar hypoventilation** is indicated by elevated PaCO<sub>2</sub> (ie, >45 mm Hg).
-   **Low PiO**<sub>**2**</sub>, such as high altitude, is usually accompanied by low PaCO<sub>2</sub> due to hyperventilation.

## Step 3b:  If A-a gradient is elevated

Hypoxemia with elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  These can be differentiated by the response to supplemental oxygen.

-   **V/Q mismatch** or **diffusion limitation**:  The hypoxemia responds quickly to supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide but remains relatively constant at all levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    -   On room air:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    -   On 40% FiO<sub>2</sub>:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 240 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 190, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg still.  (The higher starting PiO<sub>2</sub> can "overcome" the A-a gradient to normalize the PaO<sub>2</sub>.)
-   **Right-to-left shunting**:  Hypoxemia does not respond to any level of supplemental oxygen.  The A-a gradient is wide and continues to increase at higher levels of supplemental oxygen.  For example:
    -   On room air:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50, so A-a gradient = 50 mm Hg.
    -   On 100% FiO<sub>2</sub>:  P<sub>A</sub>O<sub>2</sub> = 660 but PaO<sub>2</sub> = 50 still.  (Even pure O<sub>2</sub> is ineffective because shunted blood bypasses the alveoli entirely.)

# Effects of hypoxemia

## Tissue responses

Tissue hypoxia is sensed by hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF1ɑ) (Figure 11)).  HIF1ɑ is a transcription factor that is constitutively expressed by most cells.  In normoxic cytosol, HIF1ɑ is constantly degraded; in contrast, in hypoxic cytosol, it is posttranslationally stabilized.  HIF1ɑ can have adaptive or potentially maladaptive effects, depending on the severity and duration of hypoxia:

-   **Erythropoiesis**:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of erythropoietin in kidney juxtaglomerular cells and stimulates iron uptake in gut epithelium ((Figure 12)).
    -   Adaptively, this allows for compensatory polycythemia (generally, hematocrit >50% and hemoglobin >16.5 mg/dL) to boost oxygen-carrying capacity.
    -   Maladaptively, extreme polycythemia (eg, generally, hematocrit >60%) can cause a type of hyperviscosity syndrome in which vascular sludging produces neurologic symptoms (eg, headache, confusion), thrombosis, retinal edema, mucosal bleeding (eg, epistaxis), and heart failure.
-   **Angiogenesis**:  HIF1ɑ induces the upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor, mainly in the heart and skeletal muscle.
    -   Adaptively, this promotes the formation of collateral circulation (eg, to bypass chronic coronary artery stenosis).
    -   Maladaptively, disorganized neovascularization (eg, diabetic proliferative retinopathy) results in fragile, hemorrhage-prone vessels.
-   **Anaerobic (glycolytic) shift**:  HIF1ɑ induces upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (eg, hexokinase), mainly in the heart and brain.
    -   Adaptively, this preserves ATP production despite low O<sub>2</sub> (eg, hibernating myocardium).
    -   Maladaptively, this results in several downstream changes, such as cellular proliferation (eg, Warburg effect in cancer cells, in which glucose is converted to lactate via aerobic glycolysis in the cytosol rather than being fully metabolized in the mitochondria, fueling rapid cell growth).  This shift also results in inflammation (eg, leukocyte activation due to glycolytic products).

## Vascular responses

Effects of hypoxia on vascular resistance are not dependent on HIF1ɑ.  Instead, vessels respond directly to O<sub>2</sub> itself, reactive oxygen species, or related metabolites.

-   **Systemic vasodilation**:  Hypoxia (eg, exercising skeletal muscle) stimulates the production of anaerobic metabolites such as adenosine, lactate, and nitric oxide that promote vasodilation.  Low O<sub>2</sub> tension directly relaxes vascular smooth muscle (eg, O<sub>2</sub>\-sensitive potassium and calcium channels).  These processes increase arterial perfusion to hypoxic tissue.
-   **Pulmonary vasoconstriction** ((Figure 13)):  Hypoxia is sensed by pulmonary arterioles, likely through mitochondrial redox potential, stimulating vasoconstriction.
    -   This is adaptive for short-term, regional hypoxia (eg, atelectatic lobe), because the selective vasoconstriction limits perfusion to poorly ventilated alveoli, maintaining V/Q matching.
    -   However, it is maladaptive for chronic, global hypoxia (eg, untreated obstructive sleep apnea) because whole-lung vasoconstriction can lead to pulmonary hypertension (eg, cor pulmonale, Group 3)

## Ventilatory response

Hypoxemia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies.  These chemoreceptors signal the medullary respiratory center to increase ventilation through deeper breaths and increased RR.  Hyperventilation has a much larger impact on lowering PaCO<sub>2</sub> than on raising PaO<sub>2</sub> ((Figure 14)).

-   **Ventilation**:  Hyperventilation causes an immediate reduction in PaCO<sub>2</sub> (respiratory alkalosis) because CO<sub>2</sub> elimination is directly proportional to minute ventilation.
-   **Oxygenation**:  Hyperventilation increases PaO<sub>2</sub> by only a small amount because perfusion to well-ventilated alveoli is already maximized, so further increases in ventilation do not significantly enhance O<sub>2</sub> uptake (ie, ceiling effect).  The hemoglobin in these regions is already near full saturation.

In other words, high V/Q areas (ie, hyperventilation) cannot compensate ((Figure 15)) for low V/Q units (eg, mismatch).  Breathing faster and harder will blow down CO<sub>2</sub> but does not improve oxygenation.

## Cell death

Severe or sustained hypoxemia can result in cell death, especially when combined with ischemia (eg, hypotension).  The dual insult of hypoxemia and hypotension is much more likely to cause tissue necrosis than either alone.  Tissue tolerance varies widely:  Kidneys (eg, acute tubular necrosis) can fully recover even after 15 minutes of complete circulatory arrest, whereas hypoxic-ischemic brain injury may be irreversible after just 3-5 minutes.

# Summary

Hypoxemia (PaO<sub>2</sub> <60 mm Hg) can be caused by 5 mechanisms:  low inspired oxygen (eg, high altitude), alveolar hypoventilation (eg, opioid-induced respiratory depression), ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch (eg, lobar pneumonia), diffusion limitation (eg, interstitial lung disease), and right-to-left shunting (eg, atrial septal defect).  The alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient assesses oxygen exchange across the alveolar capillary membrane and helps to identify the underlying mechanism.  Hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient is due to low inspired oxygen or alveolar hypoventilation (ie, high PaCO<sub>2</sub>).  Hypoxemia with an elevated A-a gradient is due to V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation, or right-to-left shunting.  A poor response to 100% supplemental oxygen suggests shunt physiology.

font-size: 1.1rem;"><strong style="font-size: 1.1rem;">►Patient's A-a gradient</strong> = P<sub style="font-size: 1.1rem;">A</sub>O<sub style="font-size: 1.1rem;">2</sub> − PaO<sub style="font-size: 1.1rem;">2</sub> = 75 − 50 = 25 mm Hg</p></td></tr><tr style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><td style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><p style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><strong style="font-size: 1.1rem;">Step 4</strong></p><p style="font-size: 1.1rem;">Compare to normal</p></td><td style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><ul style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><li style="font-size: 1.1rem;">Small A-a gradient is normal due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, bronchial arteries)</li><li style="font-size: 1.1rem;">Expected A-a gradient ~ age / 3 = 48 / 3 = 16 mm Hg</li></ul><p style="margin-left: 0.1in; font-size: 1.1rem;"><strong style="font-size: 1.1rem;">►</strong>Patient's A-a gradient is <strong style="font-size: 1.1rem;">elevated</strong> (25 > 16)</p></td></tr><tr style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><td colspan="2" style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><p style="font-size: 1.1rem;"><strong style="font-size: 1.1rem;">ABG</strong> = arterial blood gas.</p></td></tr></tbody></table>
