articles.title: Hypothalamic-Pituitary Hormones
articles.markdown: # Hypothalamic-Pituitary Hormones # Introduction The hypothalamic-pituitary axis is a core component of the endocrine system, responsible for regulating various physiologic processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress responses.  The hypothalamus, located at the base of the brain, controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland, which is divided into anterior and posterior lobes.  The anterior pituitary releases several hormones that regulate peripheral endocrine glands, whereas the posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.  The interplay between these 2 organs maintains homeostasis in the body.  This article examines the hormones produced by both the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and their functions, regulatory mechanisms, and physiologic effects. # Hypothalamic hormones The hypothalamus produces releasing and inhibiting hormones that control the secretion of hormones from the anterior pituitary.  These hormones help regulate a variety of bodily functions, including reproduction, stress response, and metabolism. ## Gonadotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis** in women ((Figure 1)) and men ((Figure 2)), influencing secretion of **gonadotropins**, including luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), from the anterior pituitary. - GnRH and gonadotropins regulate the function of the gonads (testes, ovaries) and reproductive processes, including production of **sex hormones** (testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone), spermatogenesis, and ovulation. - Prepubertal GnRH secretion is **low and constant**, which suppresses anterior pituitary gonadotropin secretion and gonadal sex hormone production.  Puberty is marked by a transition to **pulsatile** GnRH secretion, which stimulates increased gonadotropin secretion (resulting in increased LH, FSH, and sex hormones). **Regulation** - **Positive feedback**:  Leading up to ovulation, a sustained increase in estrogen levels leads to positive stimulation of GnRH secretion (ie, GnRH and LH surge). - **Negative feedback**:  Elevated sex hormone levels generally inhibit GnRH secretion; this effect occurs consistently with testosterone and progesterone, but the effects of estrogen in women depend on the current phase of the menstrual cycle (see below). **Clinical applications** - **Central hypogonadism**:  Suppression of GnRH can occur in states of stress or undernutrition (eg, via suppressive effects of elevated corticotropin-releasing hormone and cortisol, discussed in the next section), leading to low GnRH and hypogonadism (eg, decreased LH, estrogen, testosterone). - **Hyperprolactinemia**:  Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH secretion ((Figure 3)), leading to hypogonadism (low LH, FSH, estrogen). - **Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism**:  Primary ovarian insufficiency or testicular failure lowers sex hormone production, which leads to hypogonadism with elevated GnRH secretion (high LH and FSH with low estrogen or testosterone). - **Polycystic ovary syndrome**:  Polycystic ovary syndrome is characterized by excessively rapid pulsatile secretion of GnRH leads to a persistent imbalance in LH relative to FSH production, resulting in increased ovarian and peripheral androgen production. ## Corticotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis** ((Figure 4)), stimulating the anterior pituitary to release **adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)**, which subsequently stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce **corticosteroids** (eg, glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids). - Corticosteroids (especially cortisol) are involved in the body's response to stress and immune function; mineralocorticoids contribute to salt and volume homeostasis.  Corticosteroids also play a crucial role in regulating circadian rhythms. **Regulation** - **Positive feedback**:  Secretion of CRH is triggered by inflammatory cytokines (eg, infection), circadian rhythms, and limbic system input in states of high physiologic or psychologic stress (eg, trauma, hypoglycemia) via input from the suprachiasmatic nucleus; CRH secretion is highest in the early morning and is lowest at night. - **Negative feedback**:  High cortisol levels lower CRH and ACTH secretion ((Figure 5)). **Clinical correlations** - **Adrenal insufficiency**:  Adrenal insufficiency is characterized by low cortisol due to either primary adrenal failure or secondary (ie, central) suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.  In primary adrenal insufficiency, cortisol is low and ACTH/CRH are high due to loss of negative feedback.  Glucocorticoid use can lead to iatrogenic central suppression, with atrophy of hypothalamic CRH-releasing neurons causing low ACTH/CRH and cortisol. - **Cushing syndrome**:  Cushing syndrome refers to the clinical manifestations of prolonged, excessive cortisol exposure.  It can result from an adrenal source, such as an autonomously functioning adrenal adenoma, which leads to elevated cortisol and suppressed ACTH and CRH (due to negative feedback).  Alternately, it may arise from a central (ACTH-dependent) source, most commonly Cushing disease, which describes an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma that causes elevated ACTH and cortisol, with suppressed CRH (due to negative feedback). ## Thyrotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis** ((Figure 6)), stimulates the release of **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** from the anterior pituitary.  TSH in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release **thyroid hormones** (T3 and T4). - Thyroid hormones are critical for regulating metabolism, growth, and development, affecting nearly every tissue in the body. **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  TRH (and TSH) secretion is suppressed by increased levels of T3 and T4.  Other inhibitors of TRH include high dopamine levels, and starvation or critical illness (due to decreased leptin levels, high cortisol, and cytokine release), - **Positive feedback**:  Cold exposure, increased leptin, estrogen levels, and alpha-adrenergic stimulation (eg, norepinephrine) increase TRH levels. **Clinical applications** TRH is not routinely measured in clinical practice. - **Hyperthyroidism**:  Hyperthyroidism may result from central causes (eg, TSH-secreting tumors) with high TSH and T3/T4 or, more commonly, from primary hyperthyroidism with high T3/T4 and low TSH (feedback inhibition). - **Hypothyroidism**:  Hypothyroidism may be due to primary thyroid dysfunction (eg, Hashimoto disease) with low T3/T4 and high TSH (from negative feedback) or due to central inhibition (in which TSH and T3/T4 are both low). - **Euthyroid sick syndrome**:  In critical illness, caloric deprivation along with glucocorticoid and inflammatory cytokine release induce several changes in thyroid physiology (known as euthyroid sick syndrome \[ESS\]).  TRH suppression causes low-normal TSH levels, and decreased peripheral 5′-deiodination of T4 to T3 causes low T3; free T4 levels are initially normal.  If the underlying illness continues, T4 and TSH levels may eventually decrease, mimicking central hypothyroidism.  Because ESS typically improves with recovery, thyroid function testing in acutely ill, hospitalized patients is generally not recommended. ## Growth hormone–releasing hormone and somatostatin **Function** Growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH) and somatostatin are important regulators of the **growth hormone (GH) axis** ((Figure 7)) involving GH and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediate growth, cell repair, and metabolism.  GHRH stimulates somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary to **release GH**.  In contrast, somatostatin is the primary inhibitor of GH secretion, counteracting the effects of GHRH.  Somatostatin also inhibits the release of other hormones (eg, TSH, insulin). **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  Elevated levels of IGF-1 inhibits GHRH release from the hypothalamus (and GH secretion from the anterior pituitary). - Other regulators:  Somatostatin suppresses GH release, whereas factors such as sleep, exercise, stress, and hypoglycemia stimulate GHRH and GH secretion. **Clinical applications** - **Dwarfism**:  Dwarfism is characterized by GH deficiency. - **Acromegaly**:  Acromegaly is characterized by GH excess. ## Dopamine **Function** - Dopamine inhibits the release of **prolactin** from the anterior pituitary.  Prolactin is primarily involved in milk production in lactating women, and dopamine prevents excessive secretion of prolactin when not needed. **Regulation** - Dopamine secretion is modulated by feedback from prolactin levels.  Elevated prolactin can reduce dopamine release, allowing prolactin levels to rise further. - **Estrogen** can increase the secretion of prolactin, especially during pregnancy. **Clinical correlations** - **Prolactin-secreting tumors**:  Pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas) autonomously secrete prolactin, bypassing hypothalamic dopamine inhibition.  Elevated prolactin can cause galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and infertility. - **Dopamine antagonist medications**:  Antipsychotics and other dopamine D2 receptor blockers inhibit hypothalamic dopamine action, removing suppression of prolactin secretion.  This can lead to medication-induced hyperprolactinemia with symptoms similar to those seen in prolactinoma. # Pituitary hormones The anterior and posterior pituitary release several hormones that influence the function of other endocrine glands and target tissues throughout the body.  These hormones include ACTH, TSH, GH, LH, FSH, prolactin, and vasopressin. ## Adrenocorticotropic hormone **Function** - Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete **cortisol** and other corticosteroids.  Cortisol is vital for managing the body's response to stress, regulating metabolism, immune response, and inflammation. **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  Suppression of ACTH (and CRH) secretion can occur with high cortisol levels (or in the setting of long-term exogenous glucocorticoid therapy). ## Thyroid-stimulating hormone **Function** - Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release **thyroid hormones** (T3 and T4).  These hormones regulate metabolism, thermogenesis, and overall growth and development. **Regulation** - Like ACTH secretion, TSH secretion is regulated by **negative feedback** from thyroid hormones.  Elevated levels of T3 and T4 inhibit TRH release from the hypothalamus and TSH secretion from the pituitary. ## Growth hormone **Function** - Growth hormone (GH) stimulates growth, particularly in bones and muscles, and regulates metabolism.  It promotes protein synthesis, lipolysis, and the growth of long bones and cartilage, mainly through the action of IGF-1. **Regulation** GH secretion is regulated by **both** positive and negative feedback mechanisms: - **Positive feedback** occurs via GHRH, which stimulates GH release. - **Negative feedback** occurs through IGF-1, which inhibits both GHRH release and GH secretion. ## Prolactin **Function** - Prolactin is essential for **milk production** in the mammary glands during lactation.  It also plays a role in regulating reproductive function, immune modulation, and metabolism. **Regulation** - Prolactin release is primarily inhibited by dopamine.  During pregnancy, estrogen increases prolactin levels, preparing the mammary glands for lactation. ## Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone **Function** - Luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) are **gonadotropins** responsible for regulating reproductive functions.  In women, LH triggers ovulation and the formation of the corpus luteum, whereas FSH stimulates the growth of ovarian follicles.  In men, LH stimulates testosterone production from Leydig cells and FSH supports spermatogenesis. **Regulation** - In women, **estrogen** and **progesterone** mediate negative feedback on LH and FSH release, but during the menstrual cycle, rising estrogen levels mediate **positive feedback** by triggering the **LH surge**, which leads to ovulation. ## Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) **Function** - Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, regulates water balance by promoting water reabsorption in the kidneys.  It also plays a role in constricting blood vessels to maintain blood pressure. **Regulation** - ADH release is primarily regulated by **osmotic pressure** and **blood volume**.  When plasma osmolarity increases (indicating dehydration), ADH release is stimulated to conserve water.  Conversely, low blood volume or blood pressure also triggers ADH secretion. ## Oxytocin **Function** - Oxytocin is involved in uterine contractions during labor and facilitates milk ejection during breastfeeding.  It also has a role in social bonding, emotional responses, and maternal behaviors. **Regulation** - Oxytocin operates through **positive feedback** during labor.  The stretching of the cervix during labor stimulates oxytocin release, which intensifies uterine contractions, leading to further cervical dilation and more oxytocin release. # Summary The hypothalamic-pituitary axis plays a central role in regulating numerous physiologic functions, including metabolism, growth, reproduction, and stress response.  The hypothalamus produces hormones that either stimulate or inhibit the release of pituitary hormones, which in turn regulate the activity of peripheral endocrine glands.  Feedback mechanisms, primarily negative feedback, maintain hormonal balance, although positive feedback plays a role in certain physiologic processes such as ovulation and labor.  Disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis can lead to a variety of endocrine disorders. ​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​

articles.title: Hypersensitivity Reactions
articles.markdown:
# Hypersensitivity Reactions # Introduction Hypersensitivity reactions represent exaggerated immune responses to an antigen or an allergen.  They explain certain allergic reactions but also other (eg, autoimmune) disease conditions.  Four main types of hypersensitivity reactions are recognized (Gell and Coombs classification), based on underlying immune mechanisms and the time course of the reaction: - Type I (immediate hypersensitivity) reactions are IgE-mediated, have rapid onset, and can be seen in atopic, allergic, and anaphylactic conditions. - Type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic hypersensitivity) reactions are characterized by IgG or IgM targeting host cells and interfering with their function or leading to damage, as seen in some autoimmune conditions (eg, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody \[ANCA\] vasculitis, Graves disease). - Type III (immune complex hypersensitivity) reactions are characterized by immune complex (antibody-antigen) deposition in tissues, leading to inflammation (eg, serum sickness, lupus, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis). - Type IV (cell-mediated hypersensitivity) reactions are T cell–mediated, delayed-type (hours to days) reactions that underlie conditions such as allergic contact dermatitis and tuberculin skin test reactions. The mnemonic ACID (type I: **A**llergic/atopic/anaphylactic; type II: **C**ytotoxic/cell-mediated; type III: **I**mmune complex–mediated; type IV: **D**elayed) is sometimes used to recall these categories. # Type I hypersensitivity ## Pathophysiology An allergen is an antigen that promotes a robust immune response only in a subset of the population.  Type I hypersensitivity reactions can occur locally (eg, cutaneous hives, allergic rhinitis \[hay fever\], bronchial asthma) or systemically (eg, anaphylaxis), depending on the allergen and its portal of entry into the body ((Video 1)). After first exposure to an allergen (eg, peanut proteins, beta-lactam antibiotic), antigen-specific **IgE** is produced by B cells (as a result of class switching) and binds to the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI) on the surface of mast cells.  This receptor normally binds the Fc portion of circulating IgE, coating the cell with various antigen-specific IgE molecules.  With repeat exposure to a multivalent antigen, multiple IgE antibodies become cross-linked ((Figure 1)), resulting in aggregation of the FcεRI receptors on the mast cell surface.  This clumping of receptors leads to the activation of nonreceptor tyrosine kinases, triggering an intracellular cascade that ultimately results in **mast cell and basophil degranulation**. Systemic type I hypersensitivity reactions can lead to a potentially fatal, distributive form of shock (anaphylactic shock).  Local reactions often have early-phase (eg, minutes after exposure) and late-phase responses ((Figure 2)).  As an example, an early-phase cutaneous type I response could be superficial dermal edema and erythema (eg, wheal and flare reaction ((Image 1))), which can progress to a more systemic response (eg, anaphylaxis).  IgE also initiates the late phase of type I hypersensitivity reactions by stimulating type 2 helper T cells to release cytokines (eg, IL-5) that activate eosinophils; cationic proteins (eg, major basic protein, eosinophil peroxidase) released from eosinophils cause tissue damage.  For example, a late-phase cutaneous type I response usually manifests as a palpable, indurated lesion 2-10 hours following the early-phase reaction. ## Representative examples Type I hypersensitivity reactions are commonly thought of as: - **Allergic or atopic**:  "Atopy" refers to the predisposition to develop local immediate hypersensitivity reactions (eg, allergic rhinitis \[hay fever\], atopic dermatitis \[eczema\], bronchial asthma). - **Anaphylactic** (eg, reaction to insect sting, peanuts, some medications) Anaphylaxis, the classic manifestation of systemic type I hypersensitivity reaction, is likely if there is rapid symptom onset and any 1 of the following criteria: - Skin/mucosa involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) and either hypotension or respiratory distress - Involvement of ≥2 organ systems after exposure to a likely allergen: - Skin/mucosa (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) - Respiratory (eg, wheezing, stridor, dyspnea) - Cardiovascular (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, syncope) - Gastrointestinal (eg, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea) - Hypotension after exposure to a known allergen The diagnosis of type I hypersensitivity reactions is often made clinically.  Complete blood count may show eosinophilia in some cases, and serum total and specific IgE levels might be elevated.  Tryptase levels, which are specific for mast cells, can be elevated after anaphylactic reactions.  Skin prick testing or specific IgE blood tests can help identify the culprit allergen.  Genetic predisposition plays a role in these reactions, so family history may be positive. ## Management - **Avoidance**:  Eliminating the trigger allergen is the cornerstone of management. - **Antihistamines**:  Blocking the action of histamine alleviates related symptoms (eg, itching, hives, rhinorrhea). - **Mast cell stabilizers**:  Preventing mast cell degranulation can reduce the release of inflammatory mediators. - **Bronchodilators**:  In patients with respiratory symptoms, bronchodilators can relax airway smooth muscle and improve airflow. - **Epinephrine**:  In severe cases, especially anaphylaxis, immediate administration of epinephrine is crucial.  Epinephrine is the only pharmacologic therapy that both decreases the release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells and addresses all other manifestations of anaphylaxis.  It binds to adrenergic receptors (eg, beta-2 receptors) on the surface of mast cells, inhibiting mast cell degranulation.  In addition, it counteracts existing inflammatory effects via widespread stimulation of alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors: - Alpha-1 receptor activation causes vasoconstriction and decreases vascular permeability, raising blood pressure and decreasing upper airway edema. - Beta-1 receptor activation increases cardiac contractility and cardiac output, improving blood pressure and peripheral perfusion. - Beta-2 receptor activation causes bronchodilation, relieving airflow obstruction. In patients with severe reactions or in those who have an increased likelihood of exposure to hymenoptera venom (eg, pest control workers), **allergen immunotherapy (AIT)** is a disease-modifying treatment often recommended.  With AIT, escalating doses of antigen are administered subcutaneously over several years.  Progressive exposure induces immune tolerance via several immunologic mechanisms, including: - Desensitization of mast cells and basophils (by triggering low-level release of intracellular granules) followed by decreased recruitment and activation of these cells (due to increased IL-10 and IgG4) - Generation of blocking antibodies:  AIT upregulates allergen-specific IgG4 antibodies.  In contrast to IgG1 and IgG2, IgG4 cannot activate the complement cascade or serve as a costimulatory ligand for natural killer cells or phagocytes.  Therefore, increased production of IgG4 helps bind and neutralize antigens without promoting additional immune activity. - Shifting T-cell differentiation away from pathogenic Th2 subsets toward Th1 cells and regulatory T cells, increasing production of immunosuppressive cytokines (eg, IL-10, TGF-beta) and ligands (eg, CTLA-4, PD1) and reducing activation of mast cells and basophils. - Decreased IgE production, which is caused by the shift from Th2 cell–driven responses to Th1-driven responses.  Detectable reduction of serum IgE often takes years because IgE-producing plasma cells in bone marrow have long lifespans. # Type II hypersensitivity ## Pathophysiology and representative examples Binding of **preformed IgM or IgG antibodies** to cell surface antigens can cause cell destruction, inflammation, or dysfunction.  These reactions can develop hours to days after exposure to an antigen (eg, medications, transfused red blood cells), resulting in destruction of erythrocytes (causing fatigue, pallor), platelets (causing petechial bleeding), or leukocytes (causing fever, sepsis) ((Video 2)). The 3 main mechanisms include: - **Opsonization and phagocytosis**:  These occur either through complement fixation or through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity via natural killer cells (which recognize antibody-coated targets through Fc receptors and lyse them directly ((Figure 3))).  Examples include acute hemolytic transfusion reactions, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, erythroblastosis fetalis, and certain drug reactions.  - **Complement- and Fc receptor–mediated inflammation**:  Antibody deposition in extracellular tissue results in inflammation.  Examples include certain forms of glomerulonephritis, Goodpasture syndrome (anti–glomerular basement membrane disease), vascular rejection (after transplant), and ANCA vasculitides. - **Antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction without injury or inflammation**:  Examples include myasthenia gravis, pemphigus vulgaris, and Graves disease (leading to antibody-mediated cell function stimulation). ## Management Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the reaction and may involve immunosuppressive medications, intravenous immune globulin, or plasma exchange.  Complications such as organ damage and bleeding complications from hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia should be managed as well. # Type III hypersensitivity ## Pathophysiology In type III hypersensitivity reactions, **immune complex–mediated** complement activation typically causes tissue damage in sites where immune complexes (ie, antibody-antigen) tend to deposit (eg, skin, joints, kidneys) ((Video 3)).  Manifestations tend to present **days to weeks after initial antigen exposure**.  Antigens can be exogenous (eg, foreign protein, bacteria) or endogenous (eg, antigenic components of cells).  Smaller immune complexes are more likely to be deposited in small vessels or sites where blood is filtered into other fluids, such as joints and kidneys.  The underlying pathophysiology is as follows: 1. Foreign proteins (eg, from a medication) or self-antigens are processed by antigen-presenting cells and displayed on major histocompatibility complex class II molecules (MHCII). 2. Patrolling CD4+ cells bind the antigen-MHCII complex, undergo activation, and stimulate B cells to form plasma cells that secrete high-affinity IgG. 3. The IgG binds the foreign proteins in the medication, thereby generating immune complexes. When large quantities of immune complexes are rapidly formed, they aggregate and deposit in the skin and joints.  Deposited immune complexes activate the classical complement cascade.  Although this generates the opsonizing protein C3b, which allows the complex to be cleared by phagocytic cells using the C3b receptor, it also generates the highly inflammatory anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a. C3a and C5a are potent chemoattractants that dramatically increase phagocyte recruitment (eg, neutrophils, macrophages) to areas of complex deposition due to effects on the vasculature (eg, vasodilation, increased permeability) and immune cells (eg, increased adhesion molecule expression).  This leads to development of local (eg, skin rash, joint pain/effusion, neutrophilic joint effusion) and systemic (eg, high fever, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate) inflammatory manifestations.  Immune complex injury leads to necrotizing vasculitis (eg, fibrinoid necrosis), and the complexes can sometimes be seen on microscopy (eg, in glomerulonephritis). ## Representative examples Similar to type I hypersensitivity, some type III hypersensitivity reactions lead to generalized/systemic diseases whereas others cause localized disease, depending on the site of immune complex deposition. **Serum sickness** is a classic example of generalized/systemic type III hypersensitivity reaction.  In the 1900s, patients injected with serum from horses immunized with diphtheria toxin developed rash, arthritis, and fever; this condition was due to patient antibodies to horse serum proteins forming complexes with the proteins in the injected serum.  In present-day settings, serum sickness can occur following administration of antigenic heterologous proteins such as chimeric monoclonal antibodies (eg, rituximab and infliximab) or nonhuman immunoglobulins (eg, venom antitoxins).  A serum sickness–like reaction is also associated with the use of certain nonprotein drugs (eg, penicillin, cefaclor, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) ((Table 1)).  Continuous exposure to an antigen can cause chronic immune deposition disease; a representative example is **systemic lupus erythematosus** (which can cause nephritis and arthritis, among other conditions). Local type III hypersensitivity is illustrated by the **Arthus reaction**.  This local, immune complex–mediated area of tissue necrosis in the skin is usually associated with intradermal injection of a vaccine.  Similar to type I hypersensitivity reactions, Arthus reaction can cause localized skin swelling, but this occurs within hours of an exposure (vs immediately with type I hypersensitivity reaction); in addition, it can progress to hemorrhage and ulceration. In **poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis**, IgG antibodies form against nephritogenic antigens expressed by certain strains of group A *Streptococcus*.  These antibodies complex with streptococcal antigens to form immune complexes that are deposited along the glomerular basement membrane.  Subsequent activation of the complement cascade leads to neutrophil recruitment and inflammatory damage to the glomeruli. # Type IV hypersensitivity ## Pathophysiology In type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reactions, CD4+ T cells release cytokines (eg, interferon gamma) that promote macrophage- and **T cell–mediated** tissue damage.  When reexposed to an antigen, previously sensitized T lymphocytes (eg, memory T cells) proliferate and release inflammatory cytokines that promote cell-mediated cytotoxicity (CD8+ T cells) and/or macrophage recruitment and activation.  The resulting tissue damage and swelling is typically evident 24-48 hours after exposure, once sufficient cellular proliferation has occurred. ## Representative examples Allergic contact dermatitis (eg, poison ivy), reactive skin testing (eg, tuberculin skin test, *Candida* extract skin reaction), and granulomatous inflammation are examples of type IV (delayed type) hypersensitivity reactions. **Allergic contact dermatitis** Allergic contact dermatitis (eg, urushiol in poison ivy) occurs in 2 phases: 1. In the sensitization phase, cutaneous Langerhans cells take up haptens (ie, allergens) and present them to naive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the regional lymph nodes, resulting in clonal expansion of hapten-sensitive T cells.  This phase takes 10-14 days and does not result in cutaneous lesions. 2. On reexposure to the hapten, cutaneous antigen-presenting cells present the hapten to sensitized T cells recruited to the skin.  When activated, these T cells mediate tissue damage that manifests as pruritic erythema, vesicles, and/or bullae.  This elicitation phase occurs 2-3 days following reexposure to the hapten. **Tuberculin skin testing** ((Figure 4)) Tuberculin skin testing (eg, purified protein derivative) introduces purified proteins from *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* into the dermis.  Because *M tuberculosis* is primarily countered by the cell-mediated immune response, previously infected patients have primed, antigen-specific CD4+ T lymphocytes that rapidly replicate and mature in response to tuberculin antigen reexposure. T-lymphocyte activation is a 2-step process: 1. T lymphocytes with specific T-cell receptors recognize antigens presented on MHCII on the surface of dendritic cells (eg, antigen-presenting cells). 2. A costimulatory interaction between CD28 on the T lymphocyte and CD80/86 on the dendritic cell allows for activation. Activated CD4+ T lymphocytes release inflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-1, IL-6, TNF alpha) that stimulate/recruit other immune cells and increase vascular permeability, forming an indurated wheal of inflammation following tuberculin skin testing exposure.  Tuberculin reactions appear 24-72 hours after antigen exposure due to delays between initial antigen processing by antigen-presenting cells, T-cell activation, and amplification of the cellular response. **Candida extract skin reaction** ((Figure 5)) Intradermal injection of *Candida* antigens triggers a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which allows for evaluation of the cell-mediated immune response.  Injected *Candida* antigens are taken up by cutaneous antigen-presenting cells, which display the antigens on MHCII molecules to naive CD4+ cells.  These cells are then induced to differentiate into Th1 cells that secrete tumor necrosis factor and interferon-gamma, which recruit and activate macrophages.  The macrophages phagocytose *Candida* antigens and secrete additional inflammatory mediators, producing a cutaneous inflammatory response that appears as an indurated wheal within 24-48 hours.  Because exposure to *Candida* is ubiquitous, all healthy patients have memory T cells against *Candida*.  Failure to generate an appropriate cutaneous response indicates that the cell-mediated immune response is impaired (ie, T-cell anergy). **Morbilliform drug reaction** Morbilliform drug eruption is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction caused by drugs or their metabolites.  It typically manifests 5-21 days following drug initiation, or within 1-3 days after reexposure in previously sensitized patients.  Lesions consist of erythematous papules and macules distributed symmetrically on the trunk and extremities, sometimes accompanied by low-grade fever, pruritis, and eosinophilia.  Unlike Stevens-Johnson syndrome, mucosal involvement (eg, conjunctivae, oropharynx) and skin tenderness are absent.  Common culprit drugs include anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), antibiotics (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), and antiretroviral therapy.  Treatment involves cessation of the offending drug; the rash typically self-resolves within 1-3 weeks. # Summary The 4 main hypersensitivity reactions have distinct immunological mechanisms ((Table 2)).  Type I reactions, mediated by IgE and mast cells, cause immediate allergic responses (eg, anaphylaxis).  Type II reactions involve binding of preformed IgM or IgG antibodies to cell surface antigens, which can cause cell destruction, inflammation, and dysfunction, potentially leading to autoimmune diseases.  Type III reactions arise from immune complex deposition and complement activation, resulting in conditions such as serum sickness.  Type IV reactions are cell-mediated by T cells and take 24-48 hours to develop, as seen in allergic contact dermatitis and tuberculin skin tests.  The mnemonic ACID (type I: **A**llergic/atopic/anaphylactic; type II: **C**ytotoxic/cell-mediated; type III: **I**mmune complex–mediated; type IV: **D**elayed) can be helpful. ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌

articles.title: Homocysteine And Homocystinuria
articles.markdown:
# Homocysteine And Homocystinuria # Introduction Homocysteine is a sulfur-containing intermediary amino acid formed during methionine metabolism.  In normal patients, homocysteine levels remain low because the amino acid is rapidly recycled via remethylation to methionine (requires vitamin B12 and folate) or broken down by transsulfuration to cysteine (requires vitamin B6).  Vitamin (cofactor) deficiency or enzymatic defect can cause homocysteine to accumulate in the blood (hyperhomocysteinemia), increasing the risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events.  The most severe form of impaired homocysteine metabolism (homocystinuria) is associated with multiorgan manifestations (eg, lens dislocation, marfanoid body habitus, developmental delay, thrombotic events) that begin in infancy or early childhood. # Homocysteine formation Homocysteine is generated from methionine via a 3-step process ((Figure 1)), as follows: - **Methionine → S-adenosyl methionine** (SAM) is a rate-limiting, magnesium- and energy-dependent step that primes SAM to become a **methyl donor** for a wide variety of reactions. - SAM → S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) is the key enzymatic step of this pathway marked by the donation of a methyl group from SAM to an acceptor molecule, such as: - Nucleic acids for gene silencing in epigenetics (DNA) or regulation of protein translation (RNA). - Proteins for regulating gene expression via histone methylation. - Small molecules (eg, creatine) and lipids (eg, phosphatidylcholine) as part of energy metabolism and cell membrane production. - Neurotransmitters (eg, epinephrine, melatonin, dopamine) as part of synthesis or deactivation. - SAH → **homocysteine** + adenosine is the final step of the process, decreasing SAH to prevent competitive inhibition of the SAM → SAH step.  Elevated homocysteine levels exert a negative feedback loop on this cycle via the buildup of SAH (which then inhibits the conversion of SAM → SAH).Homocysteine is potentially toxic at elevated levels and is metabolized through the remethylation and transsulfuration pathways. # Homocysteine metabolism Homocysteine can be recycled to methionine via remethylation or broken down into cysteine via transsulfuration. ## Remethylation pathway Homocysteine can be recycled back to methionine via remethylation. The **methionine synthase** pathway, ubiquitous in cells, is considered the primary recycling mechanism.  It uses the active form of **folate** (5-methyltetrahydrofolate \[5-MTHF\]) as a methyl donor, with **vitamin B****12** as a cofactor.  Genetic polymorphisms that reduce the generation of 5-MTHF from tetrahydrofolate, via alterations in the enzyme **methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR)**, are associated with hyperhomocysteinemia. A backup pathway that converts homocysteine to methionine without requiring folate or vitamin B12 relies on betaine–homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT).  BHMT is primarily active in the liver and kidneys and is absent in the heart and brain. ## Transsulfuration pathway Homocysteine can also be broken down into cystathionine and then cysteine via a 2-step process, as follows: - **Homocysteine** → cystathionine is mediated by **cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS)**, which requires **vitamin B****6** as a cofactor and is stimulated by the accumulation of SAM (ie, sufficient methyl donors from the methionine cycle). - Cystathionine → **cysteine** is mediated by an enzyme (cystathionase) that also requires vitamin B6 as a cofactor. Cysteine plays many important roles in metabolism, including: - Precursor for glutathione, an important antioxidant. - Disulfide bridges in complex proteins. - Precursor for coenzyme A, a cofactor required for the Krebs cycle. - Precursor for taurine, a crucial amino acid in the heart/retina and for bile salt conjugation. # Hyperhomocysteinemia Hyperhomocysteinemia is a common disorder (up to 5%-10% of the population) characterized by elevated homocysteine levels in the blood.  It is typically caused by a **vitamin** (cofactor) **deficiency** or a **genetic enzyme deficit**, which impairs homocysteine metabolism. ## Impaired remethylation - **Folate or vitamin B****12** **deficiency**:  A folate metabolite (5-MTHF) and vitamin B12 are required for methionine synthase activity. - **MTHFR polymorphisms** (**most common genetic** cause of hyperhomocysteinemia):  MTHFR converts tetrahydrofolate to 5-MTHF, which is a required precursor for methionine synthase.  A large percentage of the population (up to 30%) has a genetic polymorphism that makes MTHFR work poorly at elevated temperatures (thermolabile), leading to moderate hyperhomocysteinemia. - Methionine synthase deficiency (very rare):  Because methionine synthase is the primary enzyme that recycles homocysteine to methionine, genetic deficiency of methionine synthase is associated with marked elevations of blood and urine homocysteine (homocystinuria). ## Impaired transsulfuration - **Vitamin B****6** **deficiency**:  Vitamin B6 is a required cofactor for both enzymatic steps in transsulfuration. - **CBS deficiency**:  CBS drives the first enzymatic step in the conversion of homocysteine to cysteine.  CBS deficiency is the most common cause of **homocystinuria** (discussed in the next section), which is marked by massive elevation of homocysteine in the blood and urine. Elevations in plasma homocysteine can also be seen in chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance/impaired metabolism), as a medication adverse effect (eg, fibrates, nicotinic acid, metformin, methotrexate), and with cigarette smoking. ## Clinical consequences: Hyperhomocysteinemia and vascular injury Elevated homocysteine levels are associated with vascular injury (eg, intimal thickening, smooth muscle hypertrophy, elastic lamina disruption), possibly due to oxidative stress (which damages endothelial cells), direct endothelial toxicity, impaired nitric oxide signaling, and increased platelet activation. These effects promote a prothrombotic state, leading to an increased risk for coronary artery disease, venous thromboembolism, and ischemic stroke.  In some individuals, elevated homocysteine levels contribute to premature cardiovascular disease, particularly when traditional risk factors are absent.  However, lowering homocysteine levels has not been shown to reliably prevent cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or thrombotic events; therefore, routine testing of homocysteine levels is not typically undertaken as part of the prevention or treatment of these conditions. # Homocystinuria Homocystinuria is a rare group of genetic diseases characterized by massively elevated homocysteine levels in the blood, leading to spillover in the urine.  The most common cause is an **autosomal recessive** mutation in **CBS**.  Because this enzyme blocks the homocysteine transsulfuration pathway, its deficiency prevents conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine, leading to elevated homocysteine and methionine levels.  Homocystinuria is also seen with deficiency of methionine synthase (very rare), leading to impaired homocysteine remethylation. ## Clinical consequences: Pleiotropy Homocystinuria is a more severe and consequential form of hyperhomocysteinemia that affects multiple organ systems due to the toxic effects of homocysteine on connective tissue, vascular structures, and the nervous system.  The disease illustrates the genetic principle of pleiotropy, in which a mutation in a single gene produces diverse, unrelated phenotypic traits affecting multiple organ systems.  It typically presents in infancy or early childhood with significant abnormalities, including: - **Skeletal abnormalities**:  Patients often develop skeletal findings resembling those seen in connective tissue disorders.  Many are tall with long fingers (arachnodactyly) and may have a sunken or protruding chest (pectus excavatum/carinatum).  These features produce a marfanoid appearance, although the underlying molecular defect differs from that seen in Marfan syndrome. - **Ectopia lentis**:  A hallmark ocular finding is ectopia lentis, in which the lens of the eye becomes displaced or dislocated (most often downward and inward) due to weakened or broken zonular fibers.  This results in visual impairment (eg, myopia, astigmatism, diplopia) at a young age. - **Developmental delay**:  Patients frequently have intellectual impairment and may have seizures.  Risk is reduced with early treatment. - **Thrombotic events**:  **Thromboembolism** is the **leading cause of death** in patients with homocystinuria and may occur at an early age.  Strokes or myocardial infarction can occur in adolescents or young adults due to damage to the endothelium from massively elevated homocysteine levels. ## Differentiation from Marfan syndrome Because homocystinuria and Marfan syndrome both present with tall stature, skeletal abnormalities, and lens dislocation, the conditions share a differential diagnosis ((Table 1)).  However, homocystinuria typically has downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability/developmental delay, and increased risk of thromboembolism.  In contrast, Marfan syndrome is typically associated with upward lens dislocation (due to stretched, rather than broken, zonules), no significant thrombotic risk, and progressive aortic root dilation. # Treatment Treatment of classic homocystinuria (CBS deficiency) includes the following: - **Vitamin B****6**:  Approximately 50% of patients respond to high doses of vitamin B6, which stimulates partially active CBS.  This alone may be enough to control homocysteine levels in these cases. - **Low-methionine diet**:  Reducing dietary intake of methionine limits the amount of homocysteine produced.  Patients must avoid or strictly limit meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts, and beans; instead, they are given a "methionine-free" medical formula that contains the other 19 essential amino acids. - **Cysteine supplementation**:  Because cysteine cannot be generated from homocysteine in most patients with homocystinuria, supplementation with cysteine (an essential amino acid) is required. - **Supplements to increase homocysteine remethylation:** - **Betaine supplementation**:  Betaine supplementation increases homocysteine recycling to methionine via the BHMT pathway (does not require vitamin B12 or folate). - **Vitamin B****12****/folate supplementation**:  Supplementation with these cofactors may increase conversion of homocysteine to methionine via the methionine synthase pathway. Early initiation of these therapies helps limit or delay disease manifestations.  Therefore, testing should be undertaken as soon as possible, and genetic counseling should be provided for first-degree relatives of those who are affected. Enzyme replacement therapy and gene therapy may someday provide more durable interventions. # Summary Homocysteine is an intermediate amino acid produced during methionine metabolism.  In normal patients, homocysteine is rapidly recycled via remethylation to methionine (requires vitamin B12 and folate) or is broken down by transsulfuration to cysteine (requires vitamin B6).  Disruption of these pathways (eg, vitamin deficiency, enzyme defect) leads to the accumulation of homocysteine in the blood.  Hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with an increased risk of cerebrovascular and cardiovascular events; however, lowering homocysteine levels does not seem to reduce the risk (nonmodifiable risk factor). The most severe form of impaired homocysteine metabolism is homocystinuria.  It is caused primarily by an autosomal recessive gene mutation in cystathionine beta-synthase, which prevents conversion of homocysteine to cysteine.  Patients typically have multiorgan manifestations (eg, lens dislocation, marfanoid body habitus, thrombotic events) that begin in childhood.  Early interventions to decrease homocysteine levels, such as a vitamin B6 challenge, methionine-free diet, cysteine supplementation, and stimulation of the remethylation pathway, can reduce or delay symptoms. ​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​

Differential diagnosis of Marfanoid body habitus

Diagnosis

Overlapping features

Distinguishing features

Marfan syndrome

  • Pectus deformity
  • Tall stature
    • ↑ Arm/height ratio
    • ↓ Upper/lower segment ratio
  • Arachnodactyly
  • Joint hyperlaxity
  • Scoliosis
  • Autosomal dominant
  • Normal intellect
  • Aortic root dilation
  • Upward lens dislocation

Homocystinuria

  • Autosomal recessive
  • Intellectual disability
  • Thrombosis
  • Downward lens dislocation
  • Megaloblastic anemia
  • Fair complexion

articles.title: HIV Lifecycle
articles.markdown: # HIV Lifecycle # Introduction The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) primarily targets and destroys the immune system's CD4 T cells.  As a retrovirus, HIV carries its genetic information in RNA, which is reverse-transcribed into DNA on infection.  This process allows the virus to integrate its genetic material into the host cell's DNA, establishing a persistent infection that weakens the immune system and predisposes to opportunistic infections and malignancies. # Modes of transmission HIV is primarily transmitted through the exchange of body fluids.  The most common routes of transmission include: - **Sexual transmission**:  Unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral sex is the most common mode of transmission.  The risk for sexual transmission is greatest when mucosal disruption is present.  The risk for transmission with vaginal intercourse is lower than with receptive anal intercourse (virus passage through the thin rectal epithelium). - **Parenteral transmission**:  This includes transmission via blood or blood products (eg, needle sharing), transfusion of contaminated blood products (rare), and needlestick injuries in health care settings. - **Vertical transmission**:  Vertical transmission from an HIV-infected mother to her child can occur during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding.  Without intervention, the risk for mother-to-child transmission is significant, but it can be reduced to less than 2% with effective antiretroviral therapy  (ART) and appropriate perinatal care. Other less common modes of transmission include organ transplantation from an infected donor. # HIV lifecycle ## Binding and fusion For HIV to infect a CD4 T cell, viral envelope **glycoprotein gp120** must bind to both a CD4 molecule and a chemokine receptor (eg, **CXCR4**, **CCR5**) on the surface of the T cell ((Figure 1)).  Binding of gp120 to these receptors induces a conformational change that exposes the virus's underlying transmembrane **glycoprotein gp41**.  This mediates fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane, allowing the viral core to enter the cell. ## Reverse transcription and integration Once the HIV virion enters the host cell, viral RNA is released from the nucleocapsid and transcribed into double-stranded DNA by the viral **reverse transcriptase** enzyme (which grows DNA by adding nucleotides to the terminal 3′-hydroxyl group using a 3′-5′ phosphodiester bond).  The DNA then enters the nucleus and, through the actions of viral integrase, permanently inserts into the host cell's chromosomes to become a provirus. The host cell's RNA polymerase II transcribes viral mRNA from the proviral DNA.  Once synthesized, HIV mRNA exits through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where it uses the host cell's ribosomes to translate the enzymes, glycoproteins, structural proteins, and regulatory proteins needed to promote viral replication and transmission.  The full-length mRNA also serves as the viral genome that is packaged into newly synthesized virions. ## Transcription and translation The HIV genome contains 3 major structural genes (*env*, *gag*, and *pol*) that are transcribed as polycistronic mRNA, translated as polyproteins, and subsequently cleaved by host or viral protease into the individual proteins that comprise the HIV virus. - The ***env*** **gene** encodes the polyprotein gp160, which is glycosylated in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body and subsequently cleaved into the mature envelope proteins gp120 and gp41.  These proteins form the glycoprotein spikes on the surface of the HIV virus and are essential for viral attachment and fusion. - The ***pol*** **gene** encodes the major HIV enzymes reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease. - Reverse transcriptase converts the HIV RNA genome into complementary double-stranded DNA and destroys the HIV RNA genomic template during transcription (ribonuclease H activity). - Integrase inserts complementary viral DNA into the host chromosome. - Protease cleaves HIV polyproteins (*gag*\-*pol* gene products) into functional viral proteins (*env* gene products are cleaved by host protease). - The ***gag*** **gene** encodes a polyprotein that is then cleaved to produce the matrix, capsid, and nucleocapsid protein, among others. ## Viral assembly and release Viral assembly then occurs at the host cell surface, along with budding.  The envelope proteins (gp120, gp41) are expressed on the host cell surface, and a complex of the nucleocapsid, viral RNA, and viral proteins (gag and pol polyproteins) buds from the surface.  Further assembly then occurs once the virus is free from the host cell. # Antiretroviral therapy (ART) ART targets different phases of the HIV lifecycle.  Major classes include nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non–nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), integrase inhibitors (INSTIs), and others.  They are described in more detail in a separate article. # Latent reservoir Following infection with HIV, a latent viral reservoir develops, which can be considered in molecular and anatomical terms: - **Molecular**:  Latent HIV exists primarily as a genomically integrated viral DNA (a provirus), embedded randomly throughout the host nuclear genome.  Insertion into the genome is accomplished by integrase and occurs during the earliest stages of infection (ie, within days of acute HIV). - **Anatomical**:  A range of organs and cell types serves as depots for latently integrated HIV.  The majority of the latent HIV resides within lymphoid tissue, especially the lymph nodes, lymphatic vasculature, and gut- and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.  Other important anatomic/cellular reservoirs include the CNS (astrocytes, microglia) and lungs (alveolar macrophages). Because reservoir cells may be long-lived (brain astrocytes have extremely slow turnover), complete replacement of all infected cells is highly unlikely to occur within the patient's lifespan.  ART can only suppress production and infective spread of new HIV particles; it cannot eliminate the latent reservoir.  In addition, rebound of HIV viremia and subsequent propagation to new reservoir sites is inevitable if ART is discontinued. # Viral load Viral load measurements in blood (quantity of HIV RNA measured by PCR) are a key marker of disease progression and treatment efficacy.  Higher viral loads, particularly during the acute and late stages of infection, are associated with increased transmissibility.  Conversely, effective ART can suppress viral replication to undetectable levels ("Undetectable = Untransmittable" \[U=U\]).  Regular monitoring of viral load helps assess the effectiveness of ART and guides therapeutic decisions.  A sustained undetectable viral load is the primary goal of ART and is associated with improved clinical outcomes, including reduced risk for opportunistic infections and lower morbidity and mortality. # Summary HIV is a retrovirus that primarily targets and destroys the immune system's CD4 T cells.  Its lifecycle involves intricate processes of viral entry, integration, replication, and assembly, relying on host and viral enzymes, including reverse transcriptase, protease, and integrase.  The HIV genome contains 3 major structural genes (*env*, *gag*, and *pol*).  Antiretroviral agents such as nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors, non–nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, and integrase inhibitors disrupt specific steps in the lifecycle.  However, achieving complete eradication of the virus is difficult given the latent reservoir of the virus. ​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌

articles.title: Histology: Epithelial Tissue
articles.markdown:
# Histology: Epithelial Tissue # Introduction Epithelial tissues cover external surfaces, line internal spaces, and form the secretory units of glands.  Each epithelial cell has an apical surface facing a lumen or an external environment and a basal surface attached to underlying connective tissue.  This polarity facilitates the function of epithelial tissues as selective barriers, exchange interfaces, and secretion or absorption structures. # Polarity Cell polarity refers to a functional asymmetry that organizes the cell membrane into distinct regions specialized for different tasks.  Epithelial cells have apical-basal (or luminal-basal) polarity, which distinguishes the surface facing the lumen from the surface attached to an underlying structure called the basement membrane.  The mechanical cohesion and barrier integrity of epithelial cells rely on junctional structures that link neighboring cells and anchor them to the basement membrane. ## Apical membrane The apical membrane (ie, facing the lumen or external environment) of epithelial cells often contains specialized structures that enhance absorption or transport.  These include the following: - **Microvilli** are actin-based membrane projections that increase apical surface area.  They are prominent in absorptive epithelia, such as the intestinal mucosa (eg, intestinal brush border ((Figure 1))) and renal proximal tubule. - **Cilia** ((Figure 2)) are microtubule-based projections that produce coordinated beating motions.  Motile cilia contain a characteristic 9 + 2 microtubule arrangement (circular array of 9 microtubule doublets surrounding 2 central microtubules) and move fluid or particles across epithelial surfaces, as in the respiratory tract and uterine tubes. - **Stereocilia** are long, actin-based projections that resemble microvilli but are much longer.  They are found in the epididymis and function primarily in absorption. ## Basolateral membrane The basolateral membrane contains transporters, receptors, and adhesion molecules that interact with underlying tissues.  This polarity enables directional transport of molecules. ## Basement membrane The basement membrane is a thin extracellular layer that separates epithelium from underlying connective tissue.  Its components include: - **Basal lamina**:  Produced by epithelial cells and composed primarily of type IV collagen, laminin, and proteoglycans. - **Reticular lamina**:  Derived from underlying connective tissue and composed mainly of type III collagen. These anchor epithelial cells and regulate cell polarity and differentiation.  The basement membrane provides structural support and can serve for biochemical signaling or as a filtration barrier in specialized tissues (eg, glomerulus) ((Figure 3)). ## Junctional structures Key junctional structures include ((Figure 4)): - Tight junctions form a continuous apical seal, creating an impermeable barrier to diffusion. - Adherens junctions form a belt just beneath tight junctions, providing a dynamic (ie, calcium-dependent) but strong link between cells. - Desmosomes form discrete spot-like junctions that anchor the lateral surfaces of adjacent cells together, providing tensile strength. - Hemidesmosomes (fixed) and focal adhesion complexes (transient) attach the basal cell surface to the basement membrane. - Gap junctions enable direct cytoplasmic exchange for synchronized electrical and metabolic activity (eg, heart contraction). They are described in more detail in a separate article. # Classification: Cell layers and shapes Epithelia are classified based on the number of layers and the shape of the epithelial cells ((Figure 5)). ## Cell layers - **Simple epithelium**:  Composed of a single cell layer.  Because all cells contact the basement membrane, this organization is optimized for absorption, secretion, and exchange - **Stratified epithelium**:  Composed of multiple layers.  The different layers provide mechanical protection in areas exposed to friction or stress. ## Cell shape This organization is based on the shape of the **superficial layer** of cells: - **Squamous**:  Flattened cells with thin cytoplasm that facilitates diffusion. - **Cuboidal**:  Cells with approximately equal height and width, typically involved in secretion or absorption. - **Columnar**:  Tall cells specialized for absorption, secretion, or mucus production. The combination of these categories based on the number of layers and shape leads to the classic epithelial categories: - Simple squamous epithelium in the alveoli, optimized for gas exchange and diffusion. - Simple columnar epithelium in the intestine, optimized for secretion or absorption. - Stratified squamous epithelium in the epidermis or vagina ((Image 1)), optimized for mechanical protection. An additional characteristic could describe whether the superficial layer has keratin or not. ## Special classifications - **Pseudostratified epithelium** appears multilayered; however, all cells contact the basement membrane, but not all reach the surface.  This organization is often associated with specialized apical structures such as cilia. - **Transitional epithelium**, or urothelium, is a stratified epithelium that can distend and is found in the lower urinary tract. ## Transformation (metaplasia) Certain epithelial cells can convert from one type to another, typically as an adaptive mechanism in response to a stimulus or stress.  Most commonly, columnar-to-squamous epithelium can occur in normal pseudostratified columnar respiratory epithelium in response to smoking ((Figure 6)) or in cervical epithelium in response to infection.  Squamous-to-columnar metaplasia can occur in Barrett esophagus, in which chronic reflux esophagitis can trigger the replacement of normal squamous epithelium in the distal esophagus with metaplastic columnar epithelium ((Image 2)). ## Special naming conventions The epithelial lining of blood and lymph vessels is called **endothelium** ((Figure 7)), that of heart ventricles and atria is called **endocardium**, and that covering closed body cavities (abdominal, pericardial, pleural) is called **mesothelium**. # Epithelial renewal Epithelial tissues undergo continuous renewal because surface cells are exposed to mechanical and environmental stress.  Proliferation occurs in a basal population of stem or progenitor cells attached to the basement membrane.  Older cells migrate toward the surface and eventually undergo apoptosis or are shed. The rate of renewal varies widely.  Intestinal epithelium turns over within days, whereas epidermal keratinocytes in the skin differentiate and reach the surface over several weeks.  This renewal capacity allows epithelial tissues to maintain barrier function despite constant environmental stress (trauma, injury). # Epithelial glands Epithelia also form **glands**, structures specialized for secretion, by invaginating into underlying connective tissue and forming secretory units that retain epithelial characteristics. Two major categories are recognized:  exocrine and endocrine. ## Exocrine glands Exocrine glands ((Figure 8)) secrete products onto epithelial surfaces through ducts (eg, sweat glands, salivary glands).  They are classified as mucous (mucus secretions) or serous (watery, protein-rich secretions), with 3 mechanisms of secretion: merocrine, apocrine, and holocrine ((Table 1)). Exocrine glands can be unicellular (eg, goblet cells in the intestine) or multicellular and simple (unbranched duct) or compound (branched duct).  Depending on the shape of the secretory portion, the gland can be tubular (shaped like a tube), alveolar/acinar (shaped like a flask), or tubuloalveolar (shaped like a sac). ## Endocrine glands Endocrine glands do not have ducts and release hormones directly into the bloodstream, with the target receptor on distant cells ((Figure 9)). Secretory cells often show specialized cytologic features reflecting their products.  For example, protein-secreting cells contain abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, whereas corticosteroid-secreting cells have extensive smooth endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets. # Summary Epithelial tissues cover external surfaces, line internal spaces, and form glands.  Their structure is defined by apical-basal polarity, which organizes the membrane into regions facing the lumen and the underlying connective tissue.  Junctional complexes maintain cohesion and barrier integrity, whereas the basement membrane anchors epithelial cells and provides structural support and signaling.  Epithelia are classified by cell layering and the shape of superficial cells, producing types adapted for diffusion, absorption, secretion, or protection.  Through invagination into connective tissue, epithelial cells also form exocrine and endocrine glands specialized for secretion.  Continuous renewal from basal progenitor cells maintains epithelial integrity despite ongoing environmental stress, allowing epithelial tissues to function as barriers, regulate permeability, absorb nutrients and fluids, secrete substances, and transport material across surfaces. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​

articles.title: Glycogen Storage Diseases
articles.markdown: # Glycogen Storage Diseases # Introduction Glycogen storage diseases are inherited metabolic disorders characterized by defects in the enzymes involved in glycogen metabolism, resulting in abnormal storage and utilization of glycogen in various tissues.  These diseases vary in severity, age of onset, and organ involvement. # Normal glycogen metabolism Glycogenolysis is the process by which glycogen, a branched polysaccharide that is primarily stored in the liver and skeletal muscle, is cleaved into glucose for energy use.  Glycogenolysis involves the following steps: - **Shortening of chains**:  Glycogen phosphorylase sequentially cleaves α-1,4-glycosidic bonds between glucose residues, producing glucose 1-phosphate, until only 4 glucose residues remain before a branch point.  These 4-unit structures are known as limit dextrins, and glycogen phosphorylase cannot continue cleaving beyond this point. - **Removal of branches**:  From here, debranching enzyme transfers 3 of the 4 glucose residues to a nearby branch.  Debranching enzyme then removes the single remaining glucose residue, producing free glucose.  This allows the chain to be further shortened by glycogen phosphorylase. - **Conversion of glucose 1-phosphate to glucose** ((Figure 1)):  First, glucose 1-phosphate is converted to glucose 6-phosphate by the enzyme phosphoglucomutase.  Next, glucose 6-phosphate is converted to glucose by the enzyme glucose 6-phosphatase, which is expressed in the liver, kidneys, and intestines. - **Degradation by lysosomes**:  Approximately 1% of glycogen is continuously metabolized in lysosomes by the enzyme acid α-glucosidase.  This enzyme is particularly active in cells with relatively higher concentrations of cytoplasmic glycogen (eg, hepatocytes, myocytes). Defects in the enzymes of these metabolic pathways can impair glycogenolysis, resulting in glycogen storage diseases ((Figure 2)). # Glycogen storage disease types There are several types of glycogen storage diseases with various presentations.  The most common glycogen storage diseases demonstrate an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. ## Type V (McArdle disease) Type V (McArdle disease) occurs due to a defect in **glycogen phosphorylase**.  There are 3 isoforms of this enzyme: the skeletal muscle form, the brain form, and the liver form.  McArdle disease occurs due to a defect in only the **skeletal muscle form** (ie, myophosphorylase); the other isoforms are unaffected. The disease impairs glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle, and its clinical features include: - **Exercise intolerance**:  Patients typically present in adolescence and early adulthood with extreme muscle weakness and cramping after exercise.  Symptoms classically improve after a brief period of rest (ie, second wind phenomenon), which may be explained by increased blood flow and delivery of free fatty acids to the muscle for energy. - **No increase in serum lactate**:  Serum lactate does not increase following strenuous exercise because no glucose 6-phosphate is generated to undergo glycolysis. - **Normal serum glucose levels**:  Because the liver isoform of glycogen phosphorylase is unaffected, glycogenolysis occurs normally in the liver and patients do not develop hypoglycemia. - Rhabdomyolysis:  Strenuous exercise can lead to rhabdomyolysis, resulting in myoglobinuria (eg, red urine) that can progress to renal failure. Patients are advised to consume simple carbohydrates (eg, sucrose) prior to physical activity.  These carbohydrates are rapidly digested into monosaccharides, which can be directly utilized by muscles for energy, bypassing myophosphorylase. ## Type III (Cori disease) Type III (Cori disease) occurs due to a defect in **debranching enzyme**.  Without it, abnormal-appearing glycogen structures accumulate, containing stubby outer branches (limit dextrins) due to incomplete glycogen trimming. Patients present in infancy with hypoglycemia, ketoacidosis, and hepatomegaly due to accumulation of limit dextrins, which can lead to hepatic fibrosis.  Patients also develop weakness and hypotonia due to muscle involvement. Management includes frequent oral glucose loading (eg, uncooked cornstarch, a glucose polymer that is slowly metabolized into monomers in the intestine before being absorbed) to prevent hypoglycemia. ## Type I (von Gierke disease) Type I (von Gierke disease) occurs due to a defect in **glucose 6-phosphatase**, which is expressed primarily in the liver, kidneys, and intestinal mucosa.  Without this enzyme, glucose 6-phosphate cannot be converted to glucose, and patients develop severe hypoglycemia. The clinical presentation includes: - **Severe fasting hypoglycemia**:  Occurs due to impaired release of free glucose from glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis.  - **Lactic acidosis** and **hyperlipidemia**:  Excess glucose 6-phosphate is shunted to the glycolytic pathway, resulting in increased lactic acid production ((Figure 3)).  In addition, excess glucose 6-phosphate stimulates de novo triacylglycerol synthesis via acetyl-CoA, resulting in hypertriglyceridemia. - **No improvement with fructose and galactose**:  Because fructose and galactose metabolism also involve glucose 6-phosphatase, supplementation does not improve hypoglycemia. - Hepatomegaly and renal enlargement:  Occurs due to massive accumulation of glycogen in the liver and kidneys. - Unique physical features:  Include a **doll-like face** with rounded cheeks and thin extremities.  Hepatomegaly and renal enlargement occur due to massive accumulation of glycogen in the liver and kidneys.  Failure to thrive and short stature are also common. Management includes frequent oral glucose loading (eg, uncooked cornstarch) to prevent hypoglycemia.  Patients are also advised to avoid foods containing fructose or galactose.  Lactic acidosis and hypertriglyceridemia generally improve in patients who maintain euglycemia. ## Type II (Pompe disease) Type II (Pompe disease) occurs due to a defect in **acid α-glucosidase**.  Glycogen accumulates in lysosomes, particularly in the liver, heart, and muscle ((Image 1)).  Pompe disease is the only glycogen storage disease caused by a defect in a lysosomal enzyme. In the classic form of Pompe disease, patients present in early infancy with **generalized hypotonia** and cardiomegaly (due to **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**).  In addition, patients develop macroglossia and hepatomegaly.  Death usually occurs in infancy. However, because glucose can still be produced from glycogen, patients have **normal glucose levels**, which differentiates this condition from other glycogen storage diseases. Management involves supportive care and enzyme replacement therapy, which can improve symptoms and survival. # Diagnosis Diagnosis of a glycogen storage disease involves a thorough history and physical examination, with particular attention to signs of liver (eg, hepatomegaly), muscle (eg, hypotonia), and cardiac involvement.  Initial laboratory evaluation typically includes serum glucose, lactate, uric acid, lipids, creatine kinase, and liver enzymes (eg, AST, ALT).  In addition, periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains carbohydrates and can stain excess glycogen in hepatocytes or myocytes. Enzyme assays may be performed to measure enzyme activity.  Of note, the enzyme assay for Pompe disease is included in many newborn screening programs.  Further evaluation depends on the suspected disease, and genetic testing is generally performed to identify the underlying mutation. # Summary Glycogen storage diseases are inherited metabolic disorders that are characterized by defects in the enzymes involved in glycogen metabolism, resulting in the abnormal storage and utilization of glycogen in various tissues.  These diseases vary in severity, age of onset, and organ involvement.  Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential for a favorable outcome. ​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌
