articles.title: Genetics: DNA Damage And Repair
articles.markdown: # Genetics: DNA Damage And Repair # Introduction DNA is a double-stranded molecule made of paired nucleotide bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C).  DNA is continuously damaged by environmental radiation, chemical agents, and endogenous reactive oxygen species from normal metabolism.  Unrepaired damage can be passed on during replication, becoming a mutation (permanent change in the nucleotide sequence).  Cells rely on multiple DNA repair pathways to correct damage before it becomes fixed as a mutation.  Inherited defects in these pathways are responsible for numerous cancer syndromes. # Types of DNA damage DNA damage can range from subtle base modifications and single strand breaks (SSBs) to severe double strand breaks (DSBs).  In this section, damage is listed from relatively minor to more severe. ## Base mismatch Normal DNA base pairing is G:C and A:T.  However, during DNA replication, an incorrect nucleotide is inserted for approximately 1 in every 10 million bases copied, resulting in a mismatched pair (eg, G:T, A:C).  Most mismatches are corrected in real time by the **proofreading** function of DNA polymerase ((Figure 1)).  However, a very small percentage escape proofreading and subsequent repair processes, leading to a mutation that is passed on to daughter cells. In addition to the accidental mismatches above, incorrect base pairing also occurs when the template base has preexisting damage or modification (discussed next).  Such altered bases pair incorrectly in a way that evades DNA polymerase proofreading and are highly likely to become permanent mutations if not corrected prior to replication. ## Base modification A low level of damage to DNA bases always occurs due to spontaneous hydrolysis, normal cellular metabolism (eg, reactive oxygen species), and environmental exposures (eg, ultraviolet \[UV\] radiation).  There are 4 principal types of base damage: - A base can become **oxidized** (due to reactive oxygen species from normal metabolism) and mispair with the wrong partner base during DNA replication.  For example, guanine can be oxidized to 8-oxoguanine, which mispairs with adenine instead of cytosine. - A base can become **alkylated** (eg, due to environmental carcinogens) and mispair with the wrong base during DNA replication.  For example, guanine can be alkylated to O6\-methylguanine, which mispairs with thymine instead of cytosine. - Cytosine can be **deaminated** (eg, due to spontaneous hydrolysis), which converts it to **uracil**. - An **abasic (AP) site** can form when the base is lost due to spontaneous hydrolysis, leaving behind an empty space in the DNA backbone.  This apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site is mutagenic because it lacks base-pairing information, leading to random incorporation of A, T, G, or C during replication. ## Single strand break In addition to damage affecting the bases, the DNA backbone itself can also be broken by oxidative stress, ionizing radiation, or certain drugs (eg, topoisomerase I inhibitors).  If only one strand is affected, the lesion is referred to as an SSB.  Although the DNA is still held intact by the opposite strand, SSBs must be repaired quickly or they risk converting to much more serious DSBs during replication.  Repair is not as simple as sealing the nick because most SSBs have "dirty ends" (eg, dangling phosphate or hydroxyl groups) that DNA ligase cannot join.  Specialized end-processing enzymes are needed (eg, to trim back the termini), after which DNA polymerase and ligase restore the sequence using the complementary strand as a template. ## Double strand break If both sides of the DNA backbone are cleaved at the same location, a DSB is formed.  DSBs are among the most dangerous forms of DNA damage because the chromosome becomes discontinuous, often leading to **rearrangements** and **deletions**.  Because the complementary strand is also damaged, it is no longer available to guide repair. ## Helix-distorting lesions DNA has a helical structure because of its double stranded nature.  Helix-distorting lesions severely kink or lock DNA.  They include the following: - **Intrastrand crosslinks** are covalent bonds formed between adjacent bases on the same DNA strand, most often G-G or G-A.  They are typically induced by platinum chemotherapy (eg, cisplatin).  These crosslinks introduce a local bend in the helix. - **Thymine dimers** are a special case of intrastrand crosslink formed by covalent bonding of adjacent thymines.  They are exclusively induced by **UV-B** radiation.  The T-T dimer introduces a sharp kink in the helix. - **Interstrand crosslinks** are covalent bonds formed between complementary bases on opposite DNA strands, gluing the double helix shut. These lesions interfere with DNA replication and transcription because the normal polymerases are unable to traverse them due to steric hindrance.  To overcome this, cells use specialized translesion polymerases that bind DNA more loosely; this allows for successful replication but is more error prone.  As a result, helix-distorting lesions can be mutagenic. # Single strand repair mechanisms Single stranded lesions include: - Base modifications. - SSBs. - Intrastrand crosslinks and thymine (T-T) dimers. For these lesions, the **complementary strand** is unaffected and can be used as a template for repair. ## Base excision repair Base excision repair (BER) is a process that corrects **small, non–helix-distorting lesions** such as oxidized bases, alkylated bases, deaminated cytosine, and AP sites.  The damaged base is simply removed and replaced ((Figure 2)).  Briefly, a DNA glycosylase recognizes and excises the damaged base, leaving an AP site.  An AP endonuclease cleaves the DNA backbone at the AP site.  Then, DNA polymerase beta inserts the correct nucleotide.  Finally, DNA ligase seals the nick. **MUTYH-associated polyposis** is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the activity of DNA glycosylase (first step of the BER pathway).  Affected patients develop hundreds of colorectal adenomas and have an increased risk of colorectal cancer.  The phenotype is relatively milder compared to other colorectal cancer syndromes (such as mismatch repair \[MMR\] defects or familial adenomatous polyposis) because the underlying type of damage is less severe. ## Nucleotide excision repair Nucleotide excision repair (NER) removes intrastrand crosslinks (eg, **T-T dimers** from UV-B radiation) and other single strand bulky adducts.  In NER, DNA damage is recognized by detecting distortions in the DNA helix throughout the genome (or by sensing stalled transcription machinery at active genes).  The entire nucleotide (base + backbone) must be removed and replaced ((Figure 3)).  Briefly, a dual incision is created by endonucleases (XPA, XPG).  The damaged segment is removed.  Next, DNA polymerase delta resynthesizes DNA to fill the gap, and DNA ligase seals the nicks. **Xeroderma pigmentosum** is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in NER genes (*XPA*, *XPG*), leading to extreme UV sensitivity and early-onset skin cancers (eg, multiple squamous cell carcinomas in childhood). ## Mismatch repair MMR corrects base mismatches that escape proofreading during replication.  The complementary strand is used to restore the correct sequence ((Figure 4)).  Briefly, the mismatch is recognized by specialized complexes (eg, MSH2-MSH6).  Next, endonucleases (eg, MLH-PMS2) are directed to the replicating (new) strand to remove the mispaired base.  Finally, as with NER, DNA polymerase delta resynthesizes DNA to fill the gap, and DNA ligase seals the nicks. Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (**HNPCC**, or **Lynch syndrome**) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in MMR genes (eg, *MSH2*, *MLH1*, *PMS2*).  Patients have a markedly elevated lifetime colorectal cancer risk (eg, 50% by age 50) and are also predisposed to gastric, ovarian, endometrial, and several other malignancies.  MMR impairment greatly increases the rate of frameshift mutation, resulting in the formation of large quantities of neoantigens not seen in healthy cells.  These neoantigens are displayed on class I major histocompatibility complexes on the cancer cell surface, leading to the activation of a diverse, polyclonal pool of antitumor cytotoxic T cells; tumors are therefore particularly dependent on adaptations (eg, overexpression of immune checkpoints) to avoid cytotoxic T-cell destruction.  Adenomatous polyps are paradoxically few in HNPCC (unlike with BER), likely because the extensive genomic damage with MMR enables rapid progression directly to carcinoma. # Double strand repair mechanisms DSBs can be repaired by nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR) ((Figure 5)). ## Nonhomologous end joining NHEJ directly ligates the broken DNA ends back together.  A template is not required.  Briefly, specific protein complexes (eg, Artemis) gather the 2 ends and bring them in close proximity for DNA ligase to seal the break.  In the process, nucleotides may be lost or added, making NHEJ a relatively error-prone method.  As a result, small insertions or deletions can be produced at the repair site. Although less accurate, NHEJ functions in **all phases** of the cell cycle because it does not require a homologous sister chromatid (only available after DNA replication in late S phase and G2). Some forms of severe combined immunodeficiency **(SCID)** are caused by defects in NHEJ genes (eg, *Artemis*, *RAG1/2*).  NHEJ is essential for repairing the DSBs intentionally generated during V(D)J recombination in developing T and B lymphocytes, which is required for survival as well as T-cell receptor and B-cell receptor diversity.  Failure of this pathway leads to complete absence of T and B cells in the peripheral blood. ## Homologous recombination HR repairs DSBs with greater accuracy than NHEJ because it uses an undamaged sister chromatid as a template.  Therefore, it is restricted to late S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, after DNA replication has occurred.  The process begins with invasion of the broken strand into the intact homologous sister chromatid (mediated by *BRCA1/2* and *RAD51*).  DNA polymerase then extends the invading strand using the sister sequence as a template. Although more accurate, one disadvantage of HR is the potential for **loss of heterozygosity (LOH)**.  HR can copy a pathogenic allele from the sister template, converting an otherwise recessive defect into a homozygous one.  LOH is a major mechanism of tumor suppressor gene inactivation, serving as the "second hit" in cancer development.  (Note:  Second hits can also arise independently through random mutations, even without LOH.) Mutations in HR genes (eg, *BRCA1*, *BRCA2*) force the cell to rely solely on NHEJ, which is more error prone.  Patients have a markedly elevated risk of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and other malignancies. # DNA damage response The 5 primary repair pathways (BER, NER, MMR, HR, and NHEJ) are centrally regulated by a common DNA damage response (DDR). The DDR halts the cell cycle so the machinery described above has time to fix errors.  Specialized protein complexes (eg, ATM) continuously monitor DNA integrity.  When they encounter damage, they phosphorylate downstream cell cycle checkpoint kinases to temporarily arrest the cell cycle.  They also activate proteins from the relevant pathway to begin repair. ## Successful repair Once the lesion is corrected, the cell cycle checkpoints are unblocked, and the cell is free to replicate its DNA or to divide. ## Failed repair, cell eliminated If damage is irreparable (eg, extensive DSBs), persistent DDR signaling can **trigger apoptosis via p53**, which is encoded by the *TP53* gene.  Cells can also enter senescence, a permanent state of cell cycle arrest in which they remain metabolically active but no longer divide. ## Failed repair, cell survives Defects in DDR components (eg, p53, ATM) **compromise all** DNA repair pathways, allowing cells to continue surviving despite highly mutagenic DNA damage: - Defects in p53 lead to **Li-Fraumeni syndrome**, characterized by early-onset of often-concurrent malignancies in multiple tissues (eg, sarcomas, breast cancer, glioblastoma, leukemia). - Defects in ATM lead to **ataxia-telangiectasia**, characterized by progressive cerebellar degeneration, telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, extreme radiosensitivity, and high risk of lymphoma and breast cancer. # Summary DNA is constantly damaged by replication errors, normal oxidative stress, and environmental exposures.  If not repaired prior to replication, these lesions can become permanent mutations.  DNA damage ranges from single base modifications to large helix-distorting lesions.  Five major repair pathways are available ((Figure 6)).  Base excision repair, nucleotide exclusion repair, and mismatch repair correct single strand defects, such as base modifications (eg, oxidation), mismatches, and intrastrand crosslinks (eg, T-T dimers), using the intact complementary strand as a template.  Nonhomologous end joining and homologous recombination correct double strand breaks.  Defects in each of these 5 pathways are associated with specific hereditary cancer syndromes (eg, loss of NER results in xeroderma pigmentosum).  Upstream failure of the DNA damage response itself (eg, *ATM* or *TP53* mutations) compromises multiple repair processes and predisposes to cancer. ​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​

articles.title: Fructose Metabolism And Associated Disorders
articles.markdown: # Fructose Metabolism And Associated Disorders # Introduction Dietary carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.  Disaccharides and polysaccharides must be hydrolyzed to monosaccharides ((Figure 1)) prior to absorption and use.  Fructose is a monosaccharide obtained directly from fruits and honey and indirectly from sucrose, a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose.  Although it shares structural similarity with glucose, fructose has a distinct intermediate metabolic pathway that bypasses key regulatory steps of glycolysis.  This unique handling explains both fructose's efficient utilization and the pathophysiology of inherited disorders of fructose metabolism. # Fructose metabolism Fructose metabolism has several key differences from glucose metabolism: - **Absorption**:  Glucose is absorbed via sodium-dependent transport (sodium-glucose cotransporter-1), whereas fructose is absorbed in the proximal intestine by facilitated diffusion via glucose transporter 5 (GLUT5). - **Hepatic absorption**:  Glucose is distributed systemically, whereas fructose undergoes nearly complete hepatic extraction from the portal circulation. - **Regulated steps**:  Glucose enters glycolysis ((Figure 2)), which is tightly regulated according to cellular energy status by the rate-limiting enzyme phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).  In contrast, fructose metabolism **bypasses** PFK-1 regulatory control, entering the pathway *downstream* of PFK-1 processing. The rapid, unregulated metabolism of fructose enables it to serve as a substrate for de novo lipogenesis, gluconeogenesis, or energy production. Fructose metabolism involves the following key enzymes: - **Fructokinase**:  Phosphorylates fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, "trapping" fructose within hepatocytes. - **Aldolase B**:  Cleaves fructose 1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde (subsequently converted to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate). These products then enter the glycolytic pathway at various points as intermediates of glycolysis. Deficiency of either enzyme produces distinct clinical syndromes ((Figure 3)). # Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) ## Pathophysiology Hereditary fructose intolerance is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of aldolase B (which metabolizes fructose 1-phosphate to DHAP and glyceraldehyde for entry into glycolysis). In the absence of aldolase B, fructose 1-phosphate accumulates within hepatocytes, with the following effects: - **Sequestration of inorganic phosphate**:  This depletes intracellular phosphate and ATP availability, impairing metabolic processes. - **Reduced glucose availability**:  Fructose 1-phosphate inhibits hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, reducing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. The combined effect is an inability to maintain blood glucose levels after fructose ingestion, resulting in profound hypoglycemia. ## Clinical presentation Symptoms begin when fructose-containing foods, such as fruit juices, table sugar (sucrose, which is broken down into fructose and glucose), or fructose-containing formulas are introduced into the diet.  Typically, this occurs around age 4-6 months but can present earlier in formula-fed infants.  Symptoms occur shortly (eg, within minutes) of ingesting fructose and include: - **Nausea/vomiting**:  Followed by lethargy and diaphoresis (from hypoglycemia). - **Immediate hypoglycemia**:  Can be severe and life-threatening because gluconeogenesis is impaired. The condition can eventually lead to liver failure, poor weight gain, and renal injury. ## Diagnosis The diagnosis is suggested by the timing of symptoms and hypoglycemia relative to fructose/sucrose exposure.  Laboratory studies may show abnormal liver function tests and reducing substances in the urine.  Definitive diagnosis is by genetic testing. ## Management Treatment requires strict avoidance of fructose- and sucrose-containing food products (including sorbitol, an artificial sweetener converted to fructose); this results in an excellent prognosis if implemented before permanent organ damage. # Essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) ## Pathophysiology Essential fructosuria is a rare, benign autosomal recessive disorder caused by fructokinase deficiency, leading to the following: - **Deficient fructose phosphorylation**:  Without the phosphorylation of fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, fructose cannot be "trapped" in hepatocytes and instead circulates freely. - **Alternate metabolism of fructose**:  A portion of the ingested fructose is converted into fructose 6-phosphate by hexokinase (eg, skeletal tissue), which allows entry into glycolysis or other metabolic pathways. - **Fructosuria**:  Excess fructose is not reabsorbed, leading to excretion in urine. ## Clinical presentation Patients are often **asymptomatic**, and the condition is often undetected unless specialized testing is performed for other reasons (eg, history screening, unrelated genetic testing) because fructose metabolism can proceed through alternative pathways, so no toxic intermediates (eg, fructose 1-phosphate) accumulate. ## Diagnosis Fructose, like glucose and galactose, is a reducing sugar and can be detected by copper reduction tests.  Urine dipsticks that use glucose oxidase are specific for glucose and do not detect fructose.  Therefore, a positive copper reduction test with a negative glucose dipstick suggests the diagnosis, which can be definitively confirmed with genetic testing.  Because the copper reduction test is not routinely performed on asymptomatic individuals, essential fructosuria is often undiagnosed. ## Management No treatment is required. # Differential diagnosis Fructose metabolism disorders can be distinguished from other inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism based on clinical severity and dietary triggers.  The timing of symptom onset after specific dietary exposures remains the most useful distinguishing feature. ## Classic galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency) Like hereditary fructose intolerance, classic galactosemia is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and results in the accumulation of phosphorylated intermediates (galactose-1-phosphate).  However, symptoms (nausea, jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly) present in association with breast milk initiation in the neonatal period (eg, within days of life). ## Galactokinase deficiency Galactokinase deficiency is a milder disorder of galactose metabolism that presents with neonatal cataracts but without severe systemic illness or symptoms. ## Glycogen storage diseases Glycogen storage diseases present with fasting hypoglycemia due to impaired glycogen breakdown or use, rather than hypoglycemia associated with specific fructose-containing foods.  Hepatomegaly is common due to glycogen accumulation, and some subtypes have muscle involvement (eg, exercise intolerance). # Summary Fructose is a dietary monosaccharide rapidly metabolized in the liver via a pathway that bypasses key regulatory steps of glycolysis.  Fructokinase converts fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, and aldolase B cleaves this into glycolytic substrates.  Disorders of fructose metabolism differ in severity based on whether the defect generates a trapped phosphorylated intermediate.  Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) causes severe symptoms (eg, hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting) due to fructose 1-phosphate accumulation, occurring immediately after fructose or sucrose ingestion.  In contrast, essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) is often asymptomatic because fructose is metabolized by alternative pathways via hexokinase or excreted in urine (detected via a positive reducing sugar test with a negative urinary glucose dipstick). ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​

articles.title: Extracellular Matrix And Connective Tissue
articles.markdown:
# Extracellular Matrix And Connective Tissue # Introduction The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex structural network that supports cellular architecture and function.  It consists of structural proteins (collagens and elastin), adhesive glycoproteins (integrins), and ground substance (glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans), which together form the framework for connective tissues.  Variations in the composition and organization of ECM elements lead to different connective tissue types with specialized properties. # ECM structural proteins Structural proteins are also called fibrous proteins.  The main structural proteins are collagen and elastin. ## Collagens Collagen is a fibrous protein with a triple helix structure consisting of 3 polypeptide alpha chains braided together ((Figure 1)).  Each alpha chain is comprised of ~1,000 amino acids and features a repeating sequence with a primary structure of \[Gly-X-Y\]n where X is often proline and Y is often hydroxyproline.  Glycine, the smallest amino acid, is found at every third residue, allowing for a tight turning radius.  Synthesis of collagen is a multistep **vitamin C-dependent** process involving intracellular and extracellular stages ((Figure 2)). There are >25 types of collagen.  The 4 key isoforms can be remembered as follows:  **I = strong** (bones, tendons, skin, scars), **II = slippery** (cartilage), **III = stretchy** (skin, vessels, hollow viscus); **IV = sheets** (basement membrane) ((Table 1)). - **Type I**:  Has the strongest **tensile strength**, with a **dense fibrillar** structure that forms thick, wavy bundles on histology.  The **most abundant isoform** (~90%), type I collagen is found in bone, dentin, tendons, ligaments, the cornea, and scar tissue.  Defects are implicated in osteogenesis imperfecta (eg, spontaneous fractures, conductive hearing loss, blue sclerae). - **Type II**:  Has a **fine fibrillar** structure, forming a smooth, glassy (hyaline) appearance on histology.  Its looser arrangement confers **cushioning properties**.  It is found in cartilage pads, the nucleus pulposus, and the vitreous humor.  Defects are implicated in osteochondrodysplasias (eg, achondroplasia). - **Type III**:  Has a **reticular (lacy) structure**, forming **stretchy meshworks** ideal for cell movement (eg, marrow, lymphatics, nodes, spleen, liver, granulation tissue) and distension (eg, blood vessels, gut, skin).  Defects are implicated in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (eg, aortic dissection, bowel rupture, loose translucent skin). - **Type IV**:  Has a **flat sheetlike structure**.  It is ideal for **filtration** and is therefore the main type of collagen found in **basement membranes** (eg, alveoli, glomeruli, cochlea).  Defects are implicated in Alport syndrome (eg, glomerulonephritis, corneal dystrophy, sensorineural hearing loss). Aside from Alport syndrome (X-linked), genetic collagenopathies (eg, Ehlers-Danlos) mostly display autosomal dominant inheritance due to a **dominant negative** effect—that is, a defect in just one copy of the gene compromises the entire collagen protein because mutant alpha chains disrupt the triple helix even when normal chains are present. ## Elastin Elastin is a fibrous protein with a single filament structure that has a natural tendency to contract (recoil) after stretching.  It contains residues of **desmosine**, a unique amino acid found only in elastin, representing X-shaped interchain cross-linkages between 4 lysine residues on opposing strands, which account for elastin's rubber-like properties ((Figure 3)).  Elastin is incorporated into collagen scaffolds to impart recoil to tissues, which is advantageous for structures that constantly deform but must return to their original shape (eg, lungs, joints, vessel walls).  Defects in elastin are seen in **Marfan syndrome** (eg, long limbs, aortic dilation, mitral prolapse). # ECM glycoproteins (integrins) **Integrins** are transmembrane glycoproteins located on the basolateral surface that mediate signal transduction between the ECM and the cell ((Figure 4)).  These signals can be mechanical (eg, shear stress for blood flow autoregulation) or biochemical (eg, damaged ECM fragments as danger signals).  Integrins are **adhesive** to facilitate cell-matrix contact.  Each integrin spans the membrane on an axis that connects it to 2 binding partners: an extracellular ligand (eg, collagen) and an intracellular adaptor (eg, actin cytoskeleton). Notable integrin axes include: - **αIIbβ3 (GPIIb/IIIa) integrin – fibrinogen**:  Required for platelet aggregation and optimal adhesion.  Defects result in Glanzmann thrombasthenia (eg, prolonged bleeding time but normal platelet number and morphology). - **αLβ2 (CD18) – ICAM-1**:  Required for leukocyte attachment, rolling, and diapedesis through the vessel wall ((Figure 5)).  Defects result in leukocyte adhesion deficiency (eg, recurrent bacterial infections, "cold" abscesses with lack of pus, delayed umbilical separation).  Similarly, the **α4β7–MAdCAM-1** integrin system directs mucosal T cells to sites of intestinal inflammation.  Drugs that block this integrin (eg, vedolizumab) are used for the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease. - **α6β4 integrin – laminin**:  Necessary for hemidesmosome structure ((Figure 6)).  Defects result in **epidermolysis bullosa** (eg, blistering and desquamation with minor trauma or pressure). # ECM ground substance Ground substance is the gel-like, space-filling material of the ECM.  It consists of water, glycosaminoglycans, and proteoglycans.  Its roles include nutrient diffusion, cell migration, and extracellular signaling. ## Glycosaminoglycans Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are long, unbranched polysaccharides comprised of repeating disaccharide units.  Each disaccharide consists of a hexosamine (an aminated hexose sugar \[eg, glucosamine\]) linked to a uronic acid (a carboxylated hexose sugar \[eg, glucuronic acid\]).  Most GAGs are heavily sulfated, which, in addition to their carboxyl groups, lends a dense **negative charge** that attracts water to maintain tissue turgor (ie, hygroscopic effect).  Notable GAGs include: - **Hyaluronan** (unsulfated \[N-acetyl-glucosamine – glucuronic acid\]n):  Plays critical roles in tissue hydration and wound healing.  It is found in high levels in synovial fluid, vitreous humor, and the dermis.  Clinically, hyaluronan is used as a viscoelastic device for eye surgery and as an intraarticular injection for nonoperative osteoarthritis management. - **Chondroitin sulfate** (sulfated \[N-acetyl-galactosamine – glucuronic acid\]n):  Provides structural support for cartilage, bone, skin, and corneal tissue. - **Heparan sulfate** (sulfated \[glucosamine - iduronic acid\]n):  Has myriad functions including regulation of growth factor signaling (eg, angiogenesis), endothelial and basement membrane permeability (eg, glycocalyx), and anticoagulation (eg, as closely related hepar*in* in mast cell granules). Other GAGs include keratan sulfate (eg, cornea, intervertebral discs, brain ECM) and dermatan sulfate (eg, skin, vessel walls, cardiac valves). ## Proteoglycans Proteoglycans are huge molecules consisting of a **protein core** and numerous **GAG sidechains** (eg, aggrecan core plus hyaluronan, chondroitin sulfate, or keratan sulfate side chains), forming a "bottle brush" structure.  By virtue of their size, they immobilize the GAGs within the ECM. The **mucopolysaccharidoses** are a group of lysosomal storage disorders that involve abnormal GAG (and therefore proteoglycan) accumulation due to enzyme defects ((Table 2)).  For example, Hurler syndrome involves defective iduronidase (necessary for the cleavage of dermatan and heparan sulfate), leading to accumulation in skin (eg, coarse facies), visceral organs (eg, hepatosplenomegaly), and the brain (eg intellectual disability). # Connective tissue (ECM combinations) Connective tissue refers to various compositions of the ECM elements discussed above, each conferring distinct biomechanical properties.  Various classification systems exist, and most categorize connective tissue into 3 types (loose, dense, or cartilaginous) based on their predominant collagen isotype and relative amount of ground substance: - **Loose connective tissue**:  Type III with or without type IV collagen (at basement membranes), with a balance between collagen and ground substance. - **Dense connective tissue**:  Type I collagen with or without elastin, with minimal ground substance. - **Cartilage**:  Type II collagen, with a high amount of ground substance. ## Loose connective tissue Loose connective tissue is a generic spongy matrix that fills most interstitial spaces.  It is suited for nutrient and waste diffusion, cell mobility, and soft support.  Therefore, it has a relatively balanced mix of collagen and ground substance.  The collagen component is mainly **type III** collagen (loose fibrillar, lacy, reticular).  Loose connective tissue is further classified as: - **Areolar loose**:  Composed of type III and type IV collagen at basement membranes.  It forms the **lamina propria** that supports epithelial surfaces (eg, mucous membranes).  It also forms the innermost sheath around skeletal muscle fibers (ie, endomysium), nerve fibers (ie, endoneurium), and small blood vessels (ie, tunica adventitia). - **Reticular loose**:  Exclusively composed of type III collagen.  It forms a sieve-like mesh ideal for easy cell movement and filtration and is therefore abundant in hepatic sinusoids, splenic pulp, lymph nodes, and lymphatic vessels. ## Dense connective tissue Dense connective tissue is specialized to resist stress and strain.  It is mainly composed of **type I** collagen (dense fibrillar) and has a relatively low proportion of ground substance.  Dense connective tissue includes: - **Regular dense**:  Composed of compact **parallel** bundles of type I collagen; equipped to handle high tensile stress and strain along a **single axis**.  Therefore, it is abundant in tendons and ligaments. - **Irregular dense**:  Composed of **randomly arrayed** type I collagen fibrils; equipped to handle high stress and strain along **multiple axes**.  Therefore, it is abundant in the dermis, joint capsules, organ capsules, perichondrium and periosteum, and cardiac valves. - **Elastic dense**:  Contains a high level of **elastin** in addition to type I collagen.  It is ideal for storing and releasing potential energy through elastic recoil, returning tissues to their original shape.  It is most abundant in the tunica media of large elastic arteries (eg, aorta and main branches), the lungs, vocal cords, and postural ligaments (eg, vertebral ligamentum flavum). ## Cartilaginous connective tissue Cartilage is a firm connective tissue composed primarily of **type II** collagen, which is specialized for structural support (eg, tracheal rings), smooth movement (eg, articular cartilage), and cushioning of impact forces (eg, intervertebral discs).  Cartilage is avascular and relies on the passive diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from surrounding tissues.  There are 3 main types of cartilage, including: - **Hyaline**:  The most widespread cartilage in the body, hyaline is composed almost exclusively of type II collagen.  It has a smooth, white, porcelain-like appearance.  It forms the fetal skeleton and epiphyseal plates, serving as the template for ossification.  It is the major cartilage in joint surfaces as well as the nasal bridge, larynx, and conducting airways.  Hyaline cartilage is prone to calcification in advanced age. - **Elastic**:  Contains some elastin fibers in addition to type II collagen.  It is found in tissues that "snap" open or shut quickly, such as the vocal cords, eustachian tube, and epiglottis. - **Fibrocartilage**:  Contains some type I in addition to type II collagen, reinforcing its strength.  It is the firmest and most durable of all cartilage types and is found in areas of high compressive force, such as the intervertebral discs, menisci of the knee, public symphysis, and temporomandibular joints. ## Others **Adipose** and **blood** were traditionally classified as connective tissues due to their shared embryonic origin (mesenchyme), their high soluble glycosaminoglycan content, and their functional roles in "connecting" various tissues and organs.  However, this semantic designation holds limited clinical relevance. # Connective tissue disorders ## Marfan syndrome Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the *FBN1* gene responsible for producing fibrillin-1, a protein that regulates transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) to maintain **elastin** integrity.  In Marfan syndrome, fragmentation of elastin leads to skeletal elongation and weakened structural support in various tissues.  Manifestations may be musculoskeletal (eg, tall, slender body habitus, spider-like fingers, pectus deformity), cardiovascular (eg, aortic dilation and dissection, mitral valve regurgitation), ocular (eg, lens dislocation), and respiratory (eg, spontaneous pneumothorax due to ruptured apical blebs). ## Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a family of inherited (mainly autosomal dominant) disorders caused by mutations in collagen and collagen-related proteins such as: - **Type III collagen** (COL3A1) in **vascular** EDS:  Characterized by thin, translucent skin and weakened walls in blood vessels and hollow viscera (eg, aortic dissection, gastrointestinal perforation, uterine rupture and prolapse). - **Type V collagen** (COL5A1) in **classical** EDS:  Characterized by joint hypermobility (eg, spontaneous dislocation), profound skin laxity, and skin fragility (eg, poor wound healing). - **Procollagen lysine hydroxylase** (PLOD1) in kyphoscoliotic EDS:  Characterized by severe and progressive scoliosis since birth, delayed motor development, and vascular fragility. The most common form, known as hypermobile EDS, features highly variable symptoms, structurally normal collagen, and poorly defined genetic loci.  Its features include mild skin laxity, joint hypermobility, chronic pain, and clinical overlap with functional disorders such as chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and postural orthostatic tachycardia (POTS). ## Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS) Leoys-Dietz syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder involving mutations in the **TGF-β signaling** pathway, resulting in underproduction of elastin, collagen, and other ECM components to varying degrees.  It closely resembles Marfan syndrome but involves an aggressive vascular fragility phenotype (eg, aortic aneurysm in early childhood), cardiac defects (eg, bicuspid aortic valve), and cartilage fusion abnormalities (eg, cleft uvula, craniosynostosis). ## Alport syndrome Alport syndrome ((Table 3)) is an X-linked disorder involving mutations in **type IV collagen** (eg, COL4A5), which is found in **basement membranes**.  Defective type IV collagen leads to basement membrane splitting (dehiscence), and excessive layering (lamellation), producing a woven basket appearance.  Manifestations include sensorineural deafness (eg, cochlear basement membrane), hematuria and progressive renal failure (glomerular basement membrane), anterior lens protrusion, and retinal thinning. ## Osteogenesis imperfecta Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a group of genetic disorders (mainly autosomal dominant) caused by defective **type I collagen** production (eg, COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations).  The defining feature of OI is brittle bones that fracture with minimal or no trauma, resulting in progressive deformity.  Other aspects include blue sclerae (due to translucency of scleral collagen allowing the blue choroid to be seen beyond), conductive hearing loss (due to degeneration of the middle ear ossicles), and dental malformations. ## Scurvy Scurvy ((Table 4)) is an acquired collagen disorder resulting from severe dietary **vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency** in the setting of severe malnutrition, malabsorption, or poor citrus intake.  Vitamin C is a rate-limiting cofactor for proline and lysine hydroxylation, which are necessary for triple helix formation.  Clinical features include poor wound healing and dermal capillary fragility (eg, petechiae, ecchymoses, perifollicular hemorrhages), gingivitis, and corkscrew hairs.  Untreated scurvy can progress to hemarthroses, aortic dissection, gastrointestinal bleeding, and sepsis due to gut mucosal breakdown. # Tumor cell invasion Metalloproteinases are zinc-containing enzymes that degrade components of the ECM and basement membrane and facilitate basement membrane penetration, which distinguishes an invasive tumor from carcinoma in situ.  This includes the following steps: 1. Tumor cells detach from surrounding cells in a process commonly determined by decreased expression of adhesion molecules, including E-cadherins. 2. Tumor cells adhere to the basement membrane; this is facilitated by increased expression of laminin and other adhesion molecules. 3. Tumor cells invade the basement membrane via enhanced secretion of proteolytic enzymes (eg, metalloproteinases, cathepsin D protease). # Summary The extracellular matrix is a dynamic scaffold composed of water, structural proteins (collagen, elastin), adhesive glycoproteins (integrins), and ground substance (glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans): - Inherited collagen disorders include osteogenesis imperfecta (type I:  found in bones, skin, tendons, sclerae), achondroplasia (type II:  found in cartilage); Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type III and others; found in vessel walls), and Alport syndrome (type IV:  found in basement membranes). - The primary inherited elastin disorder is Marfan syndrome. - Inherited disorders of adhesive glycoproteins (integrins) include epidermolysis bullosa, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, and leukocyte adhesion defect. - Inherited disorders leading to the accumulation of abnormal ground substance (glycosaminoglycans or proteoglycans) are known as mucopolysaccharidoses (eg, Hunter syndrome, Hurler syndrome). The relative mix of collage, elastin, and ground substance defines the major connective tissue types (ie, loose, dense, cartilaginous). ​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌

articles.title: Endocrinology: Core Principles
articles.markdown: # Endocrinology: Core Principles # Introduction The endocrine system participates in cellular communication and regulation of responses in the body, typically over chronic periods.  It uses hormones, chemical messengers carried in the bloodstream for long-distance communication among the body's cells.  This article provides an overview of the endocrine system, with an emphasis on functional aspects.  The individual hormones and associated disorders are described in separate articles. # Hormones Hormones are signaling molecules secreted from endocrine tissues into the circulation.  They can be classified based on their structure (peptide hormones, steroid hormones, and amino acid–derived hormones, described later) or their influence on other hormones: - **Tropic** hormones target endocrine tissues to influence secretion of other hormones (eg, adrenocorticotropic hormone, produced by the anterior pituitary, stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol). - In contrast, **direct** hormones act directly on target cells to produce nonendocrine responses (eg, prolactin, released by the anterior pituitary, promotes milk secretion). Some hormones (eg, growth hormone) act as both a tropic hormone (eg, stimulate the liver to release hormones) and a direct hormone (stimulates tissues to uptake glucose). # Endocrine glands Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete hormones into the bloodstream.  The major endocrine glands are shown in the figure ((Figure 1)).  The **hypothalamic-pituitary axis** is a core component of the endocrine system; it is responsible for regulating various physiologic processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress responses.  The hypothalamus, located at the base of the brain, controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland, which is divided into anterior and posterior lobes.  The anterior pituitary releases several hormones that regulate peripheral endocrine glands (eg, thyroid, adrenal glands, gonads), whereas the posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.  The interplay between these 2 organs maintains homeostasis in the body. # Hormone transport Hormones travel to target cells via the blood; therefore, a hormone's solubility affects how it is transported and how it exerts its physiologic effects. ## Peptide hormones Peptide hormones are produced in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and stored in vesicles until a signal causes them to be released.  They typically possess an overall charge at physiologic pH, making them water soluble **(hydrophilic)**.  Therefore, they can circulate largely in a free form (ie, unbound to proteins) in the bloodstream; however, they cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid layer of the target cell plasma membrane and rely on intracellular molecules to transmit a signal to the interior of a cell.  They are relatively fast acting with relatively short-lived results. ## Steroid hormones Steroid hormones are procured in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.  Because they are derived from cholesterol, they are lipophilic **(hydrophobic)** and can diffuse through the secreting cell's membrane.  They are bound predominantly to protein carriers to increase their solubility.  Their hydrophobicity facilitates diffusion through target cell plasma membranes, after which the hormones bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus to regulate gene expression ((Figure 2)).  They are slower acting with longer-lasting results. ## Amino acid–derived hormones Amino acid–derived hormones can function similarly to peptide and steroid hormones, depending on their structure and regulation.  For example, the catecholamine hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine behave like peptide hormones, whereas thyroid hormones behave like steroid hormones. # Endocrine signaling Endocrine signaling is 1 of the 3 broad ways (autocrine, paracrine, endocrine) in which cell signaling occurs ((Figure 3)).  The reception of a signal by a target cell is the first step in endocrine signaling. Receptors for peptide hormones are located in the plasma membrane because peptide hormones are charged and cannot readily cross the phospholipid bilayer; these receptors are often coupled with a G protein.  The peptide hormone serves as a first messenger, which binds its receptor and triggers a **second messenger** (eg, cyclic adenosine monophosphate), another molecule inside the target cells that transmits the signals (often through phosphorylation) ((Figure 4)).  Signal amplification can occur along this signaling cascade due to the production of hundreds of secondary messengers. Because steroid hormones are lipophilic, they diffuse directly across the plasma membrane and bind **intracellular receptors** in the cytosol or the nucleus, typically without using second messengers.  The steroid hormone–receptor complex usually acts as a **transcription factor** and binds DNA, resulting in increased or decreased transcription of target genes.  Often, 2 steroid hormone–receptor complexes bind together (ie, dimerize) prior to DNA binding. # Regulatory organization and feedback Endocrine function is organized primarily into regulatory axes that link the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and peripheral endocrine organs (eg, hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal, hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal).  Hypothalamic hormones stimulate the anterior pituitary to release tropic hormones, which in turn regulate hormone secretion from peripheral glands. Hormone secretion within these axes is governed primarily by feedback mechanisms.  In **negative feedback**, the final hormone produced by a peripheral gland suppresses further secretion of hypothalamic and pituitary hormones, stabilizing circulating hormone levels ((Figure 5)).  For example, thyroid hormones inhibit the release of both thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary. Less commonly, **positive feedback** amplifies hormone secretion under specific physiologic conditions ((Figure 6)).  For example, rising estradiol levels during the late follicular phase stimulate a surge in LH, which triggers ovulation. Hormone secretion also follows characteristic temporal patterns.  Some hormones are released in a pulsatile manner (eg, GnRH), whereas others exhibit circadian variation (eg, cortisol, which peaks in the early morning).  These patterns are integral to normal endocrine function and can be disrupted in disease states. # Patterns of endocrine disease Disorders of the endocrine system can be broadly categorized based on abnormalities in hormone production or action. Hormone excess and deficiency can result from dysfunction at different levels of an endocrine axis. - In **primary** disorders, pathology originates in the peripheral endocrine gland itself, leading to altered hormone production. - In **secondary** or tertiary (central) disorders, abnormalities in the pituitary or hypothalamus result in inappropriate regulation of peripheral glands. These distinctions tend to produce predictable patterns of hormone levels due to feedback mechanisms.  For example, primary gland failure leads to reduced end-hormone levels with compensatory elevation of tropic hormones, whereas central dysfunction results in low levels of both. In some conditions, circulating hormone levels are normal or elevated, but target tissues fail to respond appropriately.  This end-organ resistance may result from defects in hormone receptors or downstream signaling pathways (eg, insulin resistance). # Evaluation of endocrine disorders Evaluation of endocrine disorders follows from axis physiology and feedback relationships.  Initial testing measures both the peripheral (end) hormone and its corresponding pituitary tropic hormone to determine whether feedback is intact: - In primary gland dysfunction, reduced end-hormone production removes negative feedback, resulting in elevated tropic hormone levels (eg, primary hypothyroidism: low T4, high TSH). - Conversely, excess end hormone suppresses tropic hormone secretion (eg, primary hyperthyroidism: high T4, low TSH). - In central (pituitary or hypothalamic) disorders, both tropic and end-hormone levels are inappropriately low or inappropriately normal relative to each other (eg, secondary hypothyroidism: low T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH). When baseline measurements do not clearly localize the defect, dynamic testing is used to assess how the system responds to perturbation. - **Stimulation tests** are used when hormone deficiency is suspected, evaluating whether a gland can increase hormone production when appropriately stimulated (eg, cosyntropin stimulation test: failure of cortisol to rise indicates adrenal insufficiency). - **Suppression tests** are used when hormone excess is suspected, evaluating whether normal feedback can reduce hormone secretion (eg, dexamethasone suppression test: failure to suppress cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome). # Summary The endocrine system coordinates long-range cellular communication through hormones released into the bloodstream, with effects determined by hormone structure, transport, and receptor signaling.  Peptide hormones are water soluble and act via cell-surface receptors and second messengers, whereas steroid and thyroid hormones are lipophilic, circulate protein-bound, and regulate gene transcription through intracellular receptors.  Endocrine function is organized into hypothalamic–pituitary–target gland axes governed primarily by negative feedback, with additional modulation by pulsatile and circadian secretion.  Disorders arise from hormone excess or deficiency or from end-organ resistance and can be localized within an axis by interpreting feedback relationships.  Evaluation relies on paired measurement of tropic and end hormones, with dynamic stimulation or suppression testing used to assess glandular reserve or autonomy when baseline findings are inconclusive. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​

articles.title: DNA And The Central Dogma: Gene Transcription And Translation
articles.markdown:
# DNA And The Central Dogma: Gene Transcription And Translation # Overview Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), which consists of strands of nucleotides with purine or pyrimidine nitrogenous bases, allows for the transmission of genetic information from one generation to another.  The expression of the information encoded in DNA is mediated by ribonucleic acid (RNA).  The central dogma of molecular biology describes the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein ((Figure 1)).  This directional process underlies gene expression and involves 2 major stages: transcription (from DNA to RNA) and translation (from RNA to protein).  Unlike in prokaryotes (which generally do not have membrane-bound organelles), these processes are compartmentalized in eukaryotes, with transcription occurring in the nucleus and translation occurring in the cytoplasm. # DNA structure and replication ## Nucleotide composition and base pairing DNA consists of 2 strands of nucleotides that run in opposite directions (antiparallel) and twist around each other to form a right-handed double helix.  Each DNA strand is a polymer of deoxyribonucleotides, which are composed of deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base **(adenine \[A\], guanine \[G\], cytosine \[C\], or thymine \[T\])**.  Nitrogenous bases are either purines (A and G; containing 2 rings) or pyrimidines (C and T; containing 1 ring).  Complementary **base pairing** occurs between the nitrogenous bases of opposite strands: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.  RNA is similar in structure to DNA but contains ribose sugar (instead of deoxyribose sugar) and uracil (U) (instead of T). In each nucleotide, the carbons of the sugar are numbered 1′ through 5′; the 5′ carbon is attached to a phosphate group, and the 3′ carbon carries a hydroxyl (OH) group.  This orientation (ie, a 5′ end with a free phosphate group and a 3′ end with a free OH group) defines the direction of a nucleic acid strand.  Linkage of nucleotides is the basis for both DNA synthesis (replication) and RNA synthesis (transcription).  During these processes, nucleotides are added to the 3′ OH group, resulting in strand elongation in the **5′ → 3′ direction**. ## Chromatin structure and regulation DNA wraps around **histone** octamers (which are made up of 2 copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) to form nucleosomes.  **Nucleosomes** are separated by a stretch of DNA, or linker DNA, giving them the appearance of beads on a string ((Figure 2)).  DNA in this loose structure **(euchromatin)** is about 10 nm in diameter and provides a high degree of transcriptional access.  The degree of compaction changes based on epigenetic modification (eg, histone acetylation) and binding of additional DNA structural proteins ((Figure 3)).  One such protein is **histone H1**, which, in contrast to the other histone proteins, is located **outside the nucleosome core**.  Histone H1 binds to both the nucleosome and adjacent linker DNA, which facilitates packaging of chromatin into a thicker (30 nm), **more compact** structure **(heterochromatin)** that limits transcriptional access to the DNA.  During cell division, chromatin interacts with additional proteins (eg, nuclear scaffold proteins) and undergoes further coiling, ultimately forming condensed chromosomes. ## DNA replication For a copy of genetic information to be passed to daughter cells during cell division, DNA must first be copied (replicated).  This process takes place during the S phase of the cell cycle.  DNA replication is **semiconservative**, which means that each new (daughter) strand is synthesized using one of the original (parent or parental) strands as a template.  Replication initiates at origins of replication, which are specialized nucleotide sequences that bind replication machinery. Key steps of DNA replication include the following ((Figure 4)): - **Helicase** unwinds DNA, creating a replication fork. - Single-stranded DNA–binding proteins (SSBPs) prevent reannealing (ie, they hold the 2 DNA strands apart). - **Topoisomerase** relieves DNA supercoiling (overwinding) ahead of the replication fork. - **Primase** synthesizes RNA primers that provide a free 3′ OH group for DNA polymerase to begin DNA synthesis. - **DNA polymerase** III (in prokaryotes) or DNA polymerase δ/ε (in eukaryotes) extends DNA from RNA primers by attaching uncoupled deoxynucleotide triphosphates (composed of a nitrogenous base \[A, G, C, T\] with 3 phosphate groups) to the growing DNA strand, with the 3′ OH from the last nucleotide of the growing strand "attacking" the 5′ phosphate group of the incoming deoxynucleotide triphosphate. - DNA polymerase I (prokaryotes) or RNase H and polymerase δ (eukaryotes) replace RNA primers with DNA. Because all DNA polymerases can synthesize DNA only in the 5′ → 3′ direction, one daughter strand (the **leading strand**) is synthesized continuously toward the replication fork.  The other strand (the **lagging strand**) must be synthesized discontinuously in a direction away from the replication fork, with new segments being added as more DNA is unwound.  Because of this discontinuity, replication of the lagging strand requires repeated priming and synthesis of short **Okazaki fragments**, which are subsequently ligated by DNA ligase. ## Differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic replication - Prokaryotes (eg, bacteria) have circular DNA with a single origin of replication; eukaryotes have linear DNA with multiple origins of replication. - Prokaryotes possess 3 major DNA polymerases (I, II, III), whereas eukaryotes have 5 major DNA polymerases (α, β, γ, δ, ε). - DNA replication is slower in eukaryotes than in prokaryotes. ## Telomeres and telomerase Because DNA polymerases require a free 3′ OH group, the ends of linear chromosomes cannot be fully replicated, resulting in progressive shortening with each round of replication.  Telomeres, composed of hundreds of tandem **TTAGGG repeats** at the end of the chromosome, protect coding sequences.  In most cells, telomeres progressively shorten with each cellular division, eventually reaching a critical length at which apoptosis or senescence is triggered.  However, in germ cells, stem cells, and some cancer cells, telomerase, a reverse transcriptase, replenishes telomere sequences by adding DNA repeats to the end of the telomeres, maintaining replicative capacity. ## DNA repair mechanisms - During replication, DNA polymerase III (prokaryotes) and DNA polymerase δ/ε (eukaryotes) perform 3′ → 5′ **exonucleolytic proofreading** if incorrect nucleotide pairing occurs ((Figure 5)).  Immediately after replication, the DNA **mismatch repair (MMR)** system is activated when a base mismatch is identified.  MMR enzymes recognize mismatches, excise a stretch of the daughter strand (identified via methylation status in prokaryotes and strand breaks in eukaryotes), and fill in the gap.  These enzymes have **endonuclease** (rather than exonuclease) activity because the mismatched nucleotides must be excised from within an existing DNA strand ((Figure 6)). - Although DNA mismatches can occur during replication, they can also develop spontaneously or following exposure to harmful conditions (eg, ultraviolet \[UV\]) light).  **Base excision repair** removes small, nonbulky lesions (eg, deamination, oxidation) ((Figure 7)).  **Nucleotide excision repair** removes bulky lesions (eg, UV-induced thymine dimers).  Both processes involve lesion recognition, excision, gap-filling by DNA polymerase, and ligation. - In case of a **double-stranded break**, **homologous recombination** uses a sister chromatid as a template for high-fidelity repair.  In contrast, **nonhomologous end joining** directly ligates DNA ends without a template, occasionally introducing mutations ((Figure 8)). # Transcription and RNA processing Transcription is the process by which the genetic information encoded in **DNA** is copied into a complementary **RNA** sequence by RNA polymerase.  There are 3 stages of transcription ((Figure 9)): 1. Initiation. 2. Elongation. 3. Termination. ## Initiation Most DNA is noncoding **(introns)**; therefore, boundaries exist that define where coding regions **(exons)** begin and end.  These boundaries are marked by nucleotide sequences called promoters and terminators. Transcription initiation requires the recognition of promoter sequences ((Figure 10)): - TATA box:  Located approximately 25 bases upstream of the transcription start site. - CAAT box:  Located approximately 75 bases upstream of the transcription start site. RNA polymerase II binds the promoter with the help of general transcription factors to form the transcription initiation complex ((Figure 11)).  Activator proteins can bind enhancer sequences and interact with the transcription complex to enhance transcription ((Figure 12)). Transcription is similar to DNA replication in that RNA polymerase II assembles nucleotides in the 5′ → 3′ direction; however, unlike the DNA polymerases used in DNA replication, RNA polymerase does not need an RNA primer to begin assembling nucleotides. ## Elongation When the transcription machinery is assembled at the promoter, RNA polymerase II unwinds the DNA helix and transcription begins at the transcription start site ((Figure 13)).  One DNA strand is known as the coding **(sense)** strand (5′ → 3′), and the other is the noncoding/template **(antisense)** strand (3′ → 5′).  Only the noncoding/template (antisense) strand of DNA is transcribed into RNA. ## Termination Termination occurs when the RNA polymerase encounters a **polyadenylation signal** sequence (5′-AAUAAA-3′) in the RNA transcript, leading to cleavage of the nascent transcript and release from the polymerase. ## RNA processing In prokaryotes, the messenger RNA (mRNA) transcript that detaches from the DNA is available for translation to protein with no further modification.  In contrast, eukaryotic primary transcripts (heterogeneous nuclear RNA \[hnRNA\]) must undergo the following modifications before translation: - **5′ capping**:  Capping involves the addition of 7-methylguanosine (m⁷G) via a 5′-5′ triphosphate linkage to protect RNA from degradation and facilitate ribosome binding during translation (detailed below). - **Polyadenylation**:  A poly(A) tail is added to the 3′ end downstream of the polyadenylation signal by poly-A polymerase to stabilize mRNA and assist nuclear export. - **Splicing**:  The majority of DNA in eukaryotes is noncoding, and DNA sequences that code for a particular protein (exons) may be interrupted by noncoding regions (introns).  Splicing involves the **removal of noncoding introns** and the joining of coding exons.  It is carried out by the spliceosome, a complex composed of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) and small nuclear RNA (snRNA) ((Figure 14)).  The spliceosome recognizes splice donor sites (5′ end of introns) and splice acceptor sites (3′ end of introns).  With **alternative splicing**, exons and introns can be removed in a differential manner.  Therefore, multiple distinct mRNA transcripts and protein isoforms can be generated from a single gene ((Figure 15)). After export to the cytoplasm, mature mRNA may either engage in translation by ribosomes (described next) or be sequestered in P bodies, where it can be stored, degraded, or regulated via RNA exonucleases and decapping enzymes. # Translation Translation is the process by which **mRNA** is decoded into a specific sequence of amino acids to form a polypeptide chain.  It links the nucleotide-based language of RNA to the **amino acid–based structure of proteins**.  There are 20 types of amino acids in proteins and only 4 types of nucleotides (A, C, U, G) in mRNA, so the **genetic code** helps translate combinations of 3 nucleotides (called **codons**) into amino acids ((Table 1)). The small ribosomal subunit (30S in prokaryotes, 40S in eukaryotes) binds both mRNA, which contains genetic information that serves as a **reading frame**, and transfer RNA (tRNA), which serves as an amino acid carrier.  The large ribosomal subunit (50S in prokaryotes, 60S in eukaryotes) contains peptidyltransferase, which catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids to generate proteins. Each codon in mRNA serves as a reading frame triplet that is translated into one amino acid based on the genetic code.  There are 64 codons; 61 of them code for amino acids, and 3 (UAG, UGA, and UAA) serve as termination signals.  **AUG**, which codes for **methionine**, is the **start** signal codon that initiates translation. As with transcription, there are 3 stages to translation: 1. Initiation. 2. Elongation. 3. Termination. ## Initiation Translation occurs in the cytoplasm ((Figure 16)).  Eukaryotic translation initiation requires the assembly of the following ((Figure 17)): - **Ribosomal** subunits (60S and 40S, resulting in an 80S ribosomal unit). - mRNA. - Initiation factors. - Initiator tRNA (carrying methionine). - Guanosine-5′-triphosphate. The small ribosomal subunit (40S) initially binds to the 5′ cap of mRNA and scans for the **AUG start codon**, which is positioned near the beginning of the mRNA and is surrounded by the Kozak consensus sequence.  This short sequence identifies the specific AUG codon that serves as the initiator of translation. It is analogous to the Shine-Dalgarno mRNA sequence in prokaryotes, which is located upstream from the initiation codon AUG and recognizes a tRNA carrying N-formylmethionine.  This sequence allows binding of the 30S ribosomal subunit to mRNA and this N-formylmethionine-tRNA to form the prokaryotic 30S initiation complex.  The energy for this reaction brings the 50S subunit into the initiation complex, resulting in a 70S ribosomal unit. ## Elongation During elongation, the ribosome repeats the following sequence ((Figure 18)): - tRNAs deliver amino acids. - Peptide bonds form between amino acids via the ribosome's peptidyl transferase activity. Normally, in a process catalyzed by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (AA-tRNA synthetases), the 3′ end of each tRNA is covalently attached to a specific amino acid ((Figure 19)), with each amino acid/tRNA pair having a specific AA-tRNA synthetase that links them.  tRNA recognizes the 3-base codon on the mRNA being translated through the complementary bases in the tRNA anticodon region.  A charged tRNA (ie, tRNA covalently attached to an amino acid) enters the **A (aminoacyl) site** of the ribosome, and the tRNA anticodon binds to the corresponding mRNA codon.  A peptide bond forms between the newly added amino acid and the polypeptide strand, and the peptidyl-tRNA moves to the **P (peptidyl) site** as the ribosome translocates to the next codon.  The used tRNA moves to the E (exit) site and leaves.  This cycle extends the polypeptide chain (N-terminus → C-terminus of the polypeptide chain ((Figure 20))). The cloverleaf-like secondary structure of tRNA contains the following regions that facilitate this process ((Figure 21)): - The acceptor stem is created through the base pairing of 5′-terminal nucleotides with 3′-terminal nucleotides.  The CCA tail hangs off the 3′ end, with the amino acid bound to the 3′ terminal hydroxyl group.  tRNA is "loaded" with the appropriate amino acid by AA-tRNA synthetase.  A 3′ CCA tail is added to the 3′ end of tRNA as a posttranscriptional modification in eukaryotes and most prokaryotes.  Several enzymes use this tail to help recognize tRNA molecules. - The D loop contains numerous dihydrouridine residues, which are modified bases often present in tRNA.  The D loop (along with the acceptor stem and anticodon loop) facilitates correct tRNA recognition by the proper aminoacyl tRNA synthetase. - The anticodon loop contains sequences that are complementary to the mRNA codon.  During translation, the ribosome complex selects the proper tRNA based on its anticodon sequence. - The T loop contains the TΨC sequence (ribothymidine, pseudouridine, and cytidine residues) that is necessary for binding of tRNA to ribosomes. ## Termination When a stop codon **(UAA, UAG, or UGA)** enters the A site **of the ribosome**, it is not recognized by a charged tRNA because it does not code for an amino acid.  Instead, the stop codon is recognized by releasing factor proteins, which bind the stop codon and hydrolyze the bond between the polypeptide chain and the tRNA in the P site.  The newly formed polypeptide chain is then released, and the ribosome-mRNA complex disassembles ((Figure 22)). ## Posttranslational processing Proteins undergo folding, chemical modifications (eg, phosphorylation, glycosylation), and trafficking to functional destinations.  For example, protein phosphorylation (by kinases, typically on serine/threonine residues) regulates the activity (ie, on/off switching) of proteins; ubiquitination (by ubiquitin ligases, typically on lysine residues) tags the protein for destruction in the proteasome. # Summary The flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein is known as the central dogma of molecular biology.  DNA and RNA are linear polymers of nucleotides, each consisting of a sugar, phosphate group, and nitrogenous base.  Transcription (DNA to RNA) proceeds in 3 phases: RNA polymerase II and general transcription factors initiate transcription at promoter elements, elongate the RNA strand in the 5′ → 3′ direction along the template, and terminate transcription after a polyadenylation signal.  Translation (RNA to protein), likewise, has 3 stages: initiation, elongation, and termination.  The AUG codon (which codes for methionine) serves as a start codon; elongation cycles drive aminoacyl-tRNAs through ribosomal A, P, and E sites as peptidyltransferase forms peptide bonds; and a stop codon recruits release factors that hydrolyze the peptidyl-tRNA bond, freeing the completed polypeptide. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌
