articles.title: Biochemistry: Amino Acids
articles.markdown: # Biochemistry: Amino Acids # Introduction Amino acids are the fundamental building blocks of proteins.  Protein turnover recycles amino acids while generating nitrogen that must be safely handled.  Amino acids also serve as precursors for multiple nitrogen-containing biomolecules (eg, purines, pyrimidines, heme).  This article describes the structure, classification, and metabolic pathways of amino acids; the higher-order assembly and function of proteins are described in a separate article. # Structure and chemical organization There are 20 proteinogenic amino acids serving as building blocks for proteins.  They share a common backbone consisting of an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, a central alpha-carbon, a hydrogen atom, and a variable side chain (R-group) that determines the identity and chemical behavior of each amino acid ((Figure 1)). At physiologic pH (~7.4), amino acids exist predominantly as zwitterions (molecules with a positive charge at one position canceled by a negative charge at another, resulting in overall electrical neutrality) ((Figure 2)). Amino acids are represented using standardized three-letter and one-letter codes, which generally reflect their names. - Glycine (Gly, G):  Hydrogen side chain. - Alanine (Ala, A):  Methyl (−CH3) side chain. - Serine (Ser, S):  Hydroxyl-containing (−CH2OH) side chain. - Cysteine (Cys, C):  Thiol-containing (−SH) side chain. - Threonine (Thr, T):  Secondary alcohol–containing side chain. - Valine (Val, V):  Branched aliphatic (ie, nonaromatic hydrocarbon) side chain. - Leucine (Leu, L):  Branched aliphatic side chain with additional methylene. - Isoleucine (Ile, I):  Branched aliphatic side chain (constitutional isomer of leucine). - Proline (Pro, P):  Unique structure with a cyclic side chain forming a secondary amine. - Aspartate (Asp, D):  Negatively charged carboxylate-containing side chain. - Asparagine (Asn, N):  Neutral amide-containing side chain. - Glutamate (Glu, E):  Negatively charged carboxylate-containing side chain (−COOH) with additional methylene. - Glutamine (Gln, Q):  Neutral amide-containing side chain (CONH2) with additional methylene. - Methionine (Met, M):  Thioether-containing side chain (−CH2CH2SCH3). - Lysine (Lys, K):  Positively charged terminal amino–containing side chain. - Arginine (Arg, R):  Positively charged guanidinium-containing side chain. - Phenylalanine (Phe, F):  Aromatic (phenyl) side chain. - Tyrosine (Tyr, Y):  Aromatic side chain with hydroxyl group. - Histidine (His, H):  Imidazole-containing side chain. - Tryptophan (Trp, W):  Indole-containing aromatic side chain. # Classification by side-chain properties Side-chain chemistry determines interactions with water or lipid environments, capacity for hydrogen bonding or electrostatic interactions, and participation in catalysis or structural stabilization.  These features collectively determine protein folding, localization, and function. ## Nonpolar (hydrophobic) amino acids Nonpolar side chains consist largely of C–C and C–H bonds, which do not generate significant dipoles.  These amino acids interact poorly with water and are hydrophobic. This group includes small aliphatic residues (eg, glycine, alanine), branched-chain amino acids (eg, valine, leucine, isoleucine), and hydrophobic aromatics (eg, phenylalanine, tryptophan), along with methionine and proline. Hydrophobic residues preferentially localize to protein interiors or membrane-spanning domains, where they stabilize structure through the exclusion of water and favorable interactions with lipid bilayers. ## Polar, uncharged amino acids These amino acids contain polar functional groups that create dipoles but remain uncharged at physiologic pH. Representative examples include hydroxyl-containing residues (eg, serine, threonine), amide-containing residues (eg, asparagine, glutamine), and sulfur- or aromatic-containing residues with polar character (eg, cysteine, tyrosine). These residues are commonly located on protein surfaces or in active sites, where they participate in hydrogen bonding and interactions with aqueous environments. ## Charged amino acids Basic (positively charged) residues include lysine, arginine, and histidine, whereas acidic (negatively charged) residues include aspartate and glutamate. These residues contribute to electrostatic interactions, salt bridge formation, and pH-dependent conformational changes. ## Ionizable side chains Some amino acids can reversibly change charge depending on their local environment. This includes charged residues (eg, lysine, arginine, histidine, aspartate, glutamate), as well as side chains that can ionize under certain conditions (eg, tyrosine, cysteine). Local electrostatic context can alter protonation tendencies (eg, nearby charges shifting whether a group donates or accepts a proton), allowing proteins to fine-tune charge distribution and reactivity. # Metabolic roles of amino acids ## Protein turnover and nitrogen balance Continuous protein turnover releases amino acids that are either reused for protein synthesis or degraded. Degradation separates each amino acid into a carbon skeleton and an amino group.  The carbon skeleton can be used for energy metabolism, whereas the amino group represents nitrogen that cannot be directly oxidized and must be handled carefully ((Figure 3)). ## Transamination as a nitrogen-redistribution system Transamination transfers amino groups between amino acids and alpha-keto acids without generating free ammonia. This allows nitrogen from many amino acids to be funneled onto a smaller set of molecules, particularly glutamate, which acts as a central collector of amino groups.  At the same time, the corresponding carbon skeletons are converted into intermediates of central metabolic pathways, linking amino acid metabolism to glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. ## Deamination and ammonia generation When nitrogen must be eliminated, deamination reactions release ammonia from amino acids. Because ammonia is toxic, this process is largely confined to tissues equipped to detoxify it, particularly the liver.  This spatial organization ensures that nitrogen disposal is tightly coupled to mechanisms that prevent the accumulation of toxic intermediates. ## Nitrogen transport to the liver To facilitate hepatic processing and deamination, nitrogen generated in peripheral tissues is transported to the liver in nontoxic forms rather than released locally.  The primary carriers are alanine (especially from muscle) and glutamine (from most tissues). ## Urea cycle and nitrogen elimination In the liver, nitrogen is converted to urea, which can be excreted ((Figure 4)).  The urea cycle is closely integrated with overall metabolic state:  It is upregulated when amino acid breakdown increases (eg, after protein intake or during fasting) and requires sufficient ATP to proceed. ## Carbon skeletons as metabolic intermediates After the removal of nitrogen, amino acid carbon skeletons enter central metabolic pathways.  Depending on their structure, they can form Krebs cycle intermediates, serve as substrates for gluconeogenesis, or generate acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies. Glucogenic amino acids contribute to glucose production, whereas ketogenic amino acids contribute to ketone body formation.  Some amino acids can participate in both pathways.  This versatility allows amino acids to support energy production when carbohydrate availability is limited. ## Physiologic context: Fed vs fasting states The role of amino acids varies with metabolic state.  In the fed state, excess dietary amino acids are catabolized, increasing nitrogen disposal.  In fasting, endogenous proteins are broken down, and amino acids become a major source of substrates for gluconeogenesis and energy production. This dynamic behavior allows amino acids to function as a buffer between nutrient intake and metabolic demand. # Summary Amino acids are defined by a conserved backbone and a variable side chain, which determines chemical properties and protein function.  This structural framework allows a limited set of molecules to generate substantial functional diversity in proteins.  At the same time, amino acids are central metabolic intermediates.  Their nitrogen is redistributed through transamination, transported safely to the liver, and eliminated via the urea cycle, whereas their carbon skeletons integrate into core energy pathways.  These processes link protein turnover to energy production and nitrogen balance, allowing amino acids to function as structural units and metabolic substrates. ​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​

articles.title: Bilirubin Metabolism
articles.markdown: # Bilirubin Metabolism # Introduction Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced from the breakdown of heme-containing proteins (primarily hemoglobin).  Although it can function as an antioxidant at physiologic levels (ie, bilirubin-biliverdin redox cycle), bilirubin can be toxic in excess.  Bilirubin metabolism is a multistep process that is essential for maintaining normal physiologic levels and preventing toxic accumulation of bilirubin. # Bilirubin metabolism Bilirubin production and metabolism involve production, metabolism, and excretion. ## Bilirubin production Approximately 80% of bilirubin is a by-product of hemoglobin metabolism in senescent red blood cells.  The remaining 20% is a by-product of the metabolism of other heme-containing proteins (eg, myoglobin).  The first step in bilirubin formation is the conversion of heme to biliverdin by the enzyme heme oxygenase.  Next, biliverdin is reduced to unconjugated bilirubin (indirect bilirubin) by the enzyme biliverdin reductase.  Because unconjugated bilirubin is lipophilic, it is not water-soluble and must bind albumin for transport to the liver. ## Bilirubin metabolism Within the liver, bilirubin is conjugated to glucuronic acid by the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, making it water-soluble ((Figure 1)).  Conjugated bilirubin is transported into the biliary tract for secretion into the small intestine as bile. ## Bilirubin excretion Once conjugated, bilirubin is water-soluble and cannot be reabsorbed through the lipid membrane of the intestinal epithelium.  Instead, conjugated bilirubin remains in the intestinal lumen, where it is reduced to urobilinogen by intestinal bacteria.  Most urobilinogen is further processed for excretion in the stool; however, some urobilinogen is reabsorbed and reenters the circulation, where it can be transported to the liver (ie, enterohepatic circulation) or kidneys (for excretion in urine). # Disorders of bilirubin metabolism Any disruption in bilirubin metabolism can lead to bilirubin accumulation in the serum (hyperbilirubinemia).  Hyperbilirubinemia typically manifests as jaundice (yellow discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes) and can be confirmed with laboratory evaluation (eg, total serum bilirubin level >1 mg/dL).  If hyperbilirubinemia is present, identifying the predominant type of bilirubin (eg, conjugated or unconjugated) in the plasma is generally the first step in identifying the underlying cause ((Figure 2)). ## Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is characterized by a serum conjugated (direct) bilirubin level <1 mg/dL or <20% of total serum bilirubin and can occur due to: - Excessive bilirubin production (eg, hemolysis, blood extravasation into tissues leading to destruction by tissue macrophages). - Impaired hepatic bilirubin uptake:  Occurs due to impaired hepatic blood flow (eg, congestive heart failure, portosystemic shunt) or use of medications that may compete with bilirubin for hepatic uptake (eg, rifampin). - Impaired bilirubin conjugation:  Occurs due to impaired UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity, as follows: - Crigler-Najjar syndrome:  Rare autosomal recessive disorder in which a mutation within the coding sequence of the gene for UDP-glucuronosyltransferase leads to reduced enzyme activity.  Complete loss of enzyme activity (eg, Crigler-Najjar syndrome type 1) can lead to severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia within the first few days of birth that can cause permanent neurologic deficits. - Gilbert syndrome:  Benign autosomal recessive disorder in which a mutation in the promoter sequence of the gene for UDP-glucuronosyltransferase results in mildly reduced enzyme levels.  This typically presents in adolescence with episodic jaundice triggered by stress.  Patients are generally asymptomatic between episodes. ## Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia is characterized by a serum conjugated (direct)  bilirubin level >1 mg/dL or >20% of total serum bilirubin and can occur due to any disruption in bilirubin metabolism after conjugation in the liver.  Additional laboratory testing (eg, aspartate aminotransferase \[AST\], alanine aminotransferase \[ALT\], alkaline phosphatase) is often necessary to determine the underlying cause, as follows: - Impaired transport of conjugated bilirubin into (ie, enterohepatic circulation) or out of (eg, Dubin-Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome) the liver:  These conditions are characterized by normal AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase levels. - Physical obstruction of biliary flow (eg, cholelithiasis, postsurgical strictures, malignancy, primary sclerosing cholangitis):  These conditions tend to have significantly elevated alkaline phosphatase levels (ie, cholestatic pattern of liver injury). - Other clinical conditions leading to hepatic injury (eg, viral hepatitis, medication toxicity, alcoholic hepatitis).  These conditions are characterized by predominantly elevated AST and ALT  levels. These conditions are discussed in separate dedicated articles. # Summary Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced from the breakdown of heme-containing proteins (primarily hemoglobin).  Although it can function as an antioxidant at physiologic levels (ie, bilirubin-biliverdin redox cycle), bilirubin can be toxic in excess.  Bilirubin metabolism is a multistep process that is essential in maintaining normal physiologic levels and preventing toxic accumulation of bilirubin.  If hyperbilirubinemia is present, recognizing the predominant form of bilirubin (eg, conjugated or unconjugated) in the plasma helps identify the underlying cause. ​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​

articles.title: Basic Virology
articles.markdown: # Basic Virology # Introduction Viruses are obligate intracellular agents that lack metabolic activity and rely on host cells for energy requirements and macromolecule synthesis.  A complete virus particle (virion) consists of a nucleic acid genome (RNA or DNA) enclosed in a viral-encoded protein capsid; some virions have a (host-derived) lipid-bilayer envelope studded with viral glycoproteins.  Viruses infect all forms of life and are responsible for a vast array of human illnesses.  They are classified based on size, shape (eg, helical/icosahedral), chemical composition and structure of the genome (eg, single stranded \[ss\] or double stranded \[ds\], linear/circular, monopartite/multipartite), and mode of replication. # Viral structure Virions deliver nucleic acid to a host cell to be translated by host machinery.  Outside of the host cell, they are inert.  The main structural elements of a virion are discussed next. ## Capsid Capsids are composed of viral-encoded, identical protein subunits called protomers, which **self-assemble** into a regular, well-defined array that surrounds and protects the viral nucleic acid from environmental damage.  They also assist with host cell binding and entry (in nonenveloped viruses).  There are 3 main types of capsids ((Figure 1)): - **Icosahedral**:  Protomers form oligomeric clusters (capsomeres) that self-assemble into polyhedral or spherical forms with 20 equilateral triangular faces.  Icosahedral nucleocapsids are seen in many RNA (eg, poliovirus) and DNA (eg, adenovirus, herpesvirus) viruses. - **Helical**:  Protomers form a helix of rods or flexible filaments around a very tight coil of nucleic acid.  Helical nucleocapsids are often seen with ssRNA viruses (eg, rabies, influenza, Ebola) and frequently require an envelope to increase structural stability. - **Complex**:  Protomers form complex shapes that may be irregular or may have both helical and icosahedral elements (eg, a bacteriophage with an icosahedral head and helical tail).  Complex nucleocapsids are most common in viruses with large genomes (eg, poxviruses, reoviruses). ## Envelope Some viruses have an envelope that surrounds the capsule.  Envelopes are a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane during viral budding (most common), cell lysis, or exocytosis.  Envelopes are spiked with viral glycoproteins, which assist with host cell attachment and entry.  Differences between enveloped and nonenveloped viruses follow ((Figure 2)): - **Enveloped viruses**: - More sensitive to environmental factors (eg, heat, desiccation, detergents) due to the fragile lipid bilayer; therefore, direct host-to-host contact (eg, respiratory droplets, bodily fluids) is typically required for transmission. - Better able to evade immune detection and facilitate membrane fusion due to the presence of a host-derived lipid bilayer. - Typically released from host cells by budding. - Examples:  Influenza virus, HIV, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), herpesviruses. - **Nonenveloped (naked) viruses**: - More resistant to harsh environmental conditions, allowing for diverse transmission routes (eg, fecal-oral, fomite, aerosol, water). - Typically released from host cells by lysis. - Examples:  Adenoviruses, picornaviruses (eg, poliovirus), norovirus. ## Genome Viruses have either an RNA or a DNA genome that can be organized in a variety of ways (eg, ss/ds, linear/circular, monopartite/multipartite).  The chemical composition of the genome determines the replication mechanism and classification. ## RNA viruses Approximately 70% of all viruses have an RNA genome.  Most RNA viruses (excluding retroviruses) replicate their genome in the cytoplasm using RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.  Because this enzyme has a high error rate compared to DNA polymerase, RNA viruses tend to accumulate mutations (variants) more rapidly than DNA viruses and to be more adaptable to changing host conditions.  RNA viruses are classified as follows ((Figure 3)): - **ssRNA viruses**: - **Positive-sense (+) ssRNA viruses** have genomes that can serve as mRNA; they are translated by host ribosomes in their entirety (as a viral polyprotein) and subsequently cleaved into individual viral proteins.  The virus encodes for an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which is synthesized after infection and generates a negative-sense RNA intermediate that acts as a template for a positive-sense copy of the genome.  Examples include coronaviruses (eg, SARS-CoV-2), flaviviruses (eg, dengue virus, hepatitis C virus \[HCV\]), and picornaviruses (eg, poliovirus, rhinovirus, hepatitis A virus \[HAV\]).  Retroviruses, which are also positive-sense ssRNA viruses, replicate via a DNA intermediate (as discussed later). - **Negative-sense (−) ssRNA viruses** have genomes that cannot be directly translated by host ribosomes.  Therefore, the virion must carry a preformed RNA-dependent RNA polymerase enzyme to convert the negative-sense RNA into a complementary positive-sense RNA strand.  The host ribosome then translates the positive-sense strand into viral proteins; the strand also serves as a template for new copies of negative-sense RNA as part of replication.  All known negative-sense ssRNA viruses are enveloped.  Examples include influenza, rabies, and measles viruses. - **dsRNA viruses**: - Because dsRNA cannot function as directly as mRNA, a preformed RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is packaged in the virion.  This enzyme transcribes the negative-sense strand into positive-sense mRNA, which is then translated by host ribosomes into viral proteins.  The positive-sense RNA also serves as a template for viral replication.  The most common example is rotavirus. - **Retroviruses** ((Figure 4)): - Retrovirus genomes are composed of 2 identical positive-sense ssRNA molecules; however, these are not used as mRNA.  Instead, the virus brings a reverse transcriptase enzyme, which converts the viral RNA genome into DNA.  The viral DNA then integrates into the host genome (provirus) and is subsequently transcribed by host RNA polymerase II; this generates positive-sense RNA that serves as mRNA and as a template for replication of the genome.  Examples include HIV and human T-cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV). **Segmentation** is common among RNA viruses.  The genome is divided into separate RNA molecules packaged within the virion (or sometimes variably packaged).  Classic examples include orthomyxoviridae (eg, influenza) and reoviridae (eg, rotavirus).  Segmentation enables **reassortment**, ie, exchange of whole genome segments when 2 strains coinfect the same cell. ## DNA viruses The genome of most DNA viruses is monopartite (contained in a single nucleic acid molecule), linear, and composed of dsDNA.  However, some viral species have an ssDNA genome (eg, parvovirus) or a circular double-stranded DNA genome (eg, papillomavirus).  DNA viruses use viral or host DNA polymerase to replicate, most often in the nucleus ((Figure 5)).  A broad categorization of DNA viruses is provided in this figure ((Figure 6)). # Viral life cycle Viral infection requires attachment to a host cell, penetration of the cell surface, and uncoating to make the genome accessible for translation and replication.  The viral life cycle is typically characterized by these steps. ## Attachment The surface of the virion has viral-encoded attachment proteins that bind to specific receptors (usually large glycoproteins) on a host cell.  Some viruses have attachment proteins that target many cell types across a range of species, whereas others are capable of infecting only a certain type of differentiated cell in a single species (eg, human papillomavirus \[HPV\] can infect only human keratinocytes).  Complex viruses (eg, herpesvirus) often have more than a single type of attachment protein.  Attachment efficiency is dependent on receptor availability and temperature/electrostatic interactions.  Known host cell receptor and virion/virion protein binding specificities (ie, viral tropism) include: CD4 with HIV gp120, CD21 with Epstein-Barr virus gp350, and erythrocyte P antigen with parvovirus B19. ## Penetration Penetration allows the virion (or portions of the virion) to enter the host cell.  It is an energy-dependent step, which occurs almost immediately after attachment.  Penetration typically involves one of the following mechanisms: - Translocation of the virion across the plasma membrane. - Endocytosis of the virion, leading to virion accumulation within cytoplasmic vacuoles. - Fusion of the virion envelope with the cell membrane. Nonenveloped viruses are either translocated or undergo endocytosis, whereas enveloped viruses fuse with the cell membrane. ## Uncoating After the virion enters the cell, it disaggregates to release its genome for expression with or without the assistance of cellular enzymes.  For instance, the nucleocapsids of adenovirus, herpesvirus, and HPV are transported to nuclear pores; viral DNA is then released directly into the nucleus.  In contrast, viruses that undergo endocytosis (eg, influenza) often use acidification to release their genome from the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. ## Transcription/replication The crucial event in viral replication is the synthesis of viral proteins by host cell machinery.  However, no host cell enzyme can synthesize messenger RNA from a viral RNA genome or transcribe viral DNA in the cytoplasm.  Therefore, only viruses that deliver their DNA to the nucleus can use host machinery for transcription.  All other viruses must either deliver a positive-sense ssRNA genome to the cell (which can serve as mRNA) or carry transcription enzymes (eg, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase) in the virion.  Host or viral polymerases are responsible for replicating the genome. ## Assembly/release Nonenveloped viruses assemble a procapsid in the nucleus or cytoplasm, package their genome, and then leave the cell via one of the following mechanisms ((Figure 7)): - **Host cell lysis** (majority) causes cell death.  Virions accumulate until the cell membrane is disrupted or the virus produces enzymes that damage the host cell membrane.  Examples include adenoviruses, picornaviruses, and most parvoviruses. - **Exocytosis** is marked by the release of virions in exosomes, which does not cause cell death.  This is seen with picornaviruses (eg, HAV, poliovirus) and polyomaviruses (eg, JC virus, BK virus). - **Cell-to-cell transmission** can occur in a minority of viruses, which may cause host cell death.  This is typically marked by the fusion of adjacent cells or direct contact between an infected and an uninfected cell. In contrast, enveloped viruses typically combine viral assembly with release from the host cell.  Enveloped viruses (eg, retroviruses; negative-sense ssRNA viruses) insert viral proteins into the host plasma membrane.  Viral nucleocapsids then attach to the cytoplasmic surface of these proteins, and the virus is extruded ("buds") into the extracellular environment. # Genetic variability Viruses generate diversity through several mechanisms, particularly during coinfection of a single host cell. - **Mutation**:  Replication errors, especially in RNA viruses due to low-fidelity RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, generate genetically distinct variants. - **Recombination**:  Exchange of genes between 2 chromosomes via crossing over within homologous regions can result in progeny that have recombined (chimeric) genomes, with traits from both parent viruses). - **Reassortment**:  Changes in genomic composition can occur when host cells are coinfected with 2 segmented viruses that exchange whole genome segments.  - **Phenotypic mixing (pseudotyping)**:  When a host cell is coinfected with 2 viral strains and progeny virions contain parental genome from one strain and nucleocapsid (or envelope) proteins from the other strain, this may result in progeny acquiring additional traits (eg, enhanced ability to infect new host cells due to different nucleocapsid proteins).  However, as the genome is unchanged, subsequent progeny would not retain these traits. # Effect on the host cell Viral infection can result in host cell death, persistent infection, or host cell transformation, as follows: - **Cytocidal (cytolytic) infections** cause host cell death; most viral infections are cytocidal.  Histopathology often shows rounding of the host cell, the formation of inclusion bodies in the nucleus/cytoplasm, and (in some viruses) the fusion of an infected cell with an adjacent cell to form a syncytium. - **Persistent infections** are marked by viral infection in a limited number of cells following acute infection.  Replication rate and spread are typically limited by the humoral and cell-mediated immune response.  Persistent viral infections are often categorized as follows: - **Slow infections** (eg, measles virus) are marked by a prolonged incubation period in which the infected host cell harbors the virus for months or years without developing cytopathic changes.  However, the infection eventually causes cellular injury, leading to cell death. - **Chronic infections** (eg, HCV) are characterized by continuous low-level viral replication in host cell tissues.  The virus typically causes a cytocidal reaction, but the replication cycle is slower, intermittent, or limited to a few host cells. - **Latent infections** (eg, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster virus, herpes simplex virus type 1 \[HSV-1\]) are marked by extreme restriction on viral replication and gene expression.  Host cells with latent infection typically appear normal on histopathology. - **Transforming infections** are a type of persistent infection associated with oncogenic transformation of the host cell.  DNA viruses (eg, Epstein-Barr virus, HPV) typically cause transforming infection only when viral gene expression is restricted to immediate early/early proteins because full viral replication kills the host cell.  In contrast, transforming RNA viruses (eg, HTLV) can cause oncogenesis while undergoing replication because they typically do not cause cytolysis. Type I interferons (α and β) are synthesized by most human cells in response to viral infections.  Once secreted, α and β interferons bind to type I interferon receptors found on infected and neighboring cells (autocrine/paracrine signaling).  This results in transcription of antiviral enzymes capable of halting protein synthesis, such as RNase L (endonuclease that degrades all RNA in the cell) and protein kinase R (inactivates eIF-2, inhibiting translation initiation).  However, these enzymes become active only in the presence of double-stranded RNA, which forms in infected cells as a result of viral replication.  As a result, normal metabolism and protein synthesis can continue in uninfected cells but is selectively inhibited in virally infected cells. # Major viral diseases Viruses cause a wide variety of human diseases across many organ systems.  Common examples of these viruses follow: - **Respiratory**:  Influenza virus, SARS-CoV-2, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus. - **Gastrointestinal**:  Norovirus, rotavirus, HAV, astrovirus. - **Hepatic**:  Hepatitis B virus, HCV, hepatitis E virus. - **Neurologic**:  Rabies virus, poliovirus, HSV-1 (encephalitis), arboviruses (West Nile virus, Zika virus). - **Exanthems**:  Measles virus, rubella virus, varicella-zoster virus. - **Oncogenic**:  HPV, Epstein-Barr virus, Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus. - **Immunodeficiency**:  HIV-1, HIV-2. # Summary Viruses are obligate intracellular pathogens that have a single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA genome, a virally encoded protein capsid, and (in some viruses) an outer lipid-bilayer envelope.  Viral pathogens infect all forms of life; in humans, they cause a wide variety of diseases across most organ systems.  Viral infection can result in acute, chronic, latent, and/or transforming infection. ​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌

articles.title: Basic Dermatology Vocabulary
articles.markdown: # Basic Dermatology Vocabulary # Introduction Dermatologic terminology is essential for accurate communication and clinical reasoning.  Dermatologic descriptions typically incorporate the following elements: - **Primary morphology** (eg, macule, papule). - **Size**. - **Demarcation** (eg, well demarcated, poorly demarcated). - **Color**. - **Secondary morphology** (eg, erosion, ulceration). - **Distribution** (eg, photodistributive, generalized). This article provides an overview of skin anatomy and the terminology used to describe skin rashes and cutaneous findings. # Structures of the skin The skin consists of 3 primary layers ((Figure 1)): epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue. ## Epidermis The outermost layer, the epidermis, is composed primarily of keratinocytes ((Figure 2)).  It includes (from deep to superficial): - **Stratum basale**:  Composed of a single layer of basal keratinocytes undergoing **mitosis**, melanocytes (which give skin its color), and Merkel cells (mechanoreceptors involved in the sensation of touch) ((Figure 3)). - **Stratum spinosum**:  Composed of a thick layer of living skin cells connected by **desmosomes**, which provide mechanical strength (and give the cells a spiny appearance under the microscope).  Langerhans cells (antigen-presenting immune cells) are abundant in this layer. - **Stratum granulosum**:  Contains keratohyalin **granules** rich in profilaggrin and loricrin, which contribute to keratinocyte maturation and skin barrier integrity.  Lamellar bodies release lipids that form a waterproof barrier. - **Stratum corneum**:  Composed of anucleate, flattened keratinocytes embedded in a lipid matrix, forming a protective, hydrophobic **barrier** that prevents water loss and pathogen entry. Thick skin (eg, palms, soles) has an additional layer, the stratum lucidum, between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum layers. ## Dermis The dermis is the connective tissue layer below the epidermis and consists of 2 layers: - **Reticular dermis** (deep layer):  Composed of a **thick layer of dense, irregular connective tissue**; rich in type I collagen and thick elastin fibers that provide **structural integrity** and resistance to mechanical forces.  This layer also contains larger blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, cutaneous nerves, and adnexal structures (eg, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, sweat glands). - **Papillary dermis** (superficial layer):  Consists of **loose connective tissue** rich in elastin fibers and types I and III collagen, which provide **tensile strength and elasticity**.  It also contains dermal papillae, capillary loops, and sensory nerve endings (eg, **Meissner** corpuscles) responsible for detecting light touch. The dermis plays an important role in thermoregulation (blood vessels regulate heat through vasodilation/constriction, sweat glands aid cooling), immune defense (houses dendritic cells, mast cells, lymphocytes), and wound healing (fibroblasts produce collagen). **Subcutaneous tissue** (hypodermis) Located beneath the dermis, the subcutaneous tissue is the deepest layer of the skin and consists primarily of adipose tissue interspersed with connective tissue septa, blood vessels, and lymphatics.  It has the following functions: - Insulation. - Energy storage in the form of fat. - Shock absorption:  Cushions underlying muscles, bones, and organs from mechanical trauma. - Structural support:  Anchors the skin to deeper tissues while allowing for mobility. This tissue is highly vascularized, housing larger blood vessels that supply the dermis and epidermis.  Nerve endings (eg, **Pacinian corpuscles**) in this layer contribute to the sensations of deep pressure and vibration. # Terminology for dermatologic lesions ## Primary lesions Primary lesions arise de novo, reflecting the initial pathogenic changes of a dermatologic disease process, and include: - **Macule**:  A flat, nonpalpable area of color change <1 cm (eg, freckles, lentigines). - **Patch**:  A macule >1 cm (eg, vitiligo, café au lait spots) ((Image 1)). - **Papule**:  A raised, solid lesion <1 cm (eg, lichen planus, acne, molluscum contagiosum) ((Image 2)). - **Plaque**:  A raised lesion >1 cm, often with scaling (eg, psoriasis, lichen simplex chronicus) ((Image 3)). - **Nodule**:  A deeper, solid lesion >1 cm, often involving the dermis or subcutaneous tissue (eg, dermatofibroma, lipoma) ((Image 4)). - **Vesicle**:  A small, fluid-filled blister <1 cm (eg, herpes simplex, varicella) ((Image 5)). - **Bulla**:  A large, fluid-filled blister >1 cm (eg, bullous pemphigoid, second-degree burn) ((Image 6)). - **Pustule**:  A pus-filled vesicle or papule (eg, folliculitis, pustular psoriasis) ((Image 7)). - **Wheal**:  A transient, edematous raised plaque resulting from dermal edema (eg, urticaria) ((Image 8)). These descriptive terms can be used together.  For example, a maculopapular rash contains both macular (flat) and papular (raised) components.  The underlying cause could be a viral exanthem, a bacterial infection, a drug reaction, or an inflammatory condition. ## Secondary lesions Secondary lesions result from evolution of primary lesions, trauma, or external factors and include: - **Scale**:  Excessive accumulation of stratum corneum that presents as flakes or plates on the skin's surface due to abnormal keratinization or shedding.  It is commonly seen in psoriasis, ichthyosis, and seborrheic dermatitis ((Image 9)). - **Crust**:  Accumulation of dried exudate (composed of serum, blood, or pus) on the skin surface following the rupture of vesicles, pustules, or erosions.  This lesion is commonly seen in impetigo or healing wounds ((Image 10)). - **Erosion**:  Superficial loss of the epidermis that does not penetrate the dermis, typically resulting from trauma, inflammation, or rupture of vesicles or bullae.  It heals without scarring because it does not extend beyond the basal layer of the epidermis ((Image 11)). - **Ulcer**:  Full-thickness epidermal loss extending into the dermis or beyond, often leading to scarring (eg, venous stasis ulcers, pressure ulcers) ((Image 12)). - **Fissure**:  Linear split extending into the dermis.  It is commonly seen in chronic dermatitis of the hand and tinea pedis ((Image 13)). - **Atrophy**:  Pathologic thinning of the epidermis, dermis, or subcutaneous tissue, resulting in a fragile, translucent appearance with increased susceptibility to injury.  Atrophy occurs for different reasons; chronic daily use of topical corticosteroids can cause cutaneous atrophy due to the inhibition of epidermal keratinocyte proliferation and fibroblast function.  Atrophy can also be pressure-induced and is common in aging skin ((Image 14)). - **Lichenification**:  Thickening of the skin with accentuated skin markings due to chronic rubbing or scratching.  This lesion occurs in atopic dermatitis ((Image 15)). Primary lesions typically provide the initial clues to a diagnosis, whereas secondary changes offer insight into disease progression and external influences (eg, trauma, environmental factors). # Clinical correlations The following clinical correlations highlight important dermatologic findings and their associated diseases. - **Annular lesion**:  A ring-shaped skin abnormality with a clear center and an advancing erythematous or scaly border; commonly associated with dermatologic conditions such as tinea corporis, erythema annulare centrifugum, or granuloma annulare ((Image 16)). - **Target lesion**:  A concentric skin abnormality with a dusky center (often with a small bulla or crust), a pale surrounding zone, and an erythematous peripheral border; commonly seen in erythema multiforme and drug reactions ((Image 17)). - **Koebner phenomenon**:  A pathophysiologic reaction in which new lesions of a preexisting dermatosis (eg, psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo) develop at sites of trauma ((Image 18)).  The exact mechanism of this response is unclear but likely involves immune dysregulation and epidermal turnover abnormalities. - **Auspitz sign**:  Pinpoint bleeding upon removal of psoriatic scales due to dilated underlying capillaries ((Image 19)). - **Nikolsky sign**:  Dermatologic sign characterized by superficial epidermal detachment that occurs with slight mechanical pressure (eg, lateral traction or rubbing of intact skin).  It results from the loss of desmosomal integrity and can be mediated by autoantibody targeting of cadherins (eg, in pemphigus vulgaris) or widespread keratinocyte necrosis (eg, in toxic epidermal necrolysis). - **Darier sign**:  A dermatologic response where gentle rubbing or scratching of a lesion induces localized erythema, swelling, or urtication due to mast cell degranulation and histamine release.  It is a characteristic diagnostic feature of mastocytosis ((Image 20)). # Summary Dermatologic terminology classifies skin findings based on structure, primary and secondary lesion types, and characteristic clinical patterns.  Precision of dermatologic description is essential for effective diagnosis, treatment, and communication in clinical practice. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌

articles.title: Basic Blood Cell Types: Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, And Platelets
articles.markdown: # Basic Blood Cell Types: Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, And Platelets # Introduction Blood is a specialized connective tissue containing various cell types suspended in plasma, each originating from multipotent hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.  This article reviews the basic types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells (composed of granulocytes and agranulocytes), and platelets.  Morphologic characteristics, functional roles, and common pathologic alterations are discussed.  Hematopoiesis and cell lineages are explored in detail in a separate article. # Red blood cells Red blood cells (RBCs), or erythrocytes, are the most abundant blood cells, accounting for approximately 40%-45% of blood volume ((Image 1)).  Their primary functions are to transport **oxygen** from the lungs to the tissues and to return carbon dioxide to the lungs for exhalation.  Measuring 6-8 µm in diameter, RBCs are uniquely biconcave in shape, increasing the surface area available for efficient gas exchange.  Gas exchange is facilitated by **hemoglobin**, an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen.  RBCs **lack a nucleus** and organelles, allowing more space for hemoglobin but limiting them to a **120-day lifespan** before they are recycled by the spleen and liver.  Erythropoiesis, the differentiation of RBCs from early progenitor cells, is stimulated primarily by erythropoietin produced by the kidneys.  RBC pathology includes: - Anemia:  Reduced RBC count or hemoglobin level decreases oxygen delivery. - Polycythemia:  Excessive RBC production increases blood viscosity, predisposing to thrombosis. - Sickle cell disease:  Abnormal hemoglobin distorts RBCs into a characteristic sickle shape, leading to vascular occlusion, hemolysis, and tissue damage. - Thalassemia:  Decreased hemoglobin alpha- or beta-chain production results in abnormal polymers that cause ineffective erythropoiesis and chronic hemolysis. # Granulocytes Granulocytes are a category of white blood cell (WBC) (leukocyte) characterized by cytoplasmic granules and a lobed nucleus that rapidly respond to injury or infection as a part of the **innate immune response**.  They include neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils, each containing specialized, preformed granules loaded with enzymes and inflammatory mediators for rapid defensive responses.  Their production and activation are tightly regulated by specific colony-stimulating factors (eg, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) and interleukins. ## Neutrophils Neutrophils (10-12 µm) are the most abundant granulocytes (comprising approximately 60% of WBCs) and contain **multilobed nuclei** (2-5 lobes) ((Image 2)).  The nuclear segmentation increases as neutrophils mature, with young neutrophils having band-shaped (less segmented) nuclei.  This segmental nature of the nuclei is the reason that mature neutrophils are sometimes referred to as polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Neutrophils serve as first responders to **bacterial infections**, rapidly mobilizing to sites of invasion, where they phagocytize (ie, engulf) pathogens.  Their segmented nucleus allows neutrophils to squeeze through tight spaces in blood vessel walls (diapedesis) to reach infection sites without damaging their DNA ((Figure 1)).  This nuclear architecture also positions chromatin toward the cell periphery, maximizing central cytoplasmic space available for phagocytosis.  Their characteristic neutral-staining granules contain powerful destructive enzymes, including **myeloperoxidase** and lysozyme. For example, in a patient with pneumonia, neutrophils are recruited from the systemic circulation by chemokines and are subsequently activated by microbial molecules (eg, lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan, bacterial DNA) and opsonizing factors (eg, IgG, complement) to phagocytize and destroy the pathogenic bacteria.  Activated neutrophils also release cytotoxic granules (lysosomes) containing myeloperoxidase and other digestive enzymes that destroy extracellular bacteria and recruit additional immune components to the area.   However, these enzymes also cause significant damage to the pulmonary parenchyma and can result in liquefying necrosis of lung tissue and (potentially) lung abscess. Increased neutrophil counts (neutrophilia) are seen in infection or inflammation.  Decreased neutrophil counts (neutropenia) can occur due to various reasons—including chemotherapy, severe infections, and vitamin B12/folate deficiency—increasing susceptibility to infections. ## Eosinophils Eosinophils (12-17 µm) comprise approximately 2%-4% of WBCs and contain bilobed nuclei, resembling a pair of connected lobes ((Image 3)).  This bilobed nuclear structure facilitates cellular mobility and flexibility, allowing eosinophils to migrate efficiently into inflamed tissues.  Their prominent eosinophilic (red-orange staining) granules contain cytotoxic molecules (eg, **major basic protein**, eosinophil peroxidase) optimized for combating **parasitic** infections by disrupting pathogen cell membranes.  Eosinophil proliferation and activation is stimulated by IL-5 produced by TH2 and mast cells (not to be confused with IL-4, which stimulates IgE production).  When a parasite invades the mucosa or enters the bloodstream, it is coated by IgG and IgA antibodies that bind the Fc receptors located on the eosinophil cell surface.  This triggers eosinophil degranulation and release of cytotoxic proteins and reactive oxygen intermediates, substances that damage and destroy antibody-bound parasites.  This mechanism is an example of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, which is also used by macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer cells. Eosinophils also regulate **allergic** reactions by modulating inflammatory responses.  They synthesize prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines that contribute to the inflammation seen in late-phase type 1 hypersensitivity and chronic allergic reactions. Increased eosinophil counts (eosinophilia) suggest an allergic process (eg, asthma, hay fever), parasitic infection (eg, helminths such as *Ascaris* \[Loffler syndrome, intestinal obstruction\] and *Angiostrongylus* \[eosinophilic meningitis\]), drug reaction (eg, DRESS \[**D**rug **R**eaction with **E**osinophilia and **S**ystemic **S**ymptoms\]), or certain autoimmune disorders (eg, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis). ## Basophils Basophils (12-15 µm), the rarest granulocytes (comprising <1% of WBCs), have bilobed nuclei often obscured by dense, dark purple granules ((Image 4)).  These large granules store **histamine** and heparin, critical mediators of allergic reactions and inflammation.  The basophil's granule-packed cytoplasm enables rapid, controlled release of histamine to induce **vasodilation** and enhance immune cell access to affected tissues, facilitating a prompt inflammatory response.  Increased basophil counts (basophilia) are rare but can be seen in certain types of malignancy (eg, chronic myeloid leukemia, myeloproliferative disorders). # Agranulocytes Agranulocytes, another category of WBCs, lack prominent cytoplasmic granules compared to granulocytes and are critical for **cell-mediated immunity** and antigen recognition.  They consist of lymphocytes and monocytes. ## Lymphocytes Lymphocytes (6-15 µm), constituting an estimated 20%-40% of WBCs, typically feature a large, round nucleus surrounded by a narrow rim of basophilic cytoplasm ((Image 5)).  This **high nucleus/cytoplasm ratio** allows for the storage of a **large amount of genetic information** essential for generating **adaptive immunity** processes (eg, antigen recognition, immune memory).  Subtypes include **B cells** (producing specific antibodies through plasma cell differentiation), **T cells** (targeting infected or cancerous cells through cytotoxicity or helper functions), and **natural killer cells** (recognizing and eliminating virus-infected cells via perforin and granzyme release).  Lymphocyte differentiation is driven by antigen exposure and cytokines (eg, IL-2, IL-7) that stimulate maturation into effector or memory cells (with heightened response capabilities on reexposure). Lymphocytosis can be seen in viral infections and lymphoid malignancies (eg, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).  In contrast, lymphopenia is seen in immunodeficiencies and, occasionally, certain viral infections (eg, HIV, COVID-19). ## Monocytes Monocytes (12-20 µm), comprising approximately 3%-8% of WBCs, contain large, irregularly shaped, kidney-bean nuclei with **abundant gray-blue cytoplasm** ((Image 6)).  Their expansive cytoplasmic volume facilitates **phagocytosis** of pathogens and debris.  On migration into tissues, monocytes differentiate into **macrophages and dendritic cells**—specialized antigen-presenting cells crucial for coordinating immune responses by processing and presenting antigens to T cells.  The differentiation of monocytes is promoted by macrophage colony-stimulating factor. Monocytosis can be seen in chronic infections (particularly bacterial infections \[eg, tuberculosis\]), chronic inflammatory conditions (eg, sarcoidosis), and certain malignancies (eg, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, acute monocytic leukemia).  In contrast, monocytopenia is less common but may occur in hairy cell leukemia and as an adverse effect of certain medications (eg, chemotherapy agents). # Platelets Platelets (thrombocytes) are the **smallest** blood cells (2-4 µm) and are irregularly shaped fragments derived from **megakaryocytes** in the bone marrow ((Image 7)).  Their differentiation is regulated primarily by thrombopoietin produced by the liver.  The small size of platelets and the **lack of nuclei** optimize rapid circulation and facilitate quick adhesion to damaged vessel walls, forming initial **platelet plugs**.  Platelets contain numerous **granules filled with clotting factors** (eg, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor) and growth factors (eg, platelet-derived growth factor), enabling prompt secretion on activation to stabilize blood clots and promote tissue healing.  With a **7- to 10-day lifespan**, their production and function are tightly regulated to prevent excessive bleeding or clotting. Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) increases the risk for bleeding.  Thrombocytosis (high platelets) may lead to thrombosis.  Platelet dysfunction (eg, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia) impairs clotting, even in the setting of normal counts, due to molecular defects in platelet adhesion or aggregation. # Summary Blood consists of 3 main cell types, each with specialized functions. Red blood cells (erythrocytes), the most abundant blood cells, are responsible for oxygen transport via hemoglobin.  Common disorders include anemia (low red blood cell count), polycythemia (excess red blood cells), and sickle cell disease (abnormal hemoglobin). White blood cells (leukocytes) are key to immunity and are divided into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes).  Neutrophils fight bacterial infections, eosinophils combat parasites and allergies, and basophils release histamine in allergic responses.  Lymphocytes (B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells) mediate adaptive immunity, whereas monocytes mature into macrophages and dendritic cells, aiding in pathogen clearance.  Abnormal white blood cell counts can indicate infections, inflammation, or malignancies. Platelets are small cell fragments essential for clotting; imbalances can lead to bleeding disorders (thrombocytopenia) or excessive clotting (thrombocytosis). ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌

articles.title: Basic Bacteriology: Structure, Virulence Factors, And Genetics
articles.markdown:
# Basic Bacteriology: Structure, Virulence Factors, And Genetics # Introduction Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms that lack an enveloped nucleus and have no membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelles.  They are classified largely by staining characteristics (eg, gram-positive/negative), shape (eg, cocci, rods), arrangement (eg, chains, clusters), growth characteristics (eg, aerobic, anaerobic, facultative), and biochemical features. # Gram stain Gram staining is one of the most common ways to broadly classify bacteria.  In this technique, bacteria are affixed to a slide, stained with crystal violet and iodine, and then exposed to a solvent (eg, ethanol, acetone) ((Figure 1)).  Gram-positive bacteria retain the stain (due to having a thick cell wall) and appear **purple**; gram-negative bacteria lose the stain (due to having a thin cell wall) and appear **pink**.  Additional information about the surface structure of gram-positive and gram-negative organisms follows ((Figure 2)). ## Gram-positive bacteria - Gram-positive bacteria have a thick, continuous cell wall, which provides structural rigidity and resistance to osmotic pressure.  The primary components of the cell wall are as follows: - **Peptidoglycan** ((Figure 3)):  Alternating glycan strands (N-acetylglucosamine \[NAM\] and N-acetylmuramic acid \[NAG\]) cross-linked by short peptide chains. - **Teichoic acids**:  Polymers with strong negative charges covalently linked to peptidoglycan. - Additional polymers (eg, polysaccharides, peptido-glycolipids):  Linked to the peptidoglycan backbone in some bacteria. - Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane and no lipopolysaccharide (except for *Listeria monocytogenes*). - Common gram-positive bacteria include *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, *Enterococcus*, *Clostridium*, and *Corynebacterium*. ## Gram-negative bacteria - Gram-negative bacteria ((Figure 4)) have a thin (5-10 nm) cell wall composed of peptidoglycan with no teichoic acids that resides in the periplasmic space between the inner and outer membrane. - Gram-negative bacteria also have an **outer membrane**, which is an asymmetric bilayer that acts as a barrier to environmental toxins (eg, antibiotics).  It is composed of the following: - Outer layer:  Glycolipids and **lipopolysaccharide** (LPS) (also called endotoxin). - Inner layer:  Phospholipids noncovalently attached to underlying peptidoglycan by lipoprotein. - Porins:  Transmembrane proteins that selectively allow molecules from the external environment to pass into the periplasmic space. - Common gram-negative bacteria include *Escherichia*, *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*, and *Neisseria*. ## Miscellaneous Bacteria with no cell wall (eg, *Mycoplasma*), very thin peptidoglycan layers (eg, *Chlamydia*), very small diameters (eg, spirochetes), or extensive mycolic acid in the cell wall (eg, *Mycobacteria*) are often unable to be visualized well with Gram stain. Further classification of bacteria based on morphology (shape and arrangement) and biochemical and growth characteristics can support initial identification. # Bacterial morphology ## Shape Shape refers to the microscopic appearance of individual bacterial cells.  There are 3 main shapes of bacteria, as follows: - **Cocci**:  Spherical or oval-shaped organisms (eg, *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*) ((Image 1)). - **Bacilli** (rods):  Cylindrical, rod-shaped organisms varying in length and width (eg*, Corynebacterium, E coli*) ((Image 2)).  Some gram-positive bacilli (eg, *Bacillus*, *Clostridium*) produce spores, which can survive at temperatures past the boiling point of water (100 C \[212 F\]) and are resistant to chemical disinfectants, and irradiation, desiccation. - **Spirochetes**:  Thin, helical organisms that are generally too narrow to be viewed with traditional light microscopy (eg, *Treponema*). Common variants include: - **Coccobacilli**:  Short, plump rods (eg, *Haemophilus influenzae*). - **Pleomorphic**:  No consistent shape due to structural variability, environmental factors, and/or the absence of a cell wall (eg, *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia*). - **Filamentous**:  Branching chains ((Image 3)) (eg, *Nocardia*). ## Arrangement Arrangement refers to the way bacterial cells group together, as follows: - **Pairs** (diplococci):  Are characteristic of some cocci (eg, *Neisseria*) ((Image 4)). - **Chains**:  Occur when bacteria divide along a single plane and arrange longitudinally along the division axis like train cars (eg, *Streptococcus*) ((Image 5)). - **Clusters**:  Resemble grape-like groupings (eg, *Staphylococcus*) ((Image 6)). - **Palisades**:  Occur when bacilli divide by snapping division (inner cell wall splits but the outer cell wall stays connected), leading to side-by-side arrangements similar to fence posts.  Organisms (eg, *Corynebacterium*) can be either parallel or at angles. Gram-staining characteristics, along with bacterial shape and arrangement, are typically used in combination to assist with the initial identification and classification of bacteria.  For example, gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest *Staphylococcus*, which can colonize the anterior nares; whereas gram-positive rods in palisades suggest *Corynebacterium*, which can colonize the upper airway. # Biochemical and growth characteristics Testing for growth requirements and enzyme activity can differentiate organisms with similar morphologic characteristics. ## Oxygen requirements - **Obligate aerobes**:  Require oxygen to generate energy.  They use enzymes (eg, superoxide dismutase, catalase) to convert reactive oxygen species into harmless intermediates.  Obligate aerobes often infect superficial skin or the respiratory tract. - **Obligate anaerobes**:  Use fermentation or anaerobic respiration (sulfate or nitrate can act as electron acceptors) for energy generation.  They are unable to convert reactive oxygen species into harmless intermediates; therefore, exposure to oxygen is toxic.  Obligate anaerobes often infect deep tissue/wounds or the gastrointestinal/urinary tract. - **Facultative anaerobes**:  Generate energy in either the presence or absence of oxygen using aerobic respiration or fermentation, respectively. - **Microaerophiles**:  Require low levels of oxygen for energy metabolism; excessive oxygen exposure is generally toxic (due to low levels of catalase). ## Metabolic and enzymatic properties The presence or absence of enzyme activity or the ability to ferment sugar can also assist with identification, as follows: - **Catalase test**:  This test detects the presence of catalase, an enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.  Catalase-positive bacteria generate bubbles in solution (due to oxygen being released).  It is most often used to differentiate staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative). - **Oxidase test**:  This test uses a reagent to detect the presence of cytochrome c oxidase, an enzyme used in the electron transport chain.  It can differentiate oxidase-positive (eg, *Neisseria*, *Pseudomonas*) from oxidase-negative (eg, *Enterobacteriaceae*) organisms. - **Indole test**:  This test determines whether bacteria can convert tryptophan to indole.  It is primarily used to differentiate bacteria within the Enterobacteriaceae family (gram-negative gastrointestinal rods).  *E coli* is generally indole-positive. - **Carbohydrate fermentation test**:  Fermentation of sugar is detected by a pH change in the culture medium.  For example, on MacConkey agar, lactose fermentation produces pink colonies (eg, *E coli*), whereas nonfermenting organisms (eg, *Salmonella*) remain colorless. Additional enzymatic tests are sometimes used to detect the ability of a bacterium to generate urease (eg, *Proteus*) or hydrogen sulfide (H2S) (eg, *Salmonella*).  Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) is a bacterial enzyme that helps identify group A *Streptococcus* (*Streptococcus* *pyogenes*) and *Enterococcus* species; most other streptococci are PYR negative. # Algorithmic identification Biochemical and morphologic characteristics are used in combination for preliminary identification and confirmatory testing, in a somewhat algorithmic fashion.  For example: ## Gram-positive organisms **Gram-positive cocci** - **Clusters**:  Suggest *Staphylococcus* spp., which can be confirmed with a positive catalase test.  A coagulase test can then be performed to differentiate *S aureus* (coagulase-positive) from other staphylococci ((Figure 5)). - **Chains or pairs**:  Suggest *Streptococcus* or *Enterococcus*, which can be differentiated by hemolysis patterns on blood agar (altered agar appearance around the colony) and Lancefield group patterns (carbohydrate antigens on the bacterial cell wall) ((Figure 6)). **Gram-positive rods (bacilli)** - **Spores**:  Seen with *Bacillus* and *Clostridium* but not with *Corynebacterium* or *Listeria* spp. - **Filamentous, fungus-like growth** ((Image 7)):  Seen with *Nocardia* and *Actinomyces*; these species do not form spores.  In addition, *Actinomyces* forms sulfur granules (calcified mycelial fragments) that grossly appear yellow; but have a basophilic (purple/blue) appearance under light microscopy with hematoxylin and eosin staining. ## Gram-negative organisms **Gram-negative rods** - **Lactose-fermenting organisms** (eg, *E coli*, *Klebsiella*):  Can be distinguished from nonfermenting organisms (eg, *Salmonella*, *Pseudomonas*) based on MacConkey agar growth. - **Oxidase testing**:  Helps separate *Pseudomonas* (oxidase-positive) from *Enterobacteriaceae* (oxidase-negative). **Others** Other features of gram-negative organisms are described in the figure ((Figure 7)). # Virulence factors Virulence factors are bacterial adaptations that promote survival; they often enhance bacterial colonization/invasion, evasion of the immune response, or tissue damage.  Common virulence factors include: ## Surface appendages **Flagella** - Flagella are long, filamentous appendages found on some gram-negative and gram-positive organisms. - Flagella contain 3 components: - A long, external, cylindrical filament composed of protein subunits (flagellins). - A basal body that traverses the outer wall/membrane of the bacterium. - A hook structure between the basal body and filament. - Counterclockwise rotation of the basal body causes the filament to spin, which results in **propulsion** of the bacteria (similar to a motor).  The number and distribution of flagella is typically preserved within a given bacterial species and can be used to assist in identification.  Notably, flagellins are antigenic (H antigen). **Pili** - Pili (also called fimbriae) are thin, rigid, hair-like appendages found on many gram-negative bacteria. - Short (common) pili allow bacteria to **adhere** to the surface of epithelial cells, erythrocytes, and yeast/fungal cells, which assists with colonization; some bacteria are coated in common pili (eg, *Shigella*, *E coli*). - In contrast to short pili, sex pili are lengthy and few in number; they attach donor and recipient bacteria during conjugation and are encoded on plasmids (discussed more below). ## Capsules Some gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria are surrounded by a capsule, an outermost layer typically composed of polysaccharides that coalesce into a thick, viscous gel.  Capsules hide bacterial surface antigens from immune recognition, prevent phagocytosis, and impair intracellular killing by phagocytes ((Figure 8)).  For example, the major virulence factor of *S pneumoniae* is a thick antiphagocytic polysacchardie capsule that swells and appears as a halo around blue-stained bacterial cells when specific anticapsular antibodies and methylene blue dye are added ("quellung reaction").  Infection can lead to antibodies to that strain but not necessarily others. ## Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) Gram-negative bacteria contain LPS, a cell-bound, heat-stable, amphipathic toxin composed of the following parts: - **Lipid A**:  Hydrophobic portion that resides in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane and is responsible for **toxicity**. - **O antigen**:  Repeating distal oligosaccharide that differs significantly between species. - Hydrophilic core polysaccharide:  Links lipid A and the O antigen. LPS is a potent activator of the innate immune system through toll-like receptor 4; it also activates the complement and the coagulation cascades and triggers the release of inflammatory cytokines (tumor necrosis factor, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8), nitric oxide, and eicosanoids.  Exposure to even a small quantity of endotoxin can have an outsized physiologic effect (eg, septic shock). ## Exotoxins Exotoxins are proteins released from viable gram-positive or gram-negative bacteria.  They are the most potent toxic substances known to exist per unit of weight.  Although the benefit of exotoxin to bacterial growth is largely unknown, the adverse effect on the host can be profound.  Neurotoxins (eg, botulinum toxin), cytotoxins (diphtheria toxin), and enterotoxins (eg, cholera toxin) can cause life-threatening effects. Exotoxins can be categorized in a variety of ways, but a common classification is based on the mechanism of action, as follows: - **Enzymes** (eg, proteases, hyaluronidases, coagulases, fibrinolysins):  Contribute to tissue destruction and abscess formation. - **AB toxins** (eg, cholera, anthrax, botulinum, tetanus toxins):  Alter intracellular signaling or regulatory pathways; in most cases, the A subunit has enzymatic activity, and the B subunit binds to the cell surface and mediates entry of the A subunit. - **Superantigens** (eg, toxic shock syndrome toxin-1):  Bind conserved portions of the T-cell receptor, resulting in extensive T-lymphocyte activation and cytokine release. Exotoxins are antigenic, and, in some cases, the humoral antibody response can neutralize toxin activity.  Examples and mechanisms of action of select exotoxins are shown in this table ((Table 1)). ## Iron capture Most bacteria require iron for growth and metabolism.  Because free iron is often scarce in tissue fluids and blood (instead bound to heme or transferrin), some bacteria express receptors for eukaryotic iron-binding proteins (eg, transferrin-binding proteins) or release siderophores, which extract iron from host proteins. # Bacterial genetics The bacterial chromosome is typically a circular loop of double-stranded DNA.  Extrachromosomal genetic elements (eg, plasmids, bacteriophages) may also be present and frequently provide genes that confer survival benefits (eg, antimicrobial resistance, virulence factors).  Bacteria replicate via binary fission. ## Extrachromosomal elements - **Plasmids**:  Discrete, extrachromosomal, self-replicating genetic elements (replicons).  They typically encode traits (eg, antibiotic resistance, toxin production, adherence/colonization structures) not required for bacterial survival.  Most are supercoiled, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules.  Conjugative (F+) plasmids encode for genes that promote the transfer of the plasmid from one bacterium to another; nonconjugative plasmids partially rely on bacterial machinery for plasmid replication. - **Bacteriophages**:  Obligate intracellular bacterial parasites that consist primarily of proteins plus nucleic acid (DNA or RNA).  Although many bacteriophages are lytic (killing the host bacteria), the genome of temperate, nonlytic phages can contribute virulence factors (eg, diphtheria toxin, botulinum toxin) to the bacterial host. ## Exchange of genetic material The transfer of genetic material from donor to recipient bacterium increases the likelihood that rare, independent genomic mutations that confer survival benefits (eg, flagella phase variation, surface antigen variation, antibiotic resistance plasmids) will spread within a colony.  Donor DNA must be part of a plasmid or undergo recombination into the recipient genome to be passed along to progeny. - **Transformation** ((Figure 9)):  Bacteria directly take up pieces of extracellular DNA.  The extracellular DNA can originate from the genome of another bacterium, a plasmid, or a bacteriophage.  Bacteria that are able to be transformed by extracellular DNA are called competent. - **Transduction** ((Figure 10)):  Bacteriophage vectors introduce DNA from a donor bacterium to a recipient bacterium in the course of infection.  This typically occurs when the bacteriophage aberrantly produces some virions that contain a random fragment of the donor genome instead of phage DNA.  In order to pass the donor DNA on to progeny, the recipient bacterium has to incorporate the donor DNA into their genome via recombination. - **Conjugation**:  Plasmids (F plasmids) encode for sex pili ((Figure 11)), long cytoplasmic bridges between donor and recipient bacteria that allow the transfer of part or all of the donor genome to the recipient.  The donor DNA forms a plasmid in the recipient bacterium or is integrated into the genome of the recipient via recombination. - **Transposition**:  Transposons are segments of DNA that can move from one location within the genome to other specific sites in the genome.  Transposons play a role in mutations, genomic rearrangement, acquisition of new genes, deletions, duplications, and inversions. # Summary Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms that lack an enveloped nucleus and have no membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelles.  They are typically categorized based on staining characteristics (eg, gram-positive/negative), shape (eg, cocci, rods), arrangement (eg, chains, clusters), growth characteristics (eg, aerobic, anaerobic, facultative), and/or biochemical features.  Pathogenicity is enhanced by the presence of virulence factors, which may include surface appendages (eg, pili, flagella), capsules, endotoxin, exotoxins, and iron capture mechanisms.  Bacteria replicate via binary fission and can exchange genetic material (eg, genes that encode virulence factors) by transformation, transduction, and conjugation.​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌

Bordetella pertussis

Pertussis toxin

Disinhibits adenylate cyclase through Gi ADP-ribosylation, increasing cAMP levels; causes edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Adenylate cyclase toxin

Functions as an adenylate cyclase, increasing cAMP levels; causes edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Clostridium botulinum

Botulinum toxin

Blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in flaccid paralysis

Clostridium difficile

Toxin A

Recruits & activates neutrophils, leading to release of cytokines that cause mucosal inflammation, fluid loss & diarrhea

Toxin B

Induces actin depolymerization, leading to mucosal cell death, bowel wall necrosis & pseudomembrane formation

Shigella dysenteriae

Shiga toxin

Halts protein synthesis by disabling the 60S ribosomal subunit, leading to intestinal epithelial cell death & diarrhea

Streptococcus pyogenes

Pyrogenic exotoxin

Acts as a superantigen, inducing fever & shock; associated with scarlet fever & streptococcal toxic shock syndrome

Streptolysin O&S

Damages erythrocyte membranes, causing beta hemolysis
